Funds do not pay different returns to different buyers. They have one NAV, and her entry and exit points differ.
Costs are modest next to a 78% gain. They cannot turn the result into a loss; her timing did.

qs.prompt: An investor bought 1,000 units at NAV 100 and 684.9 units at NAV 146. She sells all of them at NAV 96. About how much does she receive?
options: About ₹1.92 lakh, since the 96 NAV is 96% of the ₹2 lakh she put in
About ₹1.62 lakh, since 1,684.9 units are sold at a NAV of 96 each
About ₹2.00 lakh, since what she paid in is what she gets back
About ₹1.35 lakh, since the fall from 146 to 96 costs her a third
qs.why: 1,000 plus 684.9 is 1,684.9 units. Times ₹96 gives about ₹1,61,750, which is less than the ₹2 lakh she put in.
wrong: She bought part at 146, not 100, so the 96 NAV is not 96% of what she paid. Units, not rupees, are sold.
Selling at 96 returns less than she paid for units at 100 and 146. She gets units times the NAV.
The fall from 146 to 96 is about a third, but only on the second purchase. Her first units cost 100.

qs.prompt: A client with a multi-asset SIP wants to stop it after the fund falls 12% and restart when things feel safe. What is the adviser's best reply?
options: Agree, because a restart date can be chosen when the news turns calmer again
Agree, but advise a bigger SIP at restart to make up the lost months
Switch the fund to one with higher volatility, so that the gains come back faster
Show that stopping skips cheap units and restarts come late; keep the SIP
qs.why: The gap comes from skipped buying and late returns. Keeping the SIP through the fall is the habit that closes it.
wrong: Calm news usually arrives after prices have already recovered, so restarts tend to come late.
A bigger SIP later buys at higher prices. It does not recover the cheap units that were skipped.
A more volatile fund gives a client more reasons to panic. It would widen the gap, not close it.

qs.prompt: In March 2026, industry AUM fell about 10% yet equity fund inflows stayed near ₹40,000 crore. What does it suggest?
options: Investors kept investing through a fall, a good sign, though one month is no proof
It proves no investor sold any units that month and that the behaviour gap is gone
It means the market did not fall, since inflows could not stay high if prices were falling
It means funds that fall get more inflows, so a client should wait for a fall to invest
qs.why: Steady inflows during a 10% AUM fall point to calmer behaviour. One month cannot show a lasting change.
wrong: Inflows staying high does not show that nobody sold. Some investors will always redeem in a fall.
The 10% AUM fall shows prices did drop. Inflows stayed because many investors kept going.
One month does not make a rule. Waiting for a fall to invest is timing again, which feeds the gap.

title: International diversification
concept: International funds/FoFs add geographic and currency diversification.
A weaker rupee boosts INR returns on foreign assets.
SEBI's industry-wide overseas limits periodically restrict fresh inflows — check availability.
Fund-of-funds investing overseas saw ~₹904 crore inflows in Feb 2026.
talk: "A slice abroad protects you if the rupee weakens and gives access to global leaders."

qs.prompt: Rupee depreciation makes foreign fund returns in INR:
qs.why: Currency gain.

qs.prompt: Why might an international fund pause fresh SIPs?
qs.why: SEBI/RBI limits.

qs.prompt: Main benefit of international exposure:
qs.why: Different drivers.

qs.prompt: A client invests ₹1 lakh in a foreign fund when ₹80 buys a dollar. The fund gains 5% in dollars and the rupee falls to ₹86 a dollar. What is the investment worth in rupees?
options: About ₹1,05,000, since the 5% gain in dollars is the only gain that counts
About ₹1,12,500, since the 5% and the 7.5% fall in the rupee add up directly
About ₹1,07,500, since only the rupee's fall counts when the fund holds dollars
About ₹1,12,875: dollars rose 5% and each dollar now fetches more rupees
qs.why: ₹1 lakh buys $1,250, which grows to $1,312.50. At ₹86 that is ₹1,12,875, about 12.9% more.
wrong: That figure holds the rupee at ₹80. In this case it moved to ₹86, which adds to the rupee value.
The two effects multiply: 1.05 times 86 over 80. Adding them gives ₹1,12,500, slightly too low.
The fund also gained 5% in dollars. Counting only the currency move ignores half of the story.

qs.prompt: The same fund gains 5% in dollars, but the rupee strengthens from ₹80 to ₹76 a dollar. What does the investor see in rupees?
options: About a 0.25% loss, since the stronger rupee cancels the gain in dollars
A 5% gain, since the foreign asset's return is not affected by the rupee
A 10% gain, since a stronger rupee adds to the 5% earned in dollars
A 5% loss, since a stronger rupee wipes out the dollar gain and more besides
qs.why: 1.05 times 76 divided by 80 is 0.9975, about a 0.25% fall. Currency can erase a foreign gain.
wrong: The rupee value of a foreign holding does depend on the exchange rate. A 5% dollar gain is not 5% in rupees.
A stronger rupee means each dollar buys fewer rupees. It reduces the rupee value, not adds to it.
The dollar fell about 5% against the rupee, which offsets the 5% gain. The net loss is only about 0.25%.

qs.prompt: A client wants 20% in a US fund because the rupee always weakens. How should the adviser respond?
options: Agree, since the rupee has weakened in every year and will do so in every future year
Agree, as a weak rupee makes any foreign fund a sure win for an Indian investor
A weaker rupee can add to returns, but it may reverse; the real case is spreading risk
Disagree, because a global fund holds no foreign currency at all, so the rupee does not matter
qs.why: The currency effect is real but runs both ways. The sounder reasons are geographic and currency diversification.
wrong: The rupee does not weaken every year. A strong year can cut the rupee value of foreign holdings.
A weak rupee helps, but a falling foreign market can still produce a loss. Nothing is a sure win.
The rupee value of a foreign fund depends on the exchange rate, so the currency does matter.

qs.prompt: An adviser plans to invest a ₹5 lakh lump sum into an international fund of funds next week. What should he do first?
options: Check nothing, since overseas limits apply only to redemptions and never to purchases
Check whether the scheme is taking fresh money, as overseas limits can pause buying
Wait for the rupee to weaken before buying, since that is the right moment to buy
Switch the plan to an Indian equity fund, since overseas funds can never be bought
qs.why: SEBI's industry-wide overseas limits can restrict fresh inflows, so availability and the cap on lump sums come first.
wrong: The limits restrict fresh subscriptions. Redemptions of units already held are a separate matter.
Timing the rupee is a guess. It is not a condition for buying, and the rupee can move either way.
Overseas funds can be bought. They just need a check on whether the scheme is open for fresh money.

title: Objections to multi-asset
concept: 'Small caps gave 30%, why 12%?' → compare risk and drawdowns, not just returns.
'I'll do gold and debt myself' → tax on each rebalance, discipline problem.
'It's boring' → boring compounding is the point for core money.
Use the client's own worst-month memory to anchor the conversation.
talk: "Remember how you felt in March 2026? This fund is built so that month hurts much less."

qs.prompt: Best answer to 'small caps gave more':
options: Compare drawdowns and risk, not just returns
Agree and move everything to small caps
qs.why: Risk-adjusted view.

qs.prompt: Main drawback of DIY multi-asset:
options: Tax and discipline issues when rebalancing
qs.why: Behaviour + tax.

qs.prompt: Most persuasive anchor in this conversation:
options: The client's own past experience in a fall
qs.why: Personal relevance.

qs.prompt: A client says small caps gave 30% a year, so why accept 12% from a multi-asset fund? What is the best first step?
options: Tell him small caps are too dangerous for any client and refuse to discuss them
Agree, and move his core money to small caps since the past figure is the best guide
Ask which years the 30% covers, then compare the end value and the worst fall
Promise that the multi-asset fund will beat small caps over his next five years
qs.why: A quoted return is often a best window. Comparing the whole period, and the fall, gives him something to check.
wrong: A flat refusal ignores his goal. Small caps have a role, in a limited satellite, so a lecture does not help.
A past return from a best window is a weak guide. The deep falls that came with it are part of the story.
No one can promise a future ranking. A promise that later fails costs the client's trust.

qs.prompt: A client's ₹20 lakh portfolio fell 12% in her worst month when mostly in small caps. A multi-asset fund would have fallen about 4% in that month. How much less would she have lost?
options: About ₹1.6 lakh, since 12% of ₹20 lakh is ₹2.4 lakh and 4% is ₹80,000
About ₹2.4 lakh, since that is the whole loss in the small cap month
About ₹80,000, since that is the loss the multi-asset fund would have had
About ₹8 lakh, since the gap of 8 points applies to the whole ₹1 crore portfolio
qs.why: ₹2,40,000 less ₹80,000 is ₹1,60,000. The gap is 8 points of ₹20 lakh, which is ₹1.6 lakh.
wrong: ₹2.4 lakh is the small cap loss, not the difference. The multi-asset fund would still have lost something.
₹80,000 is the multi-asset loss. The saving is the small cap loss minus that figure.
The portfolio is ₹20 lakh, not ₹1 crore. Eight points of ₹20 lakh is ₹1.6 lakh.

qs.prompt: A client says he will hold gold and debt funds himself instead of a multi-asset fund. What is a fair response?
options: He cannot, because SEBI does not allow a person to hold gold and debt funds together
He can, but each rebalance may bring tax and exit load, and a crash tests nerve
He should, because rebalancing by hand is simple and never leads to any tax at all
He should never rebalance, since leaving the funds alone is always better in the end
qs.why: It is possible, but a rebalance is a sale, and the real test is buying equity after a fall. The cost depends on size.
wrong: Nothing stops an individual from holding several funds. It is a matter of cost and discipline, not permission.
Selling units to rebalance is a taxable event, so the claim of no tax at all is wrong for most sales.
Without rebalancing the mix drifts. After a big rally, equity may dominate and the risk will have risen.

qs.prompt: A client says a multi-asset fund is boring. What is the most useful reply?
options: Agree, and drop the multi-asset fund because he should not hold what bores him
Say boring funds always beat exciting ones, so he should not worry about it
Say nothing, since a client's feelings about a fund have no place in planning
Core money should compound steadily; keep excitement for a small satellite
qs.why: Core money is meant to compound quietly. A small satellite gives room for conviction bets, within a cap.
wrong: Boredom is not a reason to drop a core holding. A satellite can answer the wish for excitement.
Boring does not always beat exciting. A sweeping promise like that cannot be kept in every period.
Feelings drive behaviour, and behaviour drives results. A plan should account for what the client can hold.

title: Multi-asset pitch kit
concept: Category: ~₹1.96 lakh crore AUM, 58 months of inflows.
Three engines: equity for growth, debt for stability, gold/silver for protection.
Tax-neutral internal rebalancing.
Ideal for first-timers, retirees, and anyone who panicked in past falls.
talk: "One fund, three engines, automatic rebalancing. Let's start with this as your core."

qs.prompt: Ideal first fit for a multi-asset fund:
options: First-time investor wanting a smoother ride
qs.why: Core starter.

qs.prompt: Which statement must you never make?
qs.why: Misselling.

qs.prompt: Which is a genuine multi-asset benefit?
qs.why: Real advantage.

qs.prompt: In a made-up bad year equity falls 20%, debt earns 7% and gold rises 10%. What does a 45% equity, 30% debt, 25% gold fund return?
options: About -20%, since the biggest loss in the portfolio sets the loss for the fund
About -1%, since the plain average of -20, 7 and 10 comes to about -1 overall
About -4.4%, since -9 plus 2.1 plus 2.5 gives -4.4 on the whole fund
About -9%, since only the equity part moves and debt and gold stay still
qs.why: Each return is weighted by its share: 0.45 times -20, 0.30 times 7 and 0.25 times 10 sum to -4.4%.
wrong: Only 45% of the fund is in equity. Debt and gold also earned money, so the whole fund fell far less.
A plain average treats the three parts as equal. Equity is 45%, so the weighted figure is not -1%.
-9% is the equity part alone. Debt added 2.1 and gold added 2.5, so the fund total is higher than that.

qs.prompt: Which of these clients is the weakest fit for a multi-asset fund as a core holding?
options: A 26-year-old, 25 years ahead, who wants maximum equity growth and accepts 50% falls
A 64-year-old about to start monthly withdrawals who worries about a fall in year one
A first-time investor who sold her last fund in a panic and wants a smoother ride
A client who wants one simple fund to start with and does not want to rebalance
qs.why: He wants maximum growth and can stay through deep falls, so a fund built to cushion falls gives up the growth he wants.
wrong: A retiree facing sequence risk gains from a fund built to fall less, so a multi-asset fund fits her case well.
A panicker's problem is the behaviour gap. A smoother fund gives fewer reasons to sell at a low.
Automatic rebalancing is the very thing this client wants, so the fund suits the request.

qs.prompt: The pitch says rebalancing inside the fund is tax-neutral for you. Which wording is accurate?
options: You pay no tax at all on this fund, since the fund absorbs the cost of every sale
The fund's own switches create no bill for you; tax comes when you redeem units
You are taxed each time the fund rebalances, on your share of the gain it makes
Every multi-asset fund is taxed like an equity fund, so the rate is always 12.5%
qs.why: The fund's trades are not your sale. Your tax comes on redemption, under the fund's class, so check its mix.
wrong: You are still taxed on redemption. Saying no tax at all would mislead the client about a real liability.
Internal trades do not reach your tax return. A bill arises only when you redeem your own units.
Tax class depends on equity share, including arbitrage. Some funds are taxed differently, so always check.

qs.prompt: A client asks for your one-line pitch. Which line is accurate and fair?
options: One fund that cannot lose money, because three assets are always better than one
One fund that beats equity every year, because gold and debt are added on top
One fund that earns 12% a year, because that is what the last few years gave
One fund, three engines: growth, stability and protection, rebalanced for you
qs.why: It says what the fund is and does, and promises no return. The claim is on structure, not on results.
wrong: No fund is certain not to lose. Three assets can fall together in a bad month, so that promise is false.
Adding gold and debt usually lowers a rally's gain. Beating equity each year is not a fair claim.
A past return is not a rate to quote as a promise. The next years may give more or less.

title: Factsheet deep-dive
concept: Key fields: AUM, expense ratio (now BER + levies), benchmark, top holdings, sector mix, turnover.
Risk stats: standard deviation, beta, Sharpe ratio — compare within the category only.
Portfolio turnover above ~100% means the manager trades the whole book in a year.
Always read the fund manager's tenure — past returns belong to the person who earned them.
talk: Before recommending, spend 5 minutes on the factsheet. It saves 5 years of regret.

qs.prompt: Portfolio turnover of 150% means:
options: The manager churns the portfolio 1.5 times a year
qs.why: Trading intensity.

qs.prompt: Sharpe ratio should be compared:
qs.why: Like-for-like.

qs.prompt: Why check fund manager tenure?
options: Past returns may belong to a previous manager
qs.why: Attribution.

qs.prompt: Two flexi-cap funds, safe-asset rate 6%. Fund P: 3-year return 18% a year, standard deviation 12%. Fund Q: 25% a year, standard deviation 20%. Which gave more return for each unit of risk?
options: Fund Q, because 25% beats 18% by a wide margin
Fund P, with a Sharpe of 1.00 against Q's 0.95
Both equal, as each beat the safe-asset rate well
Neither, until the benchmark return is known
qs.why: P earned 12 points over the safe rate for 12 points of volatility. Q earned 19 for 20, so P edges ahead per unit of risk.
wrong: Higher return alone ignores the swings. Q took a standard deviation of 20% to get it, which drags its Sharpe down.
Beating the safe-asset rate is where the Sharpe sum starts, not where it ends. The two ratios, 1.00 and 0.95, still differ.
Sharpe needs only the return, the safe-asset rate and the deviation. The benchmark matters for alpha and tracking error.

qs.prompt: A client sees a liquid fund with a Sharpe of 2.4 next to a flexi-cap fund at 0.9 and asks to move his equity into the liquid fund. What is the sound reply?
options: Agree, as a higher Sharpe means a better fund in any category
Agree, provided the liquid fund also has the lower expense ratio
Decline, since Sharpe ratios are meaningful only for equity funds
Decline: Sharpe only compares funds within one category
qs.why: Peers share a risk level and a benchmark. Across categories, a small volatility makes the ratio swing and misleads.
wrong: A liquid fund's tiny volatility inflates its ratio. The two funds do different jobs, so the numbers cannot rank them.
Cost matters, but it does not repair the comparison. The ratio itself is not comparable across a liquid and an equity fund.
Sharpe is used for debt and hybrid funds too. The rule is to compare like with like, not to limit it to equity.

qs.prompt: A mid-cap fund is pitched as a patient, buy-and-hold compounder. Its factsheet shows portfolio turnover of 165%. What does that number tell you?
options: About 1.65 times the book was traded, so check the pitch
The fund returned 165% over the year, so patience paid off
It holds 165 stocks, which is wide diversification in mid-caps
Assets grew 165% in the year, which shows heavy investor demand
qs.why: Turnover above 100% means heavy trading, at odds with buy-and-hold. Ask about the process, and about trading costs.
wrong: Turnover measures trading volume against fund size. It says nothing about the return the fund delivered.
Turnover is not a stock count. A fund can trade its whole book often while holding 30 names or 80.
Asset growth sits on another line of the factsheet. Turnover is about how much the manager buys and sells.

qs.prompt: A fund tops its category on 5-year return (21% a year). The factsheet shows its manager joined 11 months ago. What is the best step before you recommend it?
options: Recommend it, because a fund's record belongs to the fund itself
Reject it, because any fund with a new manager is unsuitable
Find who earned the record, then judge today's portfolio
Wait a year, then rely on the one-year return of the new team
qs.why: The five years show what the old manager did. The holdings now, and the new manager's record, show what you would buy.
wrong: Most of the 5-year number may belong to the previous manager. The record does not transfer with the fund's name.
A new manager is not automatically a bad one. It is a reason to look closer, not a reason to reject at once.
One year is too short to judge anyone, and waiting skips the real check: who earned the record and what has changed.

title: Portfolio overlap
concept: Many large-cap and flexi-cap funds share the same top 10 — big banks, Reliance, IT leaders.
Owning 5 such funds can mean owning one portfolio five times.
Overlap above ~50% adds little diversification.
Free overlap tools compare holdings in seconds — use them in reviews.
talk: "You own five funds, but 60% of the money is in the same 15 stocks. Let's simplify."

qs.prompt: Overlap of 60% between two funds suggests:
qs.why: Same stocks twice.

qs.prompt: Why do large-cap funds overlap heavily?
options: They draw from the same top-100 universe
qs.why: Limited universe.

qs.prompt: Best action on discovering high overlap:
qs.why: Simplify.

qs.prompt: Fund X holds Bank A 10%, Bank B 6%, Reliance 7%, IT leader 5%. Fund Y holds Bank A 7%, Bank B 9%, Reliance 7%, IT leader 2%. What is the overlap on these four stocks?
qs.why: Take the lower weight of each stock: 7, 6, 7 and 2. The total is 22%, the share of money both funds hold alike.
wrong: Adding Fund Y's weights in the shared stocks gives 25%. Overlap counts the smaller weight of each stock, not one fund's.
Adding the larger weight of each stock gives 31%. That counts money in one fund that the other does not hold.
Adding Fund X's weights in the shared stocks gives 28%. Overlap uses the smaller weight, which cuts that down.

qs.prompt: Rahul, 38, runs ₹5,000 SIPs in five funds: two large-cap, two flexi-cap and one index fund. Pairwise overlaps run from 55% to 75%. What would you propose?
options: Add a sixth fund from another fund house to spread the risk
Keep all five, since five funds already means diversification
Stop all five and move the ₹25,000 to one small-cap fund
Keep one or two, redirect the rest to different assets
qs.why: It cuts duplicated bets and frees SIP money for exposure he lacks, such as debt or mid-caps, matched to his goals.
wrong: A new fund house does not mean new stocks. A sixth large-cap fund would hold the same names again and add more overlap.
Fund count is not diversification. With 55 to 75% overlap, five funds act like one portfolio held five times over.
One small-cap fund swaps duplicate risk for a concentrated, far bumpier one that Rahul never chose.

qs.prompt: A client holds a Nifty 50 index fund and an active large-cap fund. The overlap tool says 80%, and she asks if the active fund is worth keeping. What is the best answer?
options: Keep both, since two funds always diversify better than one
Sell the index fund, because active funds always beat indices
Keep it only if the other 20% earns more than its extra cost
Sell the active fund, as overlap above 50% is never acceptable
qs.why: The extra cost buys only the differing 20%, so test whether that slice has added value after fees, over rolling periods.
wrong: At 80% overlap she owns mostly the same stocks twice. The second fund adds little diversification for its cost.
No rule says active beats index. Many large-cap funds trail their index after costs, which is why the test matters.
Overlap is a prompt for questions, not an automatic sell signal. The answer depends on what the differing slice earned.

qs.prompt: Rahul wants to go from five funds to two. Three funds hold large long-term gains and one shows a small loss. Which plan is most sensible?
options: Stop SIPs into duplicates, then exit in stages, loss first
Redeem all five funds on one day so the switch is clean and fast
Keep the duplicates for good, since any exit triggers tax
Switch the gains into the new funds, which avoids tax
qs.why: New money goes to the keepers at once. Staged exits spread gains over tax years, and the loss can offset some gains.
wrong: One-day redemption crowds all the gains into one year and may trigger exit loads on recent units. Staging costs less.
Tax is a cost to weigh, not a reason to hold duplicates for good. The running cost of overlap can outweigh it.
A switch is a redemption followed by a fresh purchase, so the gain is taxed at that point, not avoided.

title: Rolling returns and consistency
concept: Point-to-point returns depend on start and end dates — easy to cherry-pick.
Rolling returns (e.g., all 3-year periods) show how consistently a fund performed.
Check % of periods the fund beat its benchmark.
For SIPs, compare SIP XIRR over the same window.
talk: "This fund beat its benchmark in 80% of all 3-year periods — not just the last one."

qs.prompt: Rolling returns help remove:
qs.why: Consistency view.

qs.prompt: A strong consistency metric is:
options: % of rolling periods beating the benchmark
qs.why: Repeatability.

qs.prompt: SIP performance is best measured by:
qs.why: Multiple cash flows.

qs.prompt: A pitch says Fund P returned 29% a year over three years against 12.6% for its benchmark. Rolling returns over ten years show P beat the benchmark in only 24 of 85 three-year windows. What is the fair reading?
options: P's record is excellent, since the latest window matters most
P has failed, because it lost to the benchmark in most windows
P's edge rests on a late burst, so one window flatters it
The 85 windows prove that P's average return is below 5%
qs.why: The headline sits on its best window. Rolling shows the gains came in one stretch, so repeatability is unproven.
wrong: Recency is one window. The same ten years show P behind its benchmark in about seven windows out of every ten.
P still ended ahead over ten years, so failed overreaches. Its edge is concentrated in one stretch, not absent.
Window counts show how often P won, not its average. P's median window was 5.8%, a different figure altogether.

qs.prompt: A rival says Fund Z beat its benchmark in 80% of 85 rolling 3-year windows from ten years of monthly data, so that is 68 independent wins. What is wrong with that claim?
options: Windows overlap; ten years hold about three separate spans
Rolling windows can only be built from yearly data, never monthly
Eighty percent is too low a share to count as consistent
Three-year windows are meaningless; only one-year windows count
qs.why: Each window shares 35 of its 36 months with its neighbour, so the 68 wins are near-copies and the evidence is thin.
wrong: Monthly steps are normal practice. The weakness of the count is overlap, not the size of the step between windows.
A high share is useful, but the number of independent spans matters more than the percentage the windows produce.
Three-year windows suit many investors' holding periods. The issue is how many separate spans exist, not their length.

qs.prompt: Over the same ten years, Fund P shows a lump-sum return of 11.4% a year but an SIP XIRR of 14.4%. The benchmark shows 10.6% and 10.2%. Why is P's SIP figure so much higher?
options: SIPs always earn more than lump sums in every fund and market
P charges lower costs to SIP investors than to lump-sum ones
XIRR counts each instalment at its own date, so it is overstated
P surged late, when a big SIP corpus was already invested
qs.why: A late surge hits every unit bought so far, so SIP XIRR rises more. It still depends on the end date, so check rolling.
wrong: SIP and lump sum differ with the path. A fund that falls late would show the reverse, so no such rule exists.
Costs are charged on the fund, not on how the money arrived. SIP and lump-sum holders pay the same expense ratio.
XIRR dates each instalment, which is the correct way to measure a SIP. The gap comes from when the gains arrived.

qs.prompt: A client will invest for at least seven years. Fund R beat its benchmark in 88% of rolling 1-year windows but only 52% of rolling 5-year windows. Which figure should guide the choice?
options: The 1-year figure, as it has far more windows to learn from
The 5-year figure, since it matches her holding period
The better of the two, which shows what the fund can do
The average of the two, which gives a balanced overall view
qs.why: Match the window to the holding period. For a seven-year investor, the 5-year result is closest to what she will experience.
wrong: One-year windows are noisier and reflect luck as much as skill. A client holding for seven years lives through longer windows.
Choosing the better number is the cherry-picking that rolling returns are meant to stop, now done across window lengths.
Averaging mixes two horizons and fits neither. Choose the window first, from the client's holding period, then read it.

title: Upside and downside capture
concept: Downside capture below 100: the fund falls less than its benchmark.
Upside capture above 100: it rises more than its benchmark.
Ideal: upside capture > downside capture.
Great for explaining 'why this fund' to conservative clients.
talk: "When the market fell, this fund fell only 75% as much. That's the cushion you're paying for."

qs.prompt: Downside capture of 75 means:
options: Fund fell 75% as much as benchmark in down markets
qs.why: Cushion.

qs.prompt: Best combination:
qs.why: Asymmetric.

qs.prompt: Which client values low downside capture most?
qs.why: Comfort in falls.

qs.prompt: In months the benchmark rose it averaged 3.0% and the fund 3.3%. In months the benchmark fell it averaged 4.0% down and the fund 3.0% down. What are the capture ratios?
qs.why: Each ratio is the fund's average over the benchmark's: 3.3 over 3.0 is 110 up, 3.0 over 4.0 is 75 down.
wrong: The upside is inverted here. Fund over benchmark is 3.3 over 3.0, which is 110, not 91.
The upside is right but the downside is inverted. Fund over benchmark is 3.0 over 4.0, which is 75, not 133.
Both ratios are inverted. Capture always divides the fund's figure by the benchmark's, in up and in down months.

qs.prompt: A conservative client with an eight-year horizon is choosing between fund X (upside 95, downside 90) and fund Y (upside 88, downside 65). Which fits her better?
options: X, because 95 on the way up is the stronger number
Y, as it cushions falls far more than it trims gains
X, since it stays closest to the benchmark in both
Neither, because capture ratios cannot guide a choice
qs.why: Y keeps 88% of the gains and takes only 65% of the falls: a ratio of about 1.35 against 1.06 for X.
wrong: X takes 95% of the gains but also 90% of the falls, almost no cushion. Upside alone does not suit a client who dreads drops.
Hugging the benchmark means taking nearly all of its falls. She would pay a fund's cost for a cushion X barely offers.
Capture ratios are an input for exactly this talk, read together with the benchmark and the period behind them.

qs.prompt: Fund K shows upside capture 62 and downside capture 60. A colleague calls the downside number brilliant. What is the better reading?
options: Brilliant, because any downside capture under 100 shows skill
It reads like a part-cash fund: low on both sides
Misleading, since capture ratios suit only index funds
Poor, because a good fund needs a downside near zero
qs.why: Low on both sides with a ratio near 1 is what a part-cash fund looks like. Check its equity share before praising it.
wrong: Below 100 alone is not skill. K also gives up 38% of the gains, so the ratio of about 1.03 shows little real edge.
Capture ratios apply to any fund with a benchmark. The trouble here is what the pair of numbers says, not the method.
A downside near zero would mean almost no equity. That is not a fair test, and 60 is not poor on its own merits.

qs.prompt: A fund house quotes a downside capture of 68 over three years ending soon after a sharp fall. Which question should you ask first?
options: Nothing, since a capture ratio is a fixed property of the fund
Which benchmark and period, since both move the figure
Whether returns were taken after tax, since only those count
Whether it is below 100, which is all that matters
qs.why: A window that includes a sharp fall can flatter or hurt the number. Ask what benchmark was used and test several periods.
wrong: The ratio changes with the window and the index used. A fund can show 68 in one stretch and 85 in another.
Capture ratios are normally computed on pre-tax NAV returns. Tax differs by client, so it does not shape the ratio.
Below 100 is a start. A cash-heavy fund or a lucky window can pass that test while showing no real cushion skill.

title: Active share and benchmark weights
concept: Active share = % of the portfolio that differs from the benchmark.
Low active share (below ~60%) with high fees suggests closet indexing.
Overweight/underweight vs benchmark sectors show the manager's views.
High cash levels can signal caution — or a missed rally.
talk: You pay active fees for active decisions — check that the fund actually makes them.

qs.prompt: Active share measures:
options: How different a portfolio is from its benchmark
qs.why: Differentiation.

qs.prompt: Closet indexing means:
options: Charging active fees while mimicking the index
A hidden index fund with low fees
qs.why: Poor value.

qs.prompt: A fund 'overweight' banks holds:
options: More banks than the benchmark weight
qs.why: Relative view.

qs.prompt: A fund holds A 40%, B 30%, C 20% and X 10%. Its benchmark holds A, B, C and D at 25% each. X is not in the benchmark. What is the fund's active share?
qs.why: The gaps are 15, 5, 5, 25 and 10, which add to 60. Half is 30, the same as 100 minus the 70% that matches.
wrong: Adding every gap gives 60 points, but each rupee shifted is counted once as over and once as under, so the total must be halved.
15 is the largest single overweight, in A. Active share totals all the differences and then halves them, not just the biggest.
25% is only the weight of D, the benchmark stock that the fund skips. Active share also counts the overweights and X.

qs.prompt: A large-cap fund charges 1.7% a year and has an active share of 42%. An index fund costs 0.2%. How would you describe its cost to a client?
options: Just 1.7%, the same for any fund however it is built
About 0.7%, which is 1.7% times the 42% actively run
About 3.8% on the active slice, the rest being index-like
About 0.2%, the same as an index fund, since it tracks one
qs.why: Take 0.2% on the 58% that matches off the 1.7%, then divide by 42%: about 3.8% for the actively run part.
wrong: True as a total, but it hides what is bought. Most of the fund matches the index, which costs about 0.2% elsewhere.
Multiplying the fee by the active share understates it. The 1.7% is charged on all of the money, active or not.
It still charges 1.7% on all assets. It is not priced like an index fund, even if much of it looks like the index.

qs.prompt: Fund Z holds 9% cash and its benchmark holds none. The market rallied 20% and Z returned 18.5%. The client asks if the cash was a mistake. What is the best answer?
options: Yes, holding any cash in an equity fund is a plain mistake
No, cash always protects, so a larger cash share is better
Check if cash is its habit and how it paid across cycles
Ignore it, since cash is not counted in the fund's return
qs.why: One rally cannot judge a cash call. Look at the manager's habit of holding cash and whether it has earned its place.
wrong: Cash may be a deliberate, permitted choice. Whether it was a mistake depends on how it paid across many market phases.
Cash cost the fund in this rally. It protects only when markets fall, so more cash is not better by itself.
Cash is part of the NAV. In a rally it dilutes returns, which is why it matters when you compare with the index.

qs.prompt: A fund has an active share of 88% but has trailed its benchmark for three years. A colleague says high active share guarantees outperformance. How do you reply?
options: He is right; high active share must pay off eventually
No: it shows difference, not whether the bets are right
No: an active share that high signals closet indexing
He is right, as long as the benchmark does not change
qs.why: Active share measures the distance from the index, not whether the bets pay. Results still have to be tested over long periods.
wrong: Different does not mean better. A manager with 88% active share can be wrong for years, and the fees apply throughout.
Closet indexing is the reverse case: low active share with active fees. 88% is a high-conviction portfolio, not an index copy.
Keeping the benchmark fixed does not make the bets right. Active share only says how far the fund departs from it.

title: Small and mid-cap liquidity: stress tests
concept: Since 2024, AMCs disclose stress-test results for small and mid-cap funds.
Key metric: days needed to liquidate 50% (and 25%) of the portfolio.
More days = harder to exit in a sell-off; risk for large redemptions.
Use this to size small-cap allocations honestly.
talk: "This small-cap fund would need about a month to sell half its holdings. That's why we keep this slice small."

qs.prompt: SEBI-mandated stress test for small/mid-cap funds discloses:
options: Days to liquidate 50% and 25% of the portfolio
qs.why: Liquidity risk.

qs.prompt: More days to liquidate indicates:
qs.why: Exit difficulty.

qs.prompt: Practical use for an RM:
qs.why: Honest sizing.

qs.prompt: A small-cap fund shows 24 days to liquidate 50% of its portfolio, selling in proportion at a steady pace. How many days does the same test show for 25%?
qs.why: At a steady pace the time is proportional: half the portion needs half the days, so 12 here.
wrong: Same days for half the amount would mean the selling pace doubled, which the test does not assume.
Halving the amount does not square the time. At a fixed pace, time scales in direct proportion to what is sold.
Doubling is what you would see when selling more, not less. A smaller portion needs fewer days, not more.

qs.prompt: A client's small-cap fund shows 32 days to sell half its portfolio. She fears her own redemption will take 32 days. What is accurate?
options: Yes, every redemption waits until the fund has sold its holdings
No, it is a stress scenario for a mass exit, not a payout delay
No, the figure applies only to institutions, not to retail investors
Yes, but only for redemptions above ₹10 lakh in that fund
qs.why: The test asks how long selling half pro rata would take if many investors left together. It does not delay normal payouts.
wrong: Redemptions are normally paid in the usual time from cash and liquid holdings. The 32 days is a test, not a queue.
The figure describes the portfolio, which every investor shares. It is not split by type of investor.
The stress test sets no such threshold. It measures how liquid the portfolio is, not the size of one redemption.

qs.prompt: A client with ₹50 lakh wants 40% in two small-cap funds, both showing about 40 days to liquidate half. What is the most useful advice?
options: Accept it, since 40 days for half is standard for small caps
Spread the 40% over four small-cap funds to shorten the days
Keep 40%, but choose the fund that shows the fewest days
Size the slice to what he can hold through a deep fall
qs.why: Liquidity and volatility both argue for size. The slice should match what he can sit through, then days break ties.
wrong: No fixed standard exists. Long days flag exit risk on top of small-cap swings, so the size still needs a deliberate choice.
Four funds in the same bucket hold overlapping stocks and the same swings, so the total risk and total exit time stay much alike.
Fewer days is a better tie-breaker, but a 40% slice stays too big if a sharp fall would make him sell in a panic.

qs.prompt: A small-cap fund meets heavy redemptions by selling its most liquid stocks first. What happens to the investors who stay?
options: Their mix turns thinner, so a second exit is harder
They gain, since the manager keeps only the best stocks
Nothing changes, because every investor shares pro rata
They are repaid first, because they stayed with the fund
qs.why: The easy stocks go first, leaving a more illiquid mix. Early leavers get out at better prices than those who stay.
wrong: Best here means easiest to sell, not highest quality. What remains can be weaker on liquidity and harder to exit.
Investors do share pro rata, but the portfolio itself changes: it is left with the harder-to-sell stocks.
Redemptions are paid to those who ask, not to those who stay. Staying earns no priority in payment.

title: NFOs and the ₹10 myth
concept: NFO units at ₹10 aren't 'cheap' — returns are percentages, not NAV levels.
An NFO has no track record; judge by strategy, team, and fit.
Most NFOs replicate categories that already exist with long records.
Recommend NFOs only when they fill a genuine gap (e.g., a new index or category).
talk: "₹10 NAV or ₹500 NAV — your money grows by the same percentage. Let's judge the strategy, not the price."

qs.prompt: Fund A NAV ₹10, Fund B NAV ₹500, identical portfolios. Which is cheaper?
qs.why: Percentages matter.

qs.prompt: When does an NFO make sense?
options: When it fills a genuine gap in the client's portfolio
qs.why: Suitability.

qs.prompt: Main drawback of an NFO:
qs.why: Unknown behaviour.

qs.prompt: A client has ₹1,00,000 for an NFO at ₹10 or an existing fund at ₹250. Both hold the same portfolio at the same cost, and it rises 8%. Which ends higher?
options: The NFO, since 10,000 units beat 400 units
The existing fund, since its high NAV shows quality
Both end at ₹1,08,000; only the unit count differs
The NFO, but only once a full year has passed
qs.why: Both rise 8% on ₹1,00,000. The NAV level changes how many units you hold, never the percentage return you earn.
wrong: More units do not mean more money. 10,000 units at ₹10.80 and 400 units at ₹270 are both ₹1,08,000.
A high NAV is only the history of past gains, not a sign of quality. The portfolio is the same, so the result is the same.
Time changes nothing here. The same portfolio gives the same percentage return, so a year adds no edge for the NFO.

qs.prompt: A client prefers the NFO because the older fund's NAV has already run up while the NFO starts from scratch. What is the sound reply?
options: Higher NAV is just past growth; judge on strategy and cost
He is right: a low starting NAV leaves more room to rise
He is right, but only for funds launched in a rising market
He is wrong, because older funds always beat new ones
qs.why: NAV records past percentage gains. Room to rise depends on the portfolio and the market, so strategy and cost decide.
wrong: Room to rise belongs to the portfolio, not to the unit price. A ₹10 unit has no head start over a ₹500 one.
The market phase at launch does not change what NAV means. It still is just a starting number.
No rule says older funds win. Many records fade, and some newer funds fill gaps, so each case needs checking.

qs.prompt: Which of these NFOs could you consider recommending, after the usual checks of cost and process?
options: A flexi-cap fund much like three existing ones, launched at ₹10
A thematic fund pitched on how hot the theme is right now
A fund copying an older fund's strategy at a higher expense ratio
A new index fund covering a gap in her plan that no fund fills
qs.why: A real gap, named in her plan and checked on cost and process, is the case where an NFO can earn its place.
wrong: It duplicates what exists with a long record. The ₹10 price adds nothing, and she would hold the same stocks twice.
A hot theme is a reason for caution. A late buyer is most tempted then, and a new fund has no record to test.
The same strategy at a higher cost is worse than the older twin, which at least has a track record to examine.

qs.prompt: An AMC pitches a new mid-cap NFO by quoting the 5-year record of its older mid-cap fund, which has a different manager. What does that record tell you about the NFO?
options: It proves the NFO will repeat that record, as both are mid-cap
Some context on the house's process; judge the NFO's own team
Nothing at all, since fund houses never share a process
It matters only if the NFO's NAV is below that fund's NAV
qs.why: The house process may carry over, but the NFO's manager, size and mandate are its own, and they are what you buy.
wrong: A record belongs to its manager and mandate. Same category does not mean same people, size or portfolio, so no proof follows.
Houses do share research and risk rules. The record is not worthless, but it is not the NFO's own either.
NAV levels have no bearing on how much a record applies. The link depends on the team and mandate, not the unit price.

title: Goal-based conversations with HNIs
concept: Start with goals and cash flows: education, home, retirement, legacy.
Map each goal to time horizon → asset mix → fund choice.
HNIs care about tax, liquidity, succession and consolidation.
Ask permission to review all holdings — that's where AUM consolidation happens.
talk: "Can we look at all your investments together? Most families I meet hold 15–20 funds that do the same thing."

qs.prompt: Correct order for building a plan:
qs.why: Planning sequence.

qs.prompt: Top HNI concerns beyond returns:
qs.why: Wealth needs.

qs.prompt: Best question to unlock consolidation business:
options: "Can we review all your holdings together?"
qs.why: Whole-wallet view.

qs.prompt: A client with about ₹8 crore across 17 funds and some fixed deposits asks you to "suggest something good". What is your best opening move?
options: Show him the fund with the best 3-year return on your list
Ask for his goals, then review all holdings together
Offer a new NFO, since HNIs like being early in new ideas
Tell him to sell the weakest five funds and buy a flexi-cap
qs.why: Goals and dates tell you what each rupee is for, and a full view shows what he already holds. Recommendations come after.
wrong: Pitching a product before any goal repeats the habit that gave him 17 funds. Past return says nothing about his plan.
Being early is no virtue without a goal it serves. An NFO has no record, and he already holds many funds.
Selling the weakest five funds judges by return alone, and may trigger tax. You cannot judge a fund before you know its job.

qs.prompt: A client has ₹5 crore in one flexi-cap pot. She needs ₹2 crore for a home in 30 months and plans to retire in 18 years. What is the sound first step?
options: Split the money by goal, and move the home money to low-risk funds
Keep it all in flexi-cap, since equity beats debt over the long term
Put everything into debt, since part of it is needed soon
Switch to gold, since neither goal has a fixed amount
qs.why: Each goal has its own date. Money due in 30 months cannot depend on equity, while the 18-year money can stay invested.
wrong: Equity may win over decades, but the home money is needed in 30 months, when a fall could leave a gap that cannot be refilled.
Part of the money has a long horizon. Putting all of it in debt would starve the retirement goal of growth.
Gold can be part of a mix, but it carries its own swings. Neither goal is solved by one asset, whatever its amount.

qs.prompt: A masters abroad costs ₹1.2 crore today. Costs rise 8% a year, and the daughter leaves in 8 years. What target should the plan use?
qs.why: ₹1.2 crore grown at 8% a year for 8 years gives 1.2 times 1.08 to the power 8, about ₹2.22 crore.
wrong: This ignores eight years of rising costs. Plan for today's price and the plan will fall short by the time she leaves.
This adds 8% of the base eight times, as if simple interest. Costs compound, because each year's rise applies to a higher price.
That is the cost after only 4 years of rises, half the time. The daughter leaves in 8 years, not 4.

qs.prompt: An HNI client's 12 funds hold large gains, and consolidating at once would create a big tax bill. What do you propose?
options: Hold all 12 for good, since a tax bill is never worth paying
Stop new money into duplicates and phase exits over tax years
Redeem everything in March and rebuy at once for a clean start
Ignore the tax, because a simpler portfolio matters more than cost
qs.why: New money goes to the keepers at once, and staged exits spread gains over years. Agree the plan with his CA first.
wrong: Tax is a cost to weigh, not a reason to keep duplicates for good. The running cost of 12 overlapping funds also adds up.
One-day exits push all gains into one tax year and may trigger exit loads. A clean start is not worth that bill.
Tax is real money, and for an HNI it is large. A simpler portfolio is the aim, but cost and tax shape how you get there.

title: Handling objections — 2026 edition
concept: 'Rates went up in October — should I stop SIP?' → No; equity SIPs are for 5+ years; review debt duration instead.
'Gold gave more than my equity' → that's why we hold both; rebalance, don't chase.
'FD gives 7%' → post-tax, post-inflation it may be ~0%.
'Markets at highs' → SIP/STP removes timing stress.
talk: "Your SIP doesn't care about one rate hike. Your goal is 10 years away."

qs.prompt: Client: 'Rates rose, stop my SIP?' Best reply:
options: Continue; review the debt sleeve's duration instead
qs.why: Right tool for the issue.

qs.prompt: Client: 'Gold beat my equity, sell equity?' Best reply:
options: Rebalance to targets; don't chase last year's winner
qs.why: Discipline.

qs.prompt: 'Markets at all-time high' is best handled with:
qs.why: Removes timing risk.

qs.prompt: The RBI raised the repo rate last month. A client with a ₹25,000 equity SIP and a debt fund of duration 6 says: stop the SIP and get out of debt. What do you advise?
options: Stop the SIP, since equity falls whenever rates rise
Move all his money into a long-duration gilt fund now
Stop the SIP and the debt fund and wait in savings
Keep the SIP; check the debt fund's duration fit
qs.why: The equity SIP has a long goal, and the debt fund's hit is small and recoverable. Check whether its duration fits his horizon.
wrong: Rates can move markets for a while, but a ten-year SIP buys through such phases. Stopping reacts to one event with a long plan.
Long duration is the most exposed to a further rise. Switching into it after a hike adds the very risk he is worried about.
Waiting in savings makes two timing calls at once and earns little. A 0.25-point rise costs a duration-6 fund about 1.5% once.

qs.prompt: In a ₹10 lakh plan of 50% equity, 35% debt and 15% gold, gold gains 40%, equity 2% and debt 7% in a year. The client wants to sell equity and buy more gold. What do you say?
options: Sell about ₹46,000 of gold, add it to equity and debt
Sell equity and buy more gold, since gold is the leader
Sell all the gold, since it has clearly run too far
Do nothing, since weights need not be reset every year
qs.why: Gold is ₹2.10 lakh of ₹10.945 lakh, 19.2%. Back to 15% means about ₹1.64 lakh, so sell about ₹46,000 and restock the rest.
wrong: That chases last year's winner at a higher price, and sells equity that lagged. It breaks the plan the client agreed to follow.
Selling all the gold overshoots. The plan wants 15% in gold, so only the excess above that weight needs trimming.
Left alone, the weights drift to whatever ran most, so risk drifts too. A periodic reset keeps the plan's risk as agreed.

qs.prompt: A client in the 30% tax slab asks why he should take equity risk when his FD pays 7%. What is the most honest reply?
options: Equity always beats 7%, so the FD is simply a mistake
FD interest escapes tax, so the 7% reaches him in full
FD for near goals; its real return is about zero
Equity cannot lose money over seven years, so skip the FD
qs.why: At 31.2% tax the 7% becomes about 4.8%, near an assumed 5% inflation. The FD is safe and fits near goals, but does not grow wealth.
wrong: Equity has no guarantee. It may beat the FD over long periods or may not, and a promise would be misselling.
FD interest is added to income and taxed at his slab. That is why 7% shrinks to about 4.8% for him.
Equity can fall hard over seven years. Saying otherwise implies an assured outcome, which breaks the compliance rules.

qs.prompt: A client has ₹30 lakh from a property sale and will not invest because the Nifty is at an all-time high. He wants to wait for a 10% fall. What is the better approach?
options: Wait; every high is followed by a fall of at least 10%
Hold it safely and STP it in over 6 to 12 months
Invest it all today, since waiting has never paid
Put it all in gold until the market becomes cheaper
qs.why: Staged entry spreads the timing risk, so he is not betting on one day, and he can stay with the plan whichever way it goes.
wrong: Markets at highs can keep rising for years. A rule that a 10% fall must follow is a guess, and waiting has its own cost.
Never paid is also false: a lump sum placed just before a fall hurts. His fear of regret is a real input into the plan.
Gold is its own risky asset and can fall too. Swapping one timing bet for another is not a plan.

title: Hand-holding through falls
concept: In Mar 2026, industry AUM fell 10.1% in a month — equity inflows still hit ₹40,450 crore.
Corrections of 10% or more happen in most years; bear markets every few years.
Call clients before they call you — share context and their plan.
SIPs during falls buy more units — that's when future returns are made.
talk: "Markets fell 10% this month. Your SIP bought units 10% cheaper. Nothing in your plan needs to change."

qs.prompt: Best RM action when markets fall sharply:
qs.why: Trust building.

qs.prompt: During a fall, a continuing SIP:
options: Buys more units at lower prices
qs.why: Rupee cost averaging.

qs.prompt: Mar 2026 evidence of improved investor behaviour:
options: Equity inflows stayed ~₹40,450 crore despite a 10% AUM fall
qs.why: AMFI data.

qs.prompt: A fund's price falls 20%, from ₹100 to ₹80. How many more units does a client's fixed SIP instalment buy at ₹80 than at ₹100?
qs.why: ₹10,000 buys 100 units at ₹100 and 125 units at ₹80. That is 25% more for the same money.
wrong: The price fell 20%, but units move as the reciprocal: 1 divided by 0.8 is 1.25, so the gain in units is larger than 20%.
A fixed sum divided by a lower price always gives more units. The same number would need the price to stay unchanged.
Units do not rise by half the fall. The link is reciprocal, so a 20% fall lifts units by 25%, not about 12%.

qs.prompt: A colleague tells clients markets fell 10.1% in March 2026, quoting the fall in industry AUM from AMFI. What is the weakness in that statement?
options: AUM mixes market moves with flows; the Nifty 50's 11.3% is fairer
AUM never falls within a month, so the figure must be an error
Nothing, since industry AUM is the official measure of market return
AMFI reports AUM only for equity funds, so it cannot be used
qs.why: AUM moves with market prices and with money in or out. Debt funds saw large net outflows that month, so the index is cleaner.
wrong: AUM can fall in a month, and it did. The 10.1% is a real AMFI figure, so the issue is its meaning, not an error.
AUM is not a return measure. It changes with flows as well as prices, so it should not be passed off as a market return.
AMFI reports AUM for all fund types, debt included. That is partly why the 10.1% is not a pure equity-market figure.

qs.prompt: The Nifty is down 11% this month. A client in her third year of SIP has not called you. What do you do?
options: Wait for her to call, since contact may unsettle her
Call, restate her plan, and show what the SIP bought
Email a market outlook that predicts a recovery date
Offer to pause her SIP until the market settles
qs.why: It gives context and a plan, not a forecast. Showing the cheaper units her SIP bought turns the fall into something useful.
wrong: Waiting leaves her alone with the headlines. Clients who hear from you first tend to ask before they act.
No one can predict a date, and a wrong forecast costs trust. Context and her own plan are worth more than an outlook.
A pause skips the instalments that buy at low prices. Offering it first teaches her that the plan is to be dropped in a fall.

qs.prompt: A client who needs ₹15 lakh for a flat in 18 months wants to sell his equity fund after a 25% fall. What is the most honest approach?
options: Tell him to hold everything, since every fall recovers in time
Agree to sell everything, because any fall means the plan failed
Wait 18 months, then sell whatever the fund is worth by then
Split by goal, since the flat money needs a safer home
qs.why: Hand-holding does not mean never selling. Near-term money belongs in safer funds, while long-term money can stay with the plan.
wrong: No one can promise a recovery before his date. Money due in 18 months cannot wait for one, which is the real problem.
A fall is not proof the plan failed. Selling long-term money at the low makes a paper loss real, so only what is due soon should move.
That makes the flat depend on the market's mood in 18 months. It repeats the original mistake of holding near-term money in equity.

title: Compliance and ethics
concept: Disclose commissions; recommend only suitable products after risk profiling.
Never promise or imply assured returns on market-linked products.
Use the scheme and benchmark riskometers in every recommendation.
Under SEBI's 2026 regulations, cost transparency is higher — clients will ask, so answer clearly.
talk: Compliance is not paperwork — it's what lets you keep your ARN and your clients for 20 years.

qs.prompt: Which is misselling?
options: Implying assured returns on an equity fund
qs.why: Never guarantee.

qs.prompt: Distributors must disclose:
qs.why: Transparency.

qs.prompt: Before recommending, an RM must:
qs.why: Suitability.

qs.prompt: A client asks: "Do you earn anything if I buy this fund?" You receive a trail commission from the fund house. What is the right response?
options: Tell him the trail commission, and what service it covers
Say the fund house pays, so it is not his concern
Reply that commissions are confidential between you and the AMC
Move to the direct plan topic without saying what you earn
qs.why: Disclosure answers the question and lets him weigh your advice. Linking it to the service shows what he gets for it.
wrong: The fund house pays out of the fund's expense, which the client bears through the unit price, so it is his concern.
Distributors are expected to disclose commissions to clients. Calling them confidential hides what he has a right to know.
Talking about direct plans without answering is evasion. It looks like hiding the figure he asked for, and it erodes trust.

qs.prompt: A retired client says: "Just tell me it will give 10% so I can sleep." Which reply is compliant and still useful?
options: It has given about 10% before, so you can expect it again
It is a Moderate-risk fund, so 10% is a fair figure to rely on
A fund this old has a record, so the 10% is as good as fixed
I cannot promise 10%; let us check risk against your needs
qs.why: It declines to promise, and turns his need for comfort into a check of what risk he can truly carry. Honest and helpful.
wrong: Quoting past returns as an expectation implies the past will repeat. That is a form of assured return, which is not allowed.
A riskometer rating describes risk, not a return. Giving 10% as a figure to rely on still implies an assured return.
A long record is not a guarantee. Calling a return as good as fixed breaks the rule against implying assured returns.

qs.prompt: Meena's profile says Moderate. A fund you like carries a Very High riskometer. What do you do?
options: Recommend it, since a small share makes the riskometer moot
Choose a fund within her profile and show both riskometers
Raise her risk profile to Very High so that the fund fits
Mention the riskometer only if she asks about it first
qs.why: It starts from her profile, and showing scheme and benchmark riskometers lets her see the risk before she decides.
wrong: A small share still carries Very High risk. Suitability asks whether the product fits her, whatever the portion.
Changing a profile to fit a product is misselling. The profile must reflect what she can really bear, not what suits the sale.
The riskometer is part of every recommendation, not an optional extra. Waiting to be asked leaves out a required disclosure.

qs.prompt: A client reading the new documents asks why costs now show a base expense ratio plus brokerage and taxes. What helps him most?
options: Tell him the split is technical and he need not worry
Quote only the base ratio, as it is the lower figure
Show the base ratio and the added charges, then the total
Compare the new base ratio with old total ratios to show savings
qs.why: Showing each part and the total gives him the full cost, and lets him compare funds like for like.
wrong: Brushing it off leaves him uninformed. Under the 2026 rules cost transparency is higher, and clients will ask for a clear answer.
The base ratio alone understates what he pays, because brokerage and taxes sit outside it. Quoting only that misleads him.
Old total ratios and the new base ratio measure different things, so comparing them can suggest savings that may not exist.

title: SIP and step-up maths
concept: ₹10,000/month for 20 years at 12% ≈ ₹1 crore (invested ₹24 lakh).
With a 10% yearly step-up, the same start grows to ≈ ₹1.99 crore (invested ≈ ₹68.7 lakh).
Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ return %.
Step-up is the easiest upsell to every existing SIP client.
talk: "Just increase your SIP 10% every year with your salary — the corpus nearly doubles."

qs.prompt: ₹10,000 SIP, 20 years, 12% — approximate corpus:
Same SIP with 10% annual step-up — approximate corpus:
qs.why: ≈ ₹1.99 crore.

qs.prompt: Rule of 72 at 9% return — years to double:
Meena's ₹5 lakh grows at an assumed 9% a year. By the Rule of 72, in about how many years could it reach ₹20 lakh?
qs.why: Each doubling takes 8 years at 9%. ₹5 lakh becomes ₹10 lakh, then ₹20 lakh: two doublings, about 16 years.
wrong: At 9% the rule gives 72 divided by 9, which is 8 years, but that is one doubling only, to ₹10 lakh.
Twelve years is one doubling at 6%, not 9%. It also stops at ₹10 lakh, short of the target.
Twenty-four years is three doublings, which would reach ₹40 lakh. The target needs only two.

qs.prompt: A client says a ₹10,000 step-up SIP and a flat ₹20,000 SIP both reach about ₹2 crore in 20 years at 12%, so they are the same plan. What should you point out?
options: Flat needs ₹20,000 now and puts in ₹48 lakh; step-up ₹69 lakh
They are equal, since both end with about the same corpus
The step-up earns a higher rate, so it needs less money
The flat SIP always wins because its first instalment is bigger
qs.why: The flat SIP puts in less in total but demands ₹20,000 from day one. The step-up starts small and puts in more over time.
wrong: The corpus matches, but the paths differ. One strains the budget early, the other later, and total money in is not equal.
Both earn the same 12% by assumption. The step-up reaches the corpus by putting in more money, not by earning more on it.
Flat does need less in total here, but a bigger first instalment is not always affordable, and a SIP that is dropped wins nothing.

qs.prompt: After seeing ₹1 crore, Meena asks: "So I will have that?" If her fund earns 8% a year, not 12%, about what will her flat ₹10,000 SIP reach in 20 years?
options: About ₹80 lakh, a fifth below ₹1 crore
About ₹24 lakh, just what she invested
qs.why: At 8% the 20-year corpus is about ₹59.3 lakh, 41% lower than at 12%. A small change in return moves the result a lot.
wrong: Scaling by 8 over 12 is tempting, but compounding makes the shortfall larger than the drop in the rate suggests.
A fifth lower understates the effect. Over 20 years a four-point change in return compounds into a far larger gap.
₹24 lakh is her total investment. At 8% her money still grows, so the corpus is well above what she paid in.

qs.prompt: A client's salary rises about 5% a year and a 10% step-up feels too steep. What is the best advice?
options: Skip the step-up, since only 10% or more is worth doing
Step up 10% now and cut it back if money gets tight
Keep the SIP flat and add a lump sum later instead
Use 5%, which lifts the corpus to about ₹1.37 crore
qs.why: A step-up matched to her income is one she will keep. At 5%, the same ₹10,000 start reaches about ₹1.37 crore.
wrong: Any step-up helps. A 5% step-up lifts ₹99.9 lakh to about ₹137 lakh, so the all-or-nothing view leaves value on the table.
A step-up she cannot keep up risks a stopped SIP, which is worse than a smaller rise she can sustain every year.
A later lump sum is rarely kept, and later money has less time to grow. A modest yearly rise does the work steadily.

title: Using data in client meetings
concept: Open with one fresh fact (e.g., 'SIPs hit a record ₹32,297 crore in August').
Link it to the client's situation within 30 seconds.
Carry a one-page sheet: AUM, SIPs, defence, gold, rates.
Update numbers monthly after AMFI data (~10th).
talk: "Last month Indians invested a record ₹32,000 crore through SIPs. Where does your SIP stand?"

qs.prompt: Best way to use data with a client:
options: One fresh fact linked to their situation
qs.why: Relevance.

qs.prompt: When should your fact sheet be refreshed?
qs.why: Stay current.

qs.prompt: Which opener is strongest?
options: A fresh, relevant statistic plus a question
qs.why: Engagement.

qs.prompt: It is the 12th and AMFI's August data is out. Which opener suits a client whose ₹15,000 SIP is three years old?
options: AUM is ₹87.08 lakh crore, and SIP assets are ₹18.62 lakh crore
A record ₹32,297 crore came via SIPs in August. Same goal?
Let me start with a 20-slide deck on the industry this month
The market looks stretched, so you may want to pause this month
qs.why: One fresh fact, linked to her SIP, ends in a question about her goal. That turns the data into a conversation about her.
wrong: Two big numbers with no link to her give her nothing to answer. A statistic needs a bridge to her own SIP.
A long deck uses the meeting for slides, not for her. The client speaks last, if at all, and decisions get squeezed.
Pausing is advice with no reason behind it. A data point should open a talk, not hand her a call to stop a three-year SIP.

qs.prompt: A client reads that 81% of SIPs stop and wants to stop his. In August 2026, 53.82 lakh SIPs closed or matured against 66.39 lakh new ones. What is the best reply?
options: He is right; four in five SIPs fail, so stopping is normal
The figure is invented, since AMFI publishes no SIP data
It counts only equity SIPs, so it does not apply to his fund
It sets one month's closures against new SIPs, not all SIPs
qs.why: 53.82 divided by 66.39 is 81.1%. It sets closures, including SIPs that ended on schedule, against one month's new SIPs.
wrong: The ratio does not say four in five SIPs fail. About 5% of the 10.02 crore contributing accounts closed that month.
AMFI does publish SIP data monthly, including registrations and closures. The 81.1% comes from those figures.
The figure covers SIPs overall, not only equity ones, so that is not why it fails to apply to him.

qs.prompt: Your one-page sheet shows July's figures. It is mid-September and AMFI's August data is out. A client asks for the latest SIP flows. What do you do?
options: Refresh from AMFI's August data and quote it with its month
Quote July's figure as the latest, since it is only a month old
Quote a news site's figure, whichever you saw last
Say you will update the sheet when the quarter ends
qs.why: AMFI releases monthly data around the 10th. Refreshing then, and naming the month, keeps you accurate and credible.
wrong: July's figure is not the latest once August's is out. Quoting it as current is a stale fact that a client may check.
Pick a source and stick to it. The last site you saw may be late or may carry a slip, and the client cannot trace it.
A quarterly update is too slow for monthly data. By then the sheet would be a full three months out of date.

qs.prompt: Two reports show March 2026 net equity inflows as ₹40,366 crore and ₹40,450 crore. A client asks which is right. What is the best practice?
options: Quote the average of the two, to stay on the safe side
Quote the larger one, as it sounds more convincing
Quote AMFI's own release with its source and month
Avoid quoting numbers altogether, to prevent any slip
qs.why: The primary source settles it, and the month lets the client check. Secondary reports can slip, so go back to AMFI.
wrong: An average of two reports is a figure nobody published. It adds an error of its own, and you cannot source it.
Choosing the figure that sounds better is persuasion, not accuracy, and a client who checks will doubt your other numbers.
Numbers are what make your point credible. Avoiding them leaves you with opinions, and the client with nothing to weigh.

title: Grand revision
concept: Industry: ₹87 lakh crore AUM, 10 crore SIPs, 66 months of equity inflows, SEBI 2026 rules.
Economy: 7.7% FY26 growth; repo hiked to 5.50% on 7 Oct 2026.
Defence: ₹7.85 lakh crore budget, ₹1.78 lakh crore production, ₹38,424 crore exports.
Gold/silver: central banks buying, record ETF flows; multi-asset: 58 months of inflows.
talk: Take the grand test today. Then teach one fact to a colleague — teaching locks it in.

qs.prompt: Which is correct?
options: Repo rate cut to 4% in Oct 2026
Gold ETFs had outflows in India in 2025
qs.why: Recap.

qs.prompt: Best core fund for a nervous first-time investor:
qs.why: Smoother ride.

qs.prompt: Defence thematic funds belong in:
qs.why: Risk sizing.

qs.prompt: A nervous first-time investor with ₹5 lakh points at defence funds and silver and asks for the best fund this year. Which plan fits this course?
options: Put most into a defence fund, since exports hit a record
Begin with a multi-asset core, and keep any theme small
Buy only a silver ETF, since ETF inflows are strong
Wait for the repo rate to fall before investing at all
qs.why: A multi-asset core gives a smoother ride across assets, and a small theme slice lets him act on his interest without staking the plan.
wrong: A record export year is already in the price, and one theme swings widely. It is a poor start for a nervous first-timer.
Silver is one asset with sharp swings. Strong inflows show demand, not safety, so it should not be the whole plan.
Waiting to time rates is a guess with its own cost. A diversified start and a SIP deal with the worry more reliably.

qs.prompt: Which of these statements could you safely make to a client in November 2026?
options: SIP flows were under ₹10,000 crore a month in August 2026
India's FY26 growth was 6.1%, slower than the year before
The RBI raised the repo rate 0.25 point on 7 October 2026
Defence exports fell in FY26 after a record in FY25
qs.why: On 7 October 2026 the RBI raised the repo rate by 0.25 point to 5.50%, shifting its stance to calibrated tightening.
wrong: SIP flows were a record ₹32,297 crore in August 2026. Quoting ₹10,000 crore would be off by about a factor of three.
FY26 growth was 7.7%, up from 7.1% the year before, so it neither fell to 6.1% nor slowed.
Defence exports rose about 63% in FY26 to a record ₹38,424 crore, so a fall is the opposite of the facts.

qs.prompt: A client says defence exports of ₹38,424 crore must be about half of the ₹1.78 lakh crore output. What is the right correction?
options: Yes, exports are about half of output
No, they are about 5% of output
No, they are about 40% of output
No, they are about 22% of output
qs.why: ₹38,424 divided by ₹1,78,000 is about 21.6%, or 22%. A record figure is still a minority of output.
wrong: Half of ₹1.78 lakh crore would be ₹89,000 crore, far above the ₹38,424 crore actually exported.
Five percent would be about ₹8,900 crore. Actual exports are more than four times that.
Forty percent would be ₹71,200 crore, nearly double the actual figure, so it overstates the share.

qs.prompt: A client wants 40% of his ₹20 lakh portfolio in a defence thematic fund after reading the budget news. What is the best answer?
options: Keep the core diversified; defence is a small satellite
Agree; a 15% budget rise makes defence the safest theme
Agree, but only if he invests through a monthly SIP
Refuse any thematic fund, since themes are never suitable
qs.why: A theme can swing hard and news is already priced in. A small satellite keeps the plan safe if the theme disappoints.
wrong: A bigger budget is good news, not safety. A theme is concentrated, so a larger weight raises risk rather than lowering it.
An SIP spreads the entry, but 40% in one theme is still concentrated. The size problem remains whatever the method.
Themes can have a place as small satellites. A blanket ban ignores a client who has a view and can afford the swings.

title: What a REIT is: owning rent through a listed unit
concept: A REIT (Real Estate Investment Trust) is a trust that owns income-producing real estate, such as office parks and malls, and sells units to investors.
Units are listed on stock exchanges. You buy and sell them like shares, from a small amount, instead of buying a whole property.
Rent from tenants is collected by the trust. Most of it is passed on to unitholders as regular distributions.
REITs in India are regulated by SEBI under the REIT Regulations, 2014.
A REIT unit gives you a share in the cash flows of buildings. It does not give you a claim on any one building.

client.quote: "My brother says REITs let you earn rent without buying a flat. Is that true? Is it safe?"
client.context: Client in her 40s, owns a flat she rents out, wants more real estate exposure without another property loan.

talk: "A REIT lets you own a small slice of large office parks or malls and receive a share of the rent. It is listed, so the unit price moves every day. It is not a fixed deposit."
remember: A REIT is a listed trust that owns rent-earning property.
You own units, not a building.
Price moves daily; distributions are not guaranteed.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes a REIT?
options: A listed trust that owns income-producing real estate and passes most of its income to unitholders
A fixed deposit with a real estate company
A loan given to builders at a fixed rate
A government scheme that guarantees rent
qs.why: A REIT is a trust that owns rent-generating property and distributes income. It is a market-linked unit, not a guaranteed product.

qs.prompt: What do you actually own when you buy a REIT unit?
options: A share in the trust's pool of properties and their income
One specific flat in a building
A bond that returns your principal on a fixed date
The land under the buildings only
qs.why: Units give a proportionate claim on the trust's assets and cash flows, not title to one property.

qs.prompt: Which regulator governs REITs in India?
qs.why: REITs are regulated by SEBI under the SEBI (Real Estate Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014.

qs.prompt: What does one REIT unit give an investor?
options: A claim on one named building
A title deed to one office
A share in its cash flows
qs.why: A unit is a share in cash flows from many buildings.
wrong: It gives no claim on any one building.
No title deed passes to a unitholder.
Distributions vary, so no fixed salary is promised.

qs.prompt: Where can a retail investor buy REIT units?
options: On an exchange, in small amounts
Only at a land registry office
Only by buying a whole property
qs.why: Units are listed and trade like shares. This fits the facts given.
wrong: A builder is not the route for units. That does not match this case.
A land registry does not sell units. It does not fit the facts given.
The point of a REIT is to avoid buying a whole property.

qs.prompt: Who regulates REITs in India?
options: The RBI under the banking law

NAV (net asset value) is the value of the trust's assets less debt, per unit. Units can trade above or below NAV.

title: Distributions and tax: what the cash payout is made of

title: Risks: what can go wrong with REITs and InvITs

Interest rate risk: higher rates raise borrowing costs and make fixed-income alternatives more attractive, which can pressure unit prices.

title: Time value of money: why ₹1 today beats ₹1 later
concept: Money today can be invested, so it is worth more than the same amount received later.
Present value (PV) is what a future amount is worth today. Future value (FV) is what today's money grows into.
FV = PV × (1 + r)^n, where r is the yearly rate and n is the number of years.
PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n. Discounting is just compounding in reverse.
A rate of return only means something when you also state the period it applies to.

client.context: Client weighing a lump sum now against a bigger payment later.

talk: "Let's put both on the same date. At 8% a year, ₹10 lakh today grows to about ₹12.6 lakh in three years, so ₹12 lakh later is worth less."

title: Bonds: coupon, price, face value and yield

Yield is the return an investor earns at today's price. Coupon is fixed, yield changes with the price.
