options: Coupon is fixed at issue; yield changes as the price changes
Yield is fixed and coupon changes
qs.why: The coupon is a contract term. The yield reflects the price you pay.

qs.prompt: What extra risk does a corporate bond carry compared with a G-sec?
options: The risk the issuer cannot pay
qs.why: Credit risk is the risk of default or delay by the issuer.

qs.prompt: Meena's bond has a face value of ₹1,000 and a 7.5% coupon. She bought it in the market for ₹950. How much does the issuer pay her each year?
options: ₹75 a year, as the coupon is 7.5% of face value
₹71.25 a year, as 7.5% of the ₹950 she paid
₹79 a year, as that is the yield on her ₹950
It moves with the price, so nobody can tell her
qs.why: The coupon is a fixed share of face value, so 7.5% of ₹1,000 is ₹75, whatever price she paid for the bond.
wrong: The coupon is never worked on the price paid. A lower price changes her yield, not the rupees the issuer pays.
7.9% is the current yield (₹75 ÷ ₹950), a ratio. The issuer's payment is still ₹75; only the yield changes.
The coupon is set when the bond is issued and printed on it. The price moves and the yield with it; the coupon does not.

qs.prompt: After bad news about a company, its 5-year bond with an ₹80 coupon and ₹1,000 face value trades at ₹800. Rohan says his return is still 8%. What is closer to the truth?
options: Exactly 8%, because the coupon on a bond never changes
Lower than 8%, because a fall in the price cuts the yield
About 13.8% if all is paid, which signals the market's doubt
Zero until the price returns to ₹1,000, as interest waits for par
qs.why: He pays ₹800, gets ₹80 a year and ₹1,000 at the end, which is about 13.8%. The market wants this because it fears a default.
wrong: The coupon is fixed, but 8% is only what a ₹1,000 buyer earns. Paying less raises the yield, so 8% is wrong here.
A lower price raises the yield for a new buyer, because the same ₹80 and the ₹1,000 come back on less money.
Interest is paid on dates, whatever the price. A fall in price does not suspend the coupon unless the issuer defaults.

qs.prompt: A 10-year G-sec yields 7.1%. A company bond of the same tenor yields 8.6%. Meena sees the extra 1.5% as a bonus. What is the best reply?
options: It is a bonus, since both bonds carry a fixed coupon for the same ten years
It covers inflation, which hits company bonds more than G-secs do
It exists because company bonds have a higher face value than G-secs
It pays for the company's credit risk, the chance of a missed payment
qs.why: The G-sec has sovereign credit. The company could miss a payment, so lenders ask for extra yield as compensation.
wrong: Both have fixed coupons, but only one is backed by the government. The same tenor does not mean the same risk.
Inflation hits both kinds of bond alike. The gap between them is mainly about who might not pay.
Face value is a printed amount and does not explain a yield gap. The gap is the price of credit risk.

qs.prompt: Meena may need ₹5 lakh in 2 years but is offered a bond that matures in 8 years. Her cousin says fixed rate means safe. What should the adviser point out?
options: She cannot sell it before maturity, so the money would be stuck
In year 2 she would get the market price, possibly below face value
Her coupon would be cut if she sold the bond before maturity
She would get the ₹1,000 face value back whenever she sells
qs.why: Face value is due only at maturity. Before that, the market price applies, and it can be lower after a rate rise.
wrong: Bonds can be sold in the market. The real catch is the price she will receive, not whether a sale is allowed.
The coupon is set by the issuer and does not change when she sells. The buyer simply gets the remaining coupons.
Face value is repaid at maturity only. A seller in year 2 gets the market price, which can be above or below it.

title: Why bond prices fall when interest rates rise
concept: Existing bonds have fixed coupons. When new bonds offer higher rates, old bonds become less attractive, so their prices fall.
When rates fall, old higher-coupon bonds become more valuable, so prices rise.
The longer the bond has to maturity, the bigger the price move for the same change in rates.
If held to maturity, a bond pays face value, so interim price falls do not matter to the holder. A fund must show NAV daily, so the swing appears in NAV.
This is why debt funds can show negative returns over short periods.

client.quote: "Why did my debt fund go down? Debt funds are supposed to be safe."
client.context: Client sees a negative one-month return on a long-duration fund after a rate rise.

talk: "When market rates rise, the price of existing bonds drops. A fund holds many bonds and marks them each day, so the NAV dips. If rates stabilise the fund keeps earning the coupons."

qs.prompt: Market interest rates rise. What generally happens to the price of an existing bond?
qs.why: New bonds pay more, so older lower-coupon bonds must sell at a lower price to match.

qs.prompt: Which bond is likely to move more for the same rate change?
options: One with a longer time to maturity
qs.why: Longer-dated bonds are more sensitive to rate changes.

qs.prompt: Why can a debt fund's NAV fall even if no bond defaults?
options: Bond prices change with interest rates and the fund marks them daily
qs.why: NAV is based on daily market values, so rate-driven price moves flow into it.

qs.prompt: Meena owns a 7% ₹1,000 bond with ten years left. New 10-year bonds are now issued at 8%. A buyer offers her about ₹933 for hers. Why would anyone pay less than face value?
options: Second-hand bonds always sell at a 7% discount to face value
The issuer has cut the coupon on old bonds after the rate rise
A new bond pays ₹80, so the older ₹70 bond has to be cheaper
The buyer wants a profit before the issuer repays face value
qs.why: A new bond pays ₹80 on ₹1,000. To match that, the old ₹70 bond has to sell at a price that makes its yield about 8%.
wrong: There is no fixed discount. The price depends on the yield buyers want and the time left, here ₹933 for ten years.
Coupons on existing bonds never change. What changed is the market yield, which lowers the price of the old bond.
A buyer's profit does come from price and coupon, but the discount exists because of the new 8% yield, not a wish for profit.

qs.prompt: A client's long-duration debt fund shows -2.1% for the month after the RBI raised rates. She says debt funds are safe and wants to know if the fund has defaulted. What is the fair explanation?
options: The fund has missed coupon payments, and she should plan to exit
The fund's bonds were repriced for higher yields, and the coupons are still being earned
The fund house has charged a one-time fee that month for the rate rise
The NAV only moves when the fund sells a bond, so some sale must have gone wrong
qs.why: The NAV marks every bond to the market each day. Prices fell on the rate rise, while the fund still earns its coupons.
wrong: A missed coupon is a default, which is a credit event. Nothing in the story says that. A rate rise explains the dip.
No such fee exists. The cost of a fund is the expense ratio, spread across each day's NAV, not a lump sum for a rate move.
NAV is marked to market daily, whether or not the fund sells anything. A fall in bond prices is enough to dip it.

qs.prompt: Both a 2-year and a 10-year bond pay a 7% coupon at ₹1,000. Yields rise from 7% to 8%. About how much does each fall in price?
options: Both fall by about ₹10, one point of yield being ₹10 of price
Both fall by about ₹70, which is the full coupon on ₹1,000
About ₹67 for the 2-year and about ₹18 for the 10-year bond
About ₹18 for the 2-year and about ₹67 for the 10-year bond
qs.why: The 2-year drops to about ₹982 and the 10-year to about ₹933. Longer maturity, bigger swing.
wrong: Price moves are not the same for every bond. The longer one is hit far harder by the same rate rise.
₹70 is one year of coupon, not the loss in price. Neither bond falls that much from a 1% yield rise.
This reverses the rule. The short bond has less time to suffer the lower coupon, so it falls less, not more.

qs.prompt: Rohan's 10-year 7% bond is down on paper after a rate rise. The issuer is sound and he does not need the money for nine more years. What happens to the price if he simply holds?
options: It drifts back towards ₹1,000 as maturity nears
It stays at the lower price for as long as rates stay high
It falls further each year, as less time is left before maturity
It returns to ₹1,000 the day the RBI stops raising rates
qs.why: At maturity the issuer repays face value, so the price is pulled towards ₹1,000 and he is paid coupons all along.
wrong: With each year the bond has less time left, so the price is pulled back towards face value even if yields stay high.
Time works the other way. With fewer years left the discount shrinks, so the price rises towards face value.
A pause in rate rises does not reset prices. Price depends on yields and time left, and neither jumps back on a pause.

title: Duration: how sensitive is the fund to rates?
concept: Modified duration estimates the % change in a bond's price for a 1% (100 bps) change in yield.
Price change ≈ − Modified duration × change in yield.
A fund with modified duration of 4 would fall about 4% if yields rose 1%, and rise about 4% if yields fell 1% (approximately, ignoring coupons).
Longer duration means more rate risk and, usually, more potential reward when rates fall.
Fund factsheets show average maturity, Macaulay duration, modified duration and yield to maturity (YTM).

client.quote: "What does duration of 6 years mean for my money?"
client.context: Client asks why a gilt fund's NAV moved so much.

talk: "Roughly, if yields rise 1%, a fund with duration of 6 could fall about 6% in price terms. The coupon income offsets some of that over time. Shorter duration funds move less."

qs.prompt: A fund has a modified duration of 3. If yields rise by 1%, the approximate effect on price is:
qs.why: Price change ≈ −3 × 1% = −3%, before counting the coupon income.

qs.prompt: Which fund is more sensitive to interest rate changes?
options: The one with the higher modified duration
The one with the lower duration
The one with the lower expense ratio
qs.why: Higher duration means a larger price swing for a given yield change.

qs.prompt: Where would you look to see a debt fund's modified duration?
options: The fund factsheet or portfolio disclosure
qs.why: Factsheets list duration, maturity and YTM.

qs.prompt: Meena holds ₹20 lakh in a gilt fund with a modified duration of 6. Yields rise by 0.5% this month. About how much does the price effect take off her holding?
options: Nothing, because a month of coupons covers it
qs.why: Price change is about duration × change in yield, so 6 × 0.5% is 3%, and 3% of ₹20 lakh is ₹60,000.
wrong: That is the effect of a full 1% rise. Her fund saw a rise of 0.5%, so the hit is half of that.
That is just the change in yield applied to her money. Duration multiplies it, and here the multiplier is 6.
A month of coupons adds only about 0.6% of value for a 7% portfolio. That is far less than a 3% price drop.

qs.prompt: Meena says a duration of 6 years means her money is locked for six years. What is the sound reply?
options: It means the fund cannot repay her before six years are over
No lock-in: it shows price sensitivity, and she can redeem any day
It means every bond in the fund matures exactly six years from now
It means the fund loses 6% each year until the six years pass
qs.why: Duration estimates how much the price moves for a 1% change in yields. Open-ended funds can be redeemed on any business day.
wrong: No lock-in exists in an open-ended debt fund. Duration is a sensitivity measure, not a repayment date.
The portfolio holds many bonds with different maturities. Duration is a weighted average figure, not one date.
A fund does not lose a fixed 6% a year. Duration scales a move in yields, which can be up or down.

qs.prompt: A factsheet shows average maturity 8.2 years, Macaulay duration 5.9, modified duration 5.5 and YTM 7.4%. For a quick estimate of the price hit from a 1% rise in yields, which figure does the adviser use?
qs.why: Modified duration is Macaulay ÷ (1 + yield), which is 5.9 ÷ 1.074 = 5.5. It links price moves to yield moves directly.
wrong: Average maturity ignores when the coupons arrive. It overstates sensitivity because coupons shorten the true timing.
Macaulay duration is a weighted time to get your cash back. Divide by (1 + yield) to get the price sensitivity.
YTM is an expected annual return. It says what the portfolio earns, not how far the price moves when yields do.

qs.prompt: A 10-year 7% bond at ₹1,000 has a modified duration of 7.02. Yields rise from 7% to 8%. Which estimate of the new price is best?
options: About ₹1,070, because a higher yield means a higher price
About ₹993, since a 1% rise cuts only about 0.7% of the price
About ₹70, because that is the coupon the bond pays
qs.why: 7.02 × 1% is about 7%, or ₹70, off ₹1,000. Duration is a straight-line guide, so the exact price of ₹933 differs slightly.
wrong: Higher yields push prices down, not up. Price and yield move in opposite directions.
The 0.7% reading mixes up the decimal. With a duration of 7.02, a 1% rise cuts about 7% of the price, not 0.7%.
₹70 is the yearly coupon, and it is not a price. The price estimate is ₹1,000 less about ₹70, which is about ₹930.

title: Yield to maturity, accrual and mark-to-market
concept: Yield to maturity (YTM) is the annualised return if every bond in the portfolio is held to maturity and all payments are made as promised.
Accrual strategy: buy bonds and hold to maturity to earn the coupons. NAV rises steadily unless there are price shocks or defaults.
Duration strategy: the manager takes a view on rates and holds longer bonds if rates are expected to fall.
The portfolio YTM is a gross figure. Fund expenses and tax come out of it.
A high YTM can signal higher credit risk. It is not a free bonus.

client.quote: "The fund's YTM is 8%. So I will get 8%?"
client.context: Client reads YTM on a factsheet as a guaranteed return.

talk: "YTM is what the current portfolio would earn if held to maturity with no defaults, before expenses and tax. Your actual return can be different because prices change and the portfolio changes."
remember: Net of expenses and tax it is lower.
High YTM may mean higher risk.

qs.prompt: What does a fund's YTM represent?
options: The portfolio's expected annualised yield if held to maturity with all payments made
qs.why: YTM is a gross estimate based on today's holdings. It is not a promise.

qs.prompt: A debt fund shows YTM of 8% and expense ratio of 0.5%. What is a fair expectation?
options: Net return nearer 7.5% before tax, if nothing changes
qs.why: Expenses reduce the yield. Prices and the portfolio can also change.

qs.prompt: Why should a high YTM make you ask questions?
options: It may reflect lower-rated or less liquid bonds
It always means a good fund
It proves the manager is skilled
qs.why: Higher yields typically compensate for more risk.

qs.prompt: Meena puts ₹10 lakh in a fund whose factsheet shows YTM 8%. She expects ₹80,000 after a year. What is the fair way to put it?
options: It is guaranteed, because YTM is the rate the fund house has promised
Less than ₹80,000 only because of tax, as price moves cancel out
₹80,000 plus all coupons, because YTM covers only the price gain
₹80,000 is a gross estimate, before costs, tax and price moves
qs.why: YTM describes the current holdings if held to maturity, before expenses and tax. The real result can differ.
wrong: No rate is promised. YTM assumes every bond is held to maturity and paid in full, and the portfolio itself will change.
Price moves do not cancel out. A rate rise or a downgrade can lower returns, and new buys change the portfolio's yield.
YTM already includes both coupons and the gain or loss to par. Adding coupons on top would count them twice.

qs.prompt: A fund's portfolio YTM is 8.0%, its expense ratio is 0.6%, and the investor is in the 30% slab, which is 31.2% with cess. If the portfolio earns exactly its YTM and she redeems after a year, about what does she keep?
options: About 7.4%, which is 8.0% less the 0.6% cost
About 8.0%, because YTM is what the portfolio earns
qs.why: Costs take it to 7.4%. Tax at 31.2% on that gain leaves 5.1%. Real results will vary with prices and the portfolio.
wrong: This is after costs but before tax. A slab-rate investor pays tax on the gain, so the figure falls further.
YTM is gross. Costs and tax both come out of it, so an investor never keeps the full factsheet figure.
This skips the 0.6% cost and the 4% cess. Tax of 30% alone on 8.0% would leave 5.6%, but she also pays costs and cess.

qs.prompt: Meena's short-term accrual fund dips 0.8% in the week after yields rise. She wants to sell, though she planned to hold for about the fund's own duration of two years. What should the adviser explain?
options: The dip shows that the fund has failed to pay coupons on its bonds
Dips in accrual funds always grow, so selling now is the sound move
A mark-to-market dip; the bonds still pay and mature at face value
NAV cannot fall in an accrual fund, so the statement must be wrong
qs.why: Prices are marked daily. The bonds still pay and mature at face value, and her holding period matches the duration.
wrong: A rate rise explains the dip. A default would be a credit event, and nothing says any coupon has been missed.
Dips do not always grow. Bonds pull back towards face value as maturity nears, so a mark-to-market dip often fades.
Accrual funds still mark bonds to market each day, so the NAV can dip when yields rise, even if briefly.

qs.prompt: A manager lengthens the fund's average maturity from 2 years to 7 because she expects yields to fall. What has changed about how the fund tries to earn?
options: Nothing, since accrual and duration strategies are the same
It now makes a rate call too, so a rate rise would hurt more
It is now safer, because longer bonds pay more coupons
It now earns a fixed return, since longer bonds lock in the YTM
qs.why: A long position pays off if yields fall and hurts if they rise. She is now making a rate call as well as earning coupons.
wrong: They are different. Accrual earns the coupons, while a duration strategy bets on the path of rates.
Longer bonds do pay more yield, but they carry more rate risk. More coupons do not make a fund safer.
Nothing locks in the YTM for a fund. It buys and sells, and longer bonds swing more when yields change.

title: Credit risk and ratings
concept: Credit risk is the chance that an issuer misses an interest or principal payment.
Rating agencies grade debt: AAA is highest, then AA, A, BBB, and so on. Below BBB is below investment grade.
Ratings can be cut (downgrade). Prices usually fall on a downgrade, before any default.
Higher-rated bonds pay lower yields. Lower-rated bonds pay more to compensate for the risk.
Diversification across issuers and sectors reduces, but does not remove, credit risk.

client.quote: "This fund shows 9% yield but my friend's shows 7.5%. Same category. Why?"
client.context: Client compares two corporate bond funds.

talk: "The 9% fund holds lower-rated papers. It earns more because it is taking more credit risk. If one issuer fails, the loss lands in NAV."

qs.prompt: Which rating indicates the strongest credit quality?
qs.why: AAA is the highest rating.

qs.prompt: What usually happens to a bond's price when the issuer is downgraded?
qs.why: A downgrade means higher perceived risk, so the market demands a higher yield and the price falls.

qs.prompt: Two funds are in the same category. One has a much higher yield. What should you check first?
options: The credit quality table of the portfolio
Which fund house has a bigger office
qs.why: Higher yield often comes from lower-rated paper.

qs.prompt: Rohan's friend's corporate bond fund yields 7.5% and his own shows 9%. Same SEBI category, similar maturity. What should Rohan check first?
options: The credit table, to see how much sits in lower-rated papers
The expense ratio, since a lower fee explains most of a 1.5% gap
The last month's return, since a higher yield shows up there
Whether the plan is direct or regular, since cost sets the yield
qs.why: The gap usually comes from credit quality. The credit table shows how much sits in AAA and how much in lower grades.
wrong: Expense ratios differ by a fraction of a percent. A 1.5% gap in portfolio yield points to what the bonds are, not the fee.
One month of returns also reflects price moves, and says little about which bonds the fund holds or why it yields more.
Plan type changes cost by a small amount. The portfolio yield on the factsheet is the same for both plans.

qs.prompt: A fund holds a 4% position in a bond rated AA. Today the agency cuts it to A. No coupon has been missed. What is the likely effect?
options: No effect, since the issuer is still paying, so the price holds
The fund must sell the bond immediately at its original price
Its price usually falls now and the NAV dips, before any default
The fund cannot report the change until a payment is missed
qs.why: Buyers price in the higher risk straight away, so the price drops on the news, and the NAV marks it down that day.
wrong: Prices react to the downgrade itself. The market wants a higher yield for the added risk, so the price falls.
A forced sale at the old price cannot happen. The market sets the price, and buyers will pay less after a cut.
Funds mark holdings to market daily and disclose ratings. They do not wait for a missed payment to show a cut.

qs.prompt: A fund earns 1.8% a year more than a high-quality rival. It holds 4% in one issuer, which defaults with nothing recovered. About how many years of the extra yield does it take to repay that loss?
options: About 0.5 years, since one default is a rounding error
None, because diversification removes credit risk entirely
About 4 years, the same number as the 4% loss
About 2.2 years, since 4% divided by 1.8% a year
qs.why: A 4% loss at 1.8% a year takes about 2.2 years of extra yield to repay. Diversification limits this but does not remove it.
wrong: The loss is 4% of the fund, which is much larger than half a year of the 1.8% extra yield.
Spreading across issuers reduces credit risk but cannot remove it. A default still costs the fund its share.
Treating 4% as 4 years ignores the 1.8% yearly extra. Divide the loss by the extra yield instead.

qs.prompt: A client says a AAA rating means her debt fund cannot lose money. What is the honest reply?
options: Ratings are opinions that can be cut, and AAA prices still move
Correct, since AAA bonds are guaranteed by the rating agency
AAA applies only to government bonds, whose prices never move
The rating is irrelevant, because the coupon is what decides returns
qs.why: AAA means the lowest credit risk, not none. A rating can be cut, and even AAA bond prices fall when rates rise.
wrong: Rating agencies grade risk. They do not guarantee payment or compensate holders if an issuer fails.
AAA is a grade given to company issuers. Even government bond prices move when yields change.
The coupon is only part of it. A downgrade or default can change the price and hit NAV whatever the coupon was.

title: The yield curve and what it says
concept: The yield curve plots yields against maturity: 3 months, 1 year, 5 years, 10 years.
A normal curve slopes upward: longer bonds yield more. A flat curve means little extra for lending longer. An inverted curve means short yields exceed long yields.
The slope shows market expectations for growth, inflation and policy rates.
Fund managers pick where on the curve to hold bonds. A steep curve rewards extending maturity.
The RBI repo rate mostly anchors the short end. The long end follows growth, inflation and supply of government bonds.

client.quote: "RBI cut rates. Should I buy a long-term debt fund?"
client.context: Client reacts to a headline.

talk: "A rate cut helps long-duration funds if the market has not priced it already. But if long-term yields do not fall, you may not gain. Duration is a bet on the path of rates, so size it carefully."

qs.prompt: What does an upward-sloping yield curve usually mean?
options: Short yields are higher than long
qs.why: A normal curve pays more for lending for longer.

qs.prompt: Which rate mainly influences the short end of the yield curve in India?
qs.why: The policy repo rate anchors overnight and short-term yields.

qs.prompt: Why is buying a long-duration fund after a rate cut headline not a sure win?
options: Markets may have already priced it in, and long yields depend on more than the repo rate
Long funds cannot gain from cuts
qs.why: Expectations move prices before the cut. Long yields also depend on inflation and supply.

qs.prompt: The RBI cuts the repo rate by 0.50%. The 3-month yield falls from 6.5% to 6.0%, but the 10-year stays at 7.3%. A client wants a long-duration fund because rates are falling. What is the fair reply?
options: Do it now, since a repo cut always lowers every yield on the curve
The long end moves first, so a long fund will gain before short ones do
Avoid all debt funds for a year until the new repo rate settles in
The cut moved the short end only, so a long fund gains little from it alone
qs.why: The long end did not fall, so long bond prices did not rise. Her gain would depend on a later fall in long yields.
wrong: The repo rate mainly anchors the short end. The long end follows growth, inflation and bond supply, so it may not follow.
The short end responds first, as it tracks the repo rate. The long end responds to other things, and here it did not.
Waiting a year is not a plan. Short-duration funds could benefit from the lower short-end yields right away.

qs.prompt: The curve is inverted: the 1-year yield is 7.4% and the 10-year yield is 6.8%. A client wants a home for money she needs in one year. Which reading is sound?
options: Long bonds pay less here, so a short fund earns more with less rate risk
Go long, since the 10-year bond has the biggest price upside in a rate cut
Wait, since inverted curves mean every debt fund will fall next month
Pick the 10-year bond, as it pays 6.8% for ten years of safety
qs.why: Short yields exceed long ones, so there is no reward for taking duration. A short fund yields more and swings less.
wrong: The 10-year pays less than the 1-year, and its price would swing much more. She needs the money in a year anyway.
An inverted curve does not predict a debt fund fall next month. It only shows that short yields are above long ones.
A 10-year bond is not 'safer' for ten years. It carries more price risk than a 1-year bond, and she needs her money in one.

qs.prompt: On a steep curve, a 10-year bond yields 1.8 points more than a 1-year bond and has a duration of about 7. If yields rise 1% at once, about how long does the extra yield take to repay the price fall?
options: About 7 years, since the repayment time equals the duration
About 0.3 years, since 1.8 is much bigger than 1
About 3.9 years, which is 7% divided by 1.8% a year
It never repays, because a price fall is permanent
qs.why: A price fall of about 7% against 1.8% extra a year takes 3.9 years of extra yield to make up.
wrong: The repayment time is the fall divided by the extra yield, not simply the duration. Here that gives 3.9, not 7.
1.8% extra a year is not enough to cover a 7% fall in under a year. Dividing 1 by 1.8 is not the right sum here.
A price fall can be made up by extra income, and the bond is pulled back to face value as it nears maturity.

qs.prompt: A client with a goal in two years wants a long-duration fund because a rate cut is expected. Which advice fits what the lesson says about duration?
options: Go all in, since a cut is expected and the fund can wait out any dip
Skip debt completely, because rate cuts only help equity funds
Choose the longest fund, because longer maturity always pays more
Treat duration as a rate bet: size it small, match her horizon
qs.why: Duration is a view on the path of rates, so keep it small, and check that the horizon is not shorter than the duration.
wrong: An expected cut is not a delivered one. If yields do not fall, a long fund can dip within her two-year window.
Rate cuts can help bond prices as well as equities. The issue is sizing duration, not avoiding debt.
Longer maturity pays more only on a normal curve, and only if rates behave. It also raises risk.

title: SEBI's debt fund categories at a glance
concept: SEBI classifies debt funds mainly by portfolio duration, plus a few by credit rules.
Overnight: securities maturing in 1 day. Liquid: up to 91 days. Money market: up to 1 year. Ultra short: Macaulay duration 3–6 months. Low duration: 6–12 months.
Short duration: 1–3 years. Medium: 3–4 years. Medium to long: 4–7 years. Long duration: more than 7 years.

Gilt: at least 80% in government securities. Corporate bond: at least 80% in AA+ and above. Credit risk fund: at least 65% in AA and below. Banking and PSU: at least 80% in banks, PSUs and public financial institutions.
Dynamic bond and floater funds follow different rules. Always read the category and the scheme document.

client.quote: "Which debt fund category suits money I need in 6 months?"
client.context: Client has a goal inside a year.

talk: "For six months, we look at overnight, liquid or money market funds where the duration is short. A long-duration fund can swing in price within that time."
remember: Gilt = G-secs; credit risk = lower rated.

qs.prompt: Which category invests at least 80% in government securities?
qs.why: Gilt funds hold G-secs and carry sovereign credit, but still carry rate risk.

qs.prompt: A liquid fund invests in securities maturing within:
qs.why: SEBI defines liquid funds as holding securities with maturity up to 91 days.

qs.prompt: Which category has a minimum 65% allocation to AA-rated and below paper?
qs.why: Credit risk funds are designed to take more credit risk for higher yield.

qs.prompt: Rohan has a goal in 6 months and a bank balance he can set aside today. Which category fits that date best?
options: Long duration, because a rate cut is expected within the half-year
Liquid, because the holdings mature within 91 days and swings stay tiny
Corporate bond, because AA+ and above holdings cannot lose value
Medium duration, because it still falls inside the next four years

title: Liquidity risk and what the 2020 episode taught
concept: Liquidity risk: not being able to sell a bond quickly without a big price cut.
In April 2020, a fund house wound up six debt schemes after redemptions overwhelmed lower-rated holdings. Investors were locked in for months.
Since then, SEBI has tightened rules on liquidity, valuation and disclosure for debt funds, and has allowed segregated portfolios (side pockets) when a bond is downgraded to default.
In a side pocket, the troubled bond is separated. Investors keep units in the main portfolio and in the side pocket; recoveries are paid out as they happen.
Open-ended funds promise daily liquidity. The assets must be able to support that promise.

client.quote: "Can I withdraw from a debt fund any day?"
client.context: Client assumes redemption is always instant.

talk: "Normally yes, and the money arrives in a day or two. In an extreme stress the fund can face limits. That is one reason we avoid putting emergency money in lower-rated funds."

title: PMS: a portfolio in your own name
concept: Portfolio Management Service (PMS) is a SEBI-registered service where a manager runs a portfolio of securities held in the client's own demat account.
SEBI rules set the minimum investment at ₹50 lakh per client.
Types: discretionary (manager decides), non-discretionary (client approves each trade) and advisory (manager advises, client executes).
Because securities sit in the client's name, there is no pooling: each client's portfolio and tax position can differ.
PMS providers must be registered with SEBI as portfolio managers. Check the registration before recommending.

title: AIFs: Category I, II and III
concept: Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are privately pooled funds regulated by SEBI, for sophisticated investors.

Category I: funds supporting the economy, such as venture capital, start-ups, infrastructure and social ventures.
Category II: funds that do not fall in I or III and do not use leverage beyond day-to-day needs, such as private equity and debt funds.
Category III: funds that use complex strategies and may use leverage or trade in derivatives, such as hedge funds and long-short funds.

title: Who runs a mutual fund: sponsor, trustee, AMC, custodian
concept: A mutual fund is a trust. The sponsor sets it up, the trustees watch over it, and the asset management company (AMC) manages the money.
The custodian holds the securities, not the AMC. The registrar and transfer agent (RTA) keeps the unit records.
SEBI is the market regulator and writes the mutual fund rules. AMFI is the industry body that runs the ARN registration and the code of conduct.
Your money is invested in units of a scheme. It is not a deposit with the AMC, so the AMC's own finances do not hold your investment.
If an AMC shuts a scheme or changes it, the trustees and SEBI rules decide what unit holders are told and allowed to do.

client.quote: "What happens to my money if the AMC goes bust?"
client.context: Client worried about the fund house failing.

talk: "Your units are held in a trust, and the securities sit with a separate custodian. The AMC manages the money but does not own it. The fund can still lose value when markets fall, but a fund house failing is not the same as your money disappearing."
remember: SEBI regulates; AMFI runs the industry code.

qs.prompt: Who holds the securities a mutual fund buys?
qs.why: A separate custodian holds the securities. That separation protects unit holders if the AMC has trouble.

qs.prompt: A mutual fund is legally set up as:
qs.why: Mutual funds in India are trusts. The sponsor creates the trust, trustees oversee it and the AMC manages it.

qs.prompt: Which body runs the ARN registration for distributors?
qs.why: AMFI, the industry body, registers distributors and issues ARNs. SEBI sets the rules they follow.

qs.prompt: Meena's friend says: if the fund house shuts, your money goes with it. Where are the securities behind Meena's units actually held?
options: With the AMC, in a locked account it can use for its own bills
With AMFI, which looks after all the securities in the industry
With a custodian, which is separate from the AMC
With the registrar, which also keeps the unit records for the fund
qs.why: A custodian holds the securities, apart from the AMC. That separation is why an AMC failing does not wipe out her units.
wrong: The AMC manages the money but does not hold the securities. It cannot spend them on its own bills.
AMFI is an industry body for codes and registrations. It does not hold anyone's securities.
The registrar and transfer agent keeps the records of who owns how many units. It does not hold the securities.

qs.prompt: Rohan asks: who checks the AMC's work on behalf of unit holders, inside the fund's own structure? He thinks the fund manager is accountable to nobody.
options: The trustees, who watch over the fund and the AMC
The custodian, because it holds the securities the manager buys
The registrar, because it sends out his account statements
The sponsor alone, because it founded the fund and may change the manager
qs.why: The trustees watch over the fund for the unit holders. SEBI rules sit above this, and the AMC reports to them.
wrong: The custodian holds securities and settles trades. It does not oversee the AMC's decisions.
The registrar keeps the unit records and sends statements. It has no role in checking investment decisions.
The sponsor sets the trust up, but the trustees are the ones who watch over the fund once it is running.

qs.prompt: Dadi's statement shows how many units she holds. She asks who keeps the record of her units and sends the statement.
options: The trustees, who write each statement by hand once a month
The custodian, since it keeps everything about the fund safe
SEBI, since it keeps one record of every investor in the country
The registrar and transfer agent, called the RTA
qs.why: The RTA keeps the unit records for the fund and handles statements and changes to the folio.
wrong: Trustees watch over the fund. The record of units is kept by the RTA, not written by the trustees.
The custodian keeps the securities safe. The unit records are kept by a different party.
SEBI makes rules and supervises. It does not keep each investor's unit record for each scheme.

qs.prompt: Rohan wants to check that the person selling him a fund is properly registered. Which body runs that registration and the industry's code of conduct?
options: SEBI, which is the only body that registers every distributor
The custodian, which signs off every sale it settles
AMFI, the industry body that runs the ARN registration
The sponsor, which approves each distributor it hires
qs.why: AMFI runs the ARN registration and the code of conduct. A distributor should show the ARN on the form.
wrong: SEBI is the regulator and writes the rules. The distributor's ARN registration is run by the industry body.
A custodian settles and holds securities. It plays no part in registering the people who sell funds.
A sponsor sets up the trust. It does not run registration for distributors.

title: Categories, riskometer and true-to-label investing
concept: SEBI sorts schemes into categories such as equity, debt, hybrid, solution-oriented and others, so that two funds with the same label behave alike.
Inside equity, categories like large cap, mid cap and small cap have minimum holdings in their segment. This stops a large cap fund drifting into small caps.
The riskometer shows a scheme's risk on a scale from low to very high. It is updated regularly based on what the fund actually holds.
The label tells you what the fund must do. It does not tell you how well it will do. Two funds in one category can differ a lot in return.
Compare a fund with others in its own category and benchmark. Comparing a small cap fund with a liquid fund tells you nothing.

client.quote: "This mid cap fund gave 28% and your large cap gave 14%. Why would I hold the large cap?"
client.context: Client comparing funds across categories.

talk: "They are built for different jobs and carry different risk. The mid cap can fall much harder. Let's compare each fund with the others in its own category, and match the risk to what you can stay invested through."

qs.prompt: Why does SEBI define fund categories?
options: So funds with the same label follow similar rules
qs.why: Categories make funds of one label comparable and stop style drift. They do not promise returns.

qs.prompt: The riskometer is best used to:
options: Judge how risky the scheme's holdings are
Compare a fund with a bank FD
qs.why: It shows the risk level of what the scheme holds. It says nothing about future returns.

qs.prompt: The fairest way to judge a mid cap fund is to compare it with:
options: Other mid cap funds and its benchmark
qs.why: Same category, same benchmark. Cross-category comparison mixes up risk and return.

qs.prompt: Rohan says his mid cap fund gave 28% last year and Meena's large cap gave 14%, so the large cap should go. What is the fair reply?
options: Different jobs: a mid cap can fall far harder, so one year decides little
Agree, since the higher return shows the mid cap is better managed
Agree, but only if the mid cap beats the large cap two years in a row
Disagree, since large cap funds are always the higher earner over time
qs.why: The mid cap fund is built to take more risk. In the film it fell about 25% in a year, and ended below the large cap.
wrong: A higher return in one year can come from taking more risk, not from better management. The next year can reverse it.
Two years is still too short to judge. Risk shows in the falls, and a longer stretch includes them.
No category always earns more. Mid caps have done better in some stretches and worse in others.

qs.prompt: A scheme's riskometer reads Very High. What does it tell Meena?
options: The fund is expected to earn the highest returns of any scheme
The fund has been ranked best by SEBI among all schemes this year
The fund cannot be sold at all during the first year after buying
The fund's holdings carry a very high level of risk right now
qs.why: The riskometer reflects what the fund holds and is updated regularly. Very High means large swings are possible.
wrong: The riskometer shows risk, not return. A Very High reading means big swings, in both directions, are possible.
SEBI does not rank funds. The riskometer is a gauge of risk and not a prize for performance or quality.
The riskometer has nothing to do with lock-ins or when you can sell. Those rules sit in the scheme document.

qs.prompt: A small cap fund returned 30% this year and a liquid fund 6.5%. Rohan calls the liquid fund poor. What is a fair comparison?
options: Ignore returns and compare only the fund house's name
Compare the two directly, since the higher return always wins
Compare each fund only with others in its own category
Compare them only by the size of the NAV in rupees
qs.why: Funds in one category follow the same rules and carry similar risk, so comparing them is fair.
wrong: A fund house name does not tell you how the fund did against others of its kind.
A higher return from a riskier fund is not a better fund. The small cap took far more risk to earn it.
NAV in rupees is only the unit price. A fund with a high NAV is not better than one with a low NAV.

qs.prompt: Two large cap funds both follow SEBI's large cap rule. Over five years one gave 15% a year and the other 11%. What does the category label tell Meena?
options: That the 11% fund must now be moved to another category
That both will give 13% a year, the average of the two figures
That the 15% fund broke the rules by earning so much more
Both follow the large cap rule, though results can still differ
qs.why: The label sets rules for what the fund holds. How well the manager does inside those rules can differ.
wrong: A lower return does not change the category. The category depends on what the fund holds.
Labels do not set a return, and the average has no special meaning for either fund.
Earning more does not break any rule. Both funds can follow the category rule and still earn differently.

title: Costs: expense ratio, loads and direct vs regular
concept: The total expense ratio (TER) is the yearly fee taken from the fund's assets. It is already reflected in the NAV, so you never see a separate bill.
A direct plan has no distributor commission, so its TER is lower than the regular plan of the same scheme. The portfolio is the same.
An exit load is a fee for leaving early, charged on the amount redeemed within a stated period. Many equity funds have one for a year or less. Check the scheme document.
A small difference in TER compounds. A 1% gap over 20 years can shrink the final amount by a meaningful slice.
A regular plan pays for advice and service. The honest question is whether the advice is worth what it costs.

client.quote: "Why should I pay more through you when direct plans are cheaper?"
client.context: Client who has read about direct plans.

talk: "The direct plan is cheaper and that is a real saving. What you get from us is the plan, the review, and someone who talks you out of selling at the bottom. Let's look at the numbers and decide whether that is worth the difference to you."

qs.prompt: Where does a fund's expense ratio show up?
options: It is already deducted from the NAV
qs.why: TER is charged to the scheme and reflected in the NAV every day.

qs.prompt: Direct and regular plans of the same scheme differ in:
qs.why: The portfolio is identical. Regular carries a commission, so its TER is higher.

qs.prompt: An exit load is charged when you:
qs.why: Exit load applies to redemptions made within the period in the scheme document.

qs.prompt: A fund has an exit load of 1% for redemptions within one year. Rohan redeems ₹50,000 after 8 months. How much is cut as exit load?
options: ₹5,000, as the load applies to the whole year
₹500, which is 1% of the amount redeemed
Nothing, as the load stops after six months
₹250, as he stayed more than half the year
qs.why: He leaves inside the one-year period, so 1% of the ₹50,000 redeemed is cut: ₹500.
wrong: The load is 1% of the amount redeemed, not 10%. A year's period sets when it applies, not its size.
The period is stated in the scheme document, here one year. Leaving at eight months is still inside it.
The load does not scale with how long he stayed. It applies in full if he leaves within the period.

qs.prompt: Meena sees two NAVs for one scheme: ₹52.4 for the direct plan and ₹49.0 for the regular. Is the direct plan simply a better fund?
options: Yes, because its manager picks better shares than the regular plan's manager
No, because the higher NAV shows the direct plan costs more
Yes, because direct plans are allowed to hold riskier shares
No, the portfolio is the same, and the NAV is higher because the cost is lower
qs.why: Same portfolio, lower cost. The saving builds up in the direct plan's NAV over the years.
wrong: Both plans have the same manager and the same holdings. The cost is the difference, not the share-picking.
A higher NAV in rupees shows lower cost built up over time here, not a higher charge.
Plans of the same scheme hold the same portfolio, so risk is the same. Only the cost differs.

qs.prompt: Rohan could buy direct plans himself, but twice in a fall he sold in panic. How should he think about a regular plan's extra cost of about 1% a year?
options: It buys better performance, since regular plans earn more
It is a penalty for not knowing about direct plans, so he should always switch
A fee for service, worth it only if advice and discipline add more
It is zero in practice, since the NAV already includes it
qs.why: A regular plan pays for advice and service. The honest test is whether that is worth the cost to him.
wrong: Both plans hold the same portfolio. The regular plan earns less after cost, not more.
It is not a penalty. It pays for advice. For some investors, staying invested through a fall is worth the cost.
Being inside the NAV does not make it zero. It is a real cost that lowers what he ends up with.

qs.prompt: ₹1,00,000 grows at 11.5% in a direct plan and 10.5% in a regular plan for 20 years (assumed). About how much less does the regular plan end with?
options: About ₹1.45 lakh, because a 1% gap compounds year after year
About ₹20,000, as 1% of ₹1,00,000 is ₹1,000 for each of the 20 years
About ₹5 lakh, since the regular plan loses half of the direct plan's gain
About ₹10,000, as a 1% gap is a small amount in all
qs.why: ₹8.82 lakh against ₹7.37 lakh is a gap of about ₹1.45 lakh, or about 16% of the final amount.
wrong: That adds ₹1,000 a year without compounding. The gap grows because each year's cost also loses its future growth.
The regular plan loses much less than half. Its final amount is about 84% of the direct plan's.
A 1% gap looks small but compounds. Over 20 years it is far more than a few thousand rupees.

title: KYC, nomination and a clean paper trail
concept: KYC (know your customer) is required to invest. It is a one-time process with identity and address proof, and is valid across fund houses once done.
Nomination lets the investor name who receives the units. Not nominating, or opting out, can make claims slow and painful for the family.
Joint holding with 'either or survivor' lets one holder operate the folio. Choose the mode deliberately.
Keep the folio's mobile and email current. Account statements and alerts go there, and changes are verified through them.
A distributor must hold a valid ARN and show the ARN and EUIN on the application. Always check that it is correct.

client.quote: "Do I really need to fill the nominee? I will do it later."
client.context: Client skipping nomination on the form.

talk: "Please do it now, it takes a minute. If something happens, the nominee gets the units without a long legal process. You can change it any time."

qs.prompt: What does nomination do?
options: Names who receives the units on the holder's death
qs.why: A nominee receives the units, which makes the family's claim simpler.

qs.prompt: A distributor's application should always show:
qs.why: The ARN identifies the registered distributor.

qs.prompt: Why keep the mobile and email in a folio up to date?
options: It is needed to switch plans
qs.why: Account statements, OTPs and alerts are sent to the registered contact details.

qs.prompt: Meena skips the nominee on her form, planning to add it later. She then passes away suddenly. What is the likely result for her family?
options: The family may face a slow, painful claim through a long legal process
The units go to the nearest fund house, which shares them out equally
The units are cancelled and the money goes back to the AMC
Nothing changes, since the nominee is only needed for bank accounts
qs.why: Without a nominee, heirs usually must prove their claim through a longer legal route, which delays the units reaching them.
wrong: Units do not pass to a fund house. They remain her property and pass through her legal heirs.
The AMC does not take units back when a holder dies. The units belong to her heirs.
Nomination matters for mutual fund folios as much as bank accounts. Leaving it out can slow a claim.

qs.prompt: Rohan did KYC last year to buy a fund from one fund house. Now he wants to invest in another fund house. What should he expect?
options: He must repeat the whole KYC, since each fund house keeps its own
He needs a new KYC every year to keep investing
KYC is valid across fund houses, so he can go ahead with that same KYC
He can invest only if the first fund house sends a letter of approval
qs.why: Once done, KYC is valid across fund houses. He may still be asked for small details such as bank information.
wrong: KYC is a one-time process. A fresh round for each fund house is not needed.
KYC is done once and does not expire each year. Keep details like mobile and email current instead.
The first fund house has no say. KYC is recognised across fund houses without any letter.

qs.prompt: Meena and her husband hold a folio jointly with 'either or survivor'. Meena is travelling and her husband wants to redeem. Can he?
options: No, both holders must sign every transaction
Yes, but only after Meena has sent a letter allowing it
No, only the first holder named on the form can operate it
Yes, because either holder can operate the folio
qs.why: Either or survivor means any one holder can operate the folio, and the survivor continues if one holder dies.
wrong: That would be the case for 'joint' mode. The mode chosen here is 'either or survivor'.
No letter is needed. The choice of mode on the form already gives each holder that power.
In this mode no holder is above another. Either can operate the folio on their own.

qs.prompt: The form a distributor hands to Dadi has the ARN box empty. What should Dadi do?
options: Sign anyway, since the fund house can fill in the ARN box later
Fill the ARN herself with any number, since it is a formality
Ask for the valid ARN and EUIN to be filled in before signing
Cross out the box, since only direct investors have to use it
qs.why: A distributor must hold a valid ARN, and the form should show the ARN and EUIN. She checks them first.
wrong: An empty box on a signed form can be filled in later by anyone. She should check it before she signs.
A made-up number defeats the purpose. The ARN must be the distributor's own real and valid number.
An ARN is needed whenever a distributor is involved. Only direct applications go without one.

title: What you may and may not say: advertising and mis-selling
concept: Mutual fund advertising must carry the standard statement: mutual fund investments are subject to market risks; read all scheme related documents carefully.
Past performance can be shown only within the rules, and always with the line that it may or may not be sustained in future.
You must not promise or imply a return, guarantee capital, or call a market-linked scheme 'safe'.
Mis-selling includes pushing a product for the commission rather than the client's need, hiding costs, or recommending unsuitable risk.
Suitability comes first. Record the client's goal, horizon and risk comfort before you recommend.

client.quote: "Can you promise me at least 12% a year?"
client.context: Client asking for a guarantee.

talk: "I can't promise that and neither can anyone honest. Over long periods equity has done well, but the path is uneven. Let's build a plan that works even if returns are lower, and review it every year."

qs.prompt: Which statement is a promise you must not make?
options: "This fund will give you 12% every year."
qs.why: Promising a return in a market-linked product is mis-selling.

qs.prompt: Mis-selling includes:
options: Recommending a product mainly for commission
qs.why: Recommending for commission instead of suitability is mis-selling.

qs.prompt: Showing past returns needs which line?
options: That past performance may or may not be sustained
A guarantee of the same return
qs.why: Past performance cannot be presented as a promise of future results.

qs.prompt: A client says: I will invest if you promise 12% a year. What is the honest reply?
options: I cannot promise it, but let us plan so that it works if returns are lower
I can promise it if you hold for at least ten years, as history shows
I can promise 12% only on diversified funds, not on single ones
I cannot say it aloud, but you can read it in the fund's brochure
qs.why: No honest adviser can promise returns. A plan that survives lower returns, reviewed every year, is the fair answer.
wrong: History does not guarantee the future. A long holding period helps the odds, but it never makes a promise valid.
Diversified funds can fall as well. No type of fund carries a guaranteed return, so this promise is also false.
Brochures cannot promise returns either. Implying a return through any route is not allowed under the rules.

qs.prompt: Which of these is mis-selling?
options: Telling a client plainly that the fund's value can fall as well as rise
Showing a fund's five-year return along with the past performance line
Pushing a fund for its higher commission when a cheaper one fits better
Recording the client's goal, horizon and risk comfort before advising
qs.why: Pushing a product for commission instead of the client's need is mis-selling. Suitability must come first.
wrong: Saying a fund can fall is an honest warning. It is the opposite of mis-selling, because it shows the risk.
Past performance may be shown within the rules and with the line that it may or may not be sustained.
Recording the goal, horizon and risk comfort is suitability. It is what the rules ask an adviser to do.

qs.prompt: An advertisement says, 'Our fund gave 25% last year!' and nothing else. What is missing?
options: The fund manager's name and photo beside the figure shown
Nothing, since a one-year figure is always allowed on its own
A guarantee that the 25% will be repeated again next year
The past performance line, and the standard market risk statement
qs.why: Past performance may be shown only with the line that it may or may not be sustained, plus the standard risk statement.
wrong: A name or photo is not what the rules ask for. The risk statement and the past performance line are the missing parts.
A bare figure without the required lines is not allowed. The rules attach a disclaimer to past performance.
A guarantee would itself break the rules. Returns cannot be promised or implied, so a repeat cannot be assured.

qs.prompt: Meena, 60 and retired, needs her money in two years. She asks for the best small cap fund because her neighbour made 40%. What does suitability say you do first?
options: Place the order at once, since she is the client who asked for it
Record her goal, horizon and risk comfort, then judge if it fits
Choose the small cap fund that pays the adviser the highest commission
Tell her the 40% will repeat if she holds on for the two years
qs.why: Suitability comes first. A two-year goal for a retired client is a poor fit for a small cap fund, and the record shows why.
wrong: Just placing the order skips suitability. The adviser must check her goal, horizon and comfort with risk first.
Choosing by commission is mis-selling. The client's need, not the adviser's pay, decides the recommendation.
No return can be guaranteed, and a neighbour's 40% says nothing about the next two years. Saying so breaks the rules.

title: When things go wrong: grievances and investor protection
concept: Start with the fund house's investor service team, and keep the reference number. Most issues end here.
If the reply is late or unsatisfactory, escalate through SEBI's complaint platform, SCORES. Complaints are tracked against timelines.
SEBI's online dispute resolution (ODR) route is available once internal escalation does not work.
Unclaimed amounts sit with the fund house and can be claimed with proof. Keep KYC and bank details current.
Good records protect everyone: application copies, statements, and notes of what was discussed with the client.

client.quote: "My redemption has not arrived in a week. Who do I complain to?"
client.context: Client stuck on a delayed payout.

talk: "First, write to the fund house and note the reference. If they don't resolve it in the stated time, we escalate on SEBI's SCORES platform. I'll help you with the paperwork."

qs.prompt: Where should a complaint start?
options: With the fund house's investor service team
qs.why: Most problems are solved at the first level. Keep the reference.

qs.prompt: SEBI's online platform for complaints is:
qs.why: SCORES lets investors lodge and track complaints against listed entities and intermediaries.

qs.prompt: Why keep copies of applications and statements?
options: They are the proof if there is a dispute
qs.why: Records settle disputes quickly and protect both client and advisor.

qs.prompt: Meena's redemption has not arrived after a week. She wants to go straight to SEBI. What does the adviser suggest first?
options: Go straight to court, since even a delay of a week is already wrong
Write to the fund house's investor service team and note the reference
Wait another month or so, as such delays usually sort themselves out
Complain only to the distributor, as the fund house cannot help her
qs.why: Most issues end at the fund house, and its reference number is needed if she has to escalate later.
wrong: A court case is slow and costly, and it skips the simple steps that often solve the matter quickly.
Waiting without writing leaves no record. She should raise it now, in writing, and note the reference.
The fund house holds her redemption record, so it is the right first stop. A distributor cannot fix a payout.

qs.prompt: Meena wrote to the fund house and was promised a reply within a week. Two weeks later there is nothing. What next?
options: Ask another fund house's investor service team to step in
Write the same letter again and wait for another month or so
Close the folio and write off the amount as not worth it
File on SEBI's SCORES platform, where complaints are tracked
qs.why: After a late or unsatisfactory reply, SCORES is the next step, and complaints there are tracked against timelines.
wrong: Another fund house holds none of her records and has no power over her fund. SCORES is the escalation route.
Repeating the letter gives the fund house more time but no escalation. It adds no new record or pressure.
Closing the folio does not cure the problem. The money is still owed to her, and she should claim it.

qs.prompt: A dividend cheque came back because Dadi's old bank account was closed. Where does the money sit now?
options: It is lost for good, since a returned cheque cannot be reissued
With SEBI, which pays it out on its own after a year
With the fund house as unclaimed money, claimable with proof
With her old bank, which must be asked to reopen the account
qs.why: Unclaimed amounts sit with the fund house and can be claimed with proof. Her KYC and bank details must be current.
wrong: The money is not lost. It stays claimable with proof of identity and current bank details.
SEBI does not hold investors' money, and it pays nothing out on its own. The fund house keeps it for her.
A closed account cannot receive it, and the bank never held it. She should update her details with the fund house.

qs.prompt: A year later a client says: you told me this fund was guaranteed. What protects both client and adviser?
options: A verbal promise from the client never to raise it again
Nothing can help, since it is one person's word against another's
Only the fund house's own records, since advisers need none
Copies of the application and statements, plus notes of the meeting
qs.why: Notes of the discussion show what was said, and application copies show what was signed. Both protect everyone.
wrong: A spoken promise adds no proof and cannot stop a complaint. A written record is what helps.
Without records it is one word against another. Writing things down is exactly what removes that problem.
The fund house cannot know what was said in the meeting. Advisers need their own notes and copies of papers.

title: Large, mid and small: how the market-cap ladder works
concept: AMFI ranks listed companies by market capitalisation. The top 100 are large caps, ranks 101 to 250 are mid caps, and 251 onward are small caps.
Large caps are bigger, more liquid and usually steadier. Small caps can grow faster but fall harder and are harder to sell in a crash.
A large cap fund must keep at least 80% in large caps. Mid cap and small cap funds must keep at least 65% in their own segment.
Companies move between buckets as prices change, so a fund's mix of stocks changes without the manager doing anything.
Long-term returns tend to rise with risk across the ladder, but with long flat or negative stretches. Match the bucket to the client's horizon.

client.quote: "Small caps gave the highest return. Put everything there."
client.context: Client chasing last year's winner.

talk: "Small caps have the highest ceiling and the deepest falls. Let's keep them as one part of the portfolio, sized so a bad year doesn't push you to sell."

qs.prompt: Under AMFI's list, mid caps are companies ranked:
qs.why: Large = 1-100, mid = 101-250, small = 251 onward.

qs.prompt: A large cap fund must hold at least what share in large caps?
qs.why: SEBI's categorisation requires a minimum of 80% in large caps.

qs.prompt: Why can a fund's portfolio drift between buckets without trades?
options: Company market caps change and ranks move
qs.why: Rankings follow market value, so stocks cross the line as prices move.

qs.prompt: A company ranked 99th by market value falls in price and slips to rank 108 in the next AMFI list. A large cap fund holds it. What happens?
options: The fund must sell the shares the same day it slips below rank 100
The company is now a mid cap, and the fund's mix shifts without a trade
The fund house has to refund investors for that change of bucket
Nothing changes in the mix, because the label stays fixed for ten years
qs.why: Buckets follow rank, so the stock moves down a bucket. The fund's large cap share falls even though the manager did nothing.
wrong: No same-day sale is required. The rules are about the fund's overall mix, which is checked against the published lists.
There is no payment to investors. A change of bucket is part of normal market movement and the fund is not at fault.
Lists are reset every six months, not ten years. A company's bucket can change at each update.

qs.prompt: A client says small caps gave the highest return, so everything should go there. What is the fair reply?
options: Small caps have the highest ceiling and the deepest falls, so size them to survive a bad year
Agree, because the highest return so far is the best guide to the next ten years
Move everything to large caps, since small caps are not allowed for a client like him
Split it equally across twenty small cap funds, which takes away the risk of a fall
qs.why: It states the trade honestly: more upside, deeper falls, and a size small enough that he will not sell in a panic.
wrong: Past returns say little about the next decade. The same path that gave a high return also had the deepest fall.
There is no rule against small caps for him. The question is how much of his money, not whether to own them.
Twenty funds in the same bucket still fall together, because they hold many of the same kind of company.

qs.prompt: What is the minimum a large cap fund must hold in large cap stocks?
qs.why: SEBI sets the floor for large cap funds at 80%, and the manager chooses where the other 20% goes.
wrong: Half is too low to call a fund large cap. Half could sit in mid and small companies instead.
65% is the minimum for mid cap and small cap funds in their own bucket. Large cap funds have a higher bar.
The rule is a minimum, not a full requirement. A large cap fund may hold up to 20% outside the large cap bucket.

qs.prompt: In the made-up paths, small caps ended with the most money. What else did the small cap path show?
options: It also had the deepest fall, about 48% from a peak
It never fell below its starting value of ₹100 along the way
It fell by less than the large caps in every single year
It grew by exactly the same amount in every single year
qs.why: The path that rose the most also dropped the most. That is why the bucket must match the client's time and nerves.
wrong: The line dips well below earlier peaks, and a fall like that can leave an investor under water for years.
Large caps fell about 8% at worst here. Small caps swung much more, in both directions.
Growth was uneven, with big jumps and big drops. Smooth growth is not what smaller companies deliver.

title: Flexi cap, multi cap and focused funds
concept: A multi cap fund must keep at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps. The manager chooses the rest.
A flexi cap fund can invest in any mix of market caps with no minimum for each, so the manager has the most freedom.
A focused fund holds at most 30 stocks. High conviction means that one wrong stock hurts more.
Flexi cap suits a client who wants one core equity fund and trusts the manager to shift between segments.
Check what the fund actually holds. The label sets the range, the factsheet shows the real mix.

client.quote: "I want just one equity fund. Which type?"
client.context: Client with a single-fund mindset.

talk: "A flexi cap is a reasonable one-fund core because the manager can move between large, mid and small caps. We'll check what it really holds every year, and I'll tell you if it drifts from your risk comfort."

qs.prompt: A multi cap fund must hold at least how much in each of large, mid and small caps?
qs.why: SEBI requires a minimum 25% in each segment.

qs.prompt: A focused fund holds at most:
qs.why: SEBI caps focused funds at 30 stocks.

qs.prompt: The main risk of a focused fund is:
options: It must be sold in a year
Each stock has a larger effect on returns
qs.why: With few stocks, one bad pick moves the whole fund.

qs.prompt: What must a multi cap fund hold at the minimum?
options: At least 25% each in large, mid and small caps
At least 80% in large caps and the rest in mid caps
qs.why: Three buckets at 25% each adds up to 75%. The remaining 25% is left to the manager's choice.
wrong: The 80% large cap floor belongs to a large cap fund. A multi cap fund must spread across all three buckets.
The 65% small cap floor belongs to a small cap fund. A multi cap fund cannot be all small caps.
No such floor exists for mid caps in a multi cap fund. The rule sets a floor for each of the three buckets.

qs.prompt: A client wants one equity fund for her core money and is comfortable trusting the manager. What is a reasonable choice?
options: A sectoral fund, since one sector is simple to follow
A flexi cap fund, with a yearly check of what it actually holds
A focused fund of 10 stocks, since fewer stocks means less risk
A small cap fund, because it can grow the fastest
qs.why: A manager who can move across all caps suits a one-fund core, and the yearly check catches drift from her comfort.
wrong: A sector fund holds one corner of the market. It can fall hard for years when that corner is out of favour.
Fewer stocks means each one matters more. A mistake in one name can hurt the whole fund.
Small caps have deep falls. As a single fund it carries more risk than a one-fund core should.

qs.prompt: Which statement about a focused fund is correct?
options: It holds at most 30 stocks, so one wrong stock hurts more
It must hold at least 30 stocks, which makes it safer
It invests only in large caps, with no mid caps
It can hold any number of stocks, like a flexi cap fund
qs.why: The limit is a maximum. With few stocks, the weight of each one is larger and a single failure shows in the NAV.
wrong: The number is a ceiling, not a floor. A focused fund with a high floor would not be focused at all.
A focused fund can hold stocks from any bucket. The rule limits the count, not the size of the companies.
The cap of 30 is what makes the fund focused. A flexi cap fund has no such limit on the number of stocks.

qs.prompt: The fund's name says flexi cap. Where do you check how much of it is in small caps today?
options: The fund's name, since it states the exact mix of the fund
The factsheet, which shows the real mix by market cap
The NAV chart, which shows the mix by the colour of its line
The exit load table in the offer document of the scheme
qs.why: The factsheet lists the real mix by market cap, and the portfolio shows each stock. It is the place to look.
wrong: A name sets the range the fund may use. Two flexi cap funds can hold quite different mixes inside it.
A NAV chart shows price over time only. It carries no information about what the fund holds.
The exit load says what you pay to leave early. It tells you nothing about the stocks inside.

title: ELSS: the tax-saving equity fund
concept: An ELSS (equity linked savings scheme) is an equity fund with a three-year lock-in. It qualifies for the section 80C deduction under the old tax regime.
The lock-in is the shortest among 80C options. Each SIP instalment is locked for three years from its own date.
ELSS must invest at least 80% in equity, so it carries full equity risk. The tax benefit does not reduce market risk.
Under the new tax regime, 80C is not available. For such clients ELSS is just an equity fund with a lock-in.
Pick ELSS for the fund quality, not only the tax. Staying invested after the lock-in is usually the better choice.

client.quote: "I need to save tax before March. Which ELSS should I buy?"
client.context: Client rushing at year-end.

talk: "First, are you on the old regime? If yes, ELSS can help with 80C. Pick it for the fund, not just the deduction, and consider an SIP across the year instead of one lump sum in March."

qs.prompt: The lock-in period of an ELSS is:
qs.why: ELSS has a three-year lock-in, counted for each purchase.

qs.prompt: Does the ELSS deduction work under the new tax regime?
qs.why: 80C deductions are an old-regime benefit.

qs.prompt: An ELSS SIP of 12 monthly instalments has:
options: One lock-in from the first date
A lock-in only on the last instalment
Each instalment locked for 3 years from its date
qs.why: Every instalment has its own three-year lock-in.

qs.prompt: Rohan begins an ELSS SIP of ₹5,000 a month. In which month does his first instalment become open to redeem?
options: Month 12, when his first year ends
Month 24, after two years of instalments
Month 37, and then one more frees up each month
Month 48, when all twelve instalments unlock together
qs.why: Each instalment completes its own three years, so the first frees up in month 37 and the rest follow month by month.
wrong: A year is too early. The lock is three years for each instalment, counted from the date it was invested.
Two years leaves one more year of lock on the first instalment. The rule is three years from each date.
Not all twelve unlock together. They were invested on different dates, so they unlock on different dates.

qs.prompt: A client on the new tax regime asks for an ELSS to save tax. What is true?
options: Without 80C, ELSS is only an equity fund with a lock-in attached
ELSS still gives the full 80C deduction under either of the tax regimes
ELSS can only be bought by people who pay no income tax at all
The lock-in disappears for anyone who chooses the new tax regime
qs.why: Without the deduction, the only difference from other equity funds is the lock-in, so the choice should rest on fund quality.
wrong: The 80C deduction belongs to the old regime. Under the new one, it is not available for any investment.
ELSS can be bought by anyone. Its tax benefit applies only where the old regime and 80C apply.
The lock-in is a feature of the scheme, not of the tax regime. It stays for three years from each instalment.

qs.prompt: A buyer says ELSS must be safe because it saves tax. How do you reply?
options: It is safe, because the government stands behind the scheme
It holds at least 80% in equity, so the market risk is the same
The lock-in makes it safe, because you cannot sell in a panic
It becomes safe once the three years of lock-in are over
qs.why: An ELSS must keep at least 80% in equity. The tax benefit does not reduce what the market can do to the NAV.
wrong: No government backing exists for a mutual fund. The tax deduction is an incentive, not a guarantee.
A lock-in stops selling. It does not stop the NAV from falling, and a fall can still show on the statement.
The NAV can fall after three years just as before. The end of the lock only means you may sell.

qs.prompt: Which is the better way to buy an ELSS for the year?
options: One lump sum in the last week of March
A SIP across the year, picking the fund for its quality
Whatever fund the bank agent mentions first
Two funds, bought on the last day, to double the deduction
qs.why: A SIP spreads the entry across the year, and choosing the fund for quality means the lock-in is not a trap.
wrong: A single March purchase puts all the money in at one price, and it is often chosen in a hurry.
The first name offered is not a measure of quality. The fund is held for years, so it deserves a proper look.
The deduction has a cap, so a second fund does not double it. It only adds another holding.

title: Sectoral and thematic funds: narrow bets
concept: A sectoral fund invests at least 80% in one sector, such as banking or pharma. A thematic fund follows a wider idea, such as consumption or manufacturing.
Both are concentrated. When the theme is in favour, returns can be big. When it is out of favour, falls are deep and long.
They are usually satellite holdings, not the core of a portfolio.
Beware of buying a theme after it has already run. NFOs often arrive near the top of a theme.
Size them small, and agree beforehand when you will review or exit.

client.quote: "Defence stocks are flying. Put half my money there."
client.context: Client chasing a hot theme.

talk: "The story is real, but so is the risk of buying after a big run. Let's keep it to a small slice of the portfolio and agree when we'll review it."

qs.prompt: A sectoral fund must hold at least what share in its sector?
qs.why: Sectoral funds invest a minimum of 80% in their chosen sector.

qs.prompt: Sectoral and thematic funds are usually best as:
qs.why: Their concentration makes them unsuitable as a sole core holding.

qs.prompt: The danger of buying a theme after a big rally is:
options: You may buy near a peak and face a long fall
qs.why: Strong past performance often reflects prices already high.

qs.prompt: What must a sectoral fund hold at the minimum in its own sector?
qs.why: A sectoral fund puts at least 80% in one sector such as banking or pharma, which is why it is so concentrated.
wrong: 65% is the floor for several style funds. A sectoral fund has to be more narrowly focused than that.
Half is too low for a fund that carries a sector label. Half would leave room to hold many other sectors.
95% is not the rule. The floor is lower, with a small part left for cash and other needs.

qs.prompt: Defence stocks are up sharply, and a client wants half his money in a defence fund. What do you suggest?
options: Agree, since the trend is strong and may well continue for years
A small slice, with a date to review it, kept outside his core
Put the whole amount into the new NFO, which gives a fresh start
Avoid equity altogether until the defence theme has cooled down
qs.why: A small slice captures some of the story, and the review date agrees in advance when to hold or exit.
wrong: Buying half after a big run puts a lot of money at a high price. A bad theme year could set him back for years.
An NFO has no history, and themes often launch after a strong run. A new fund is not safer for being new.
Avoiding equity would swap one extreme for another. His core can stay invested in a diversified fund.

qs.prompt: In the made-up paths, the sector fund climbed to ₹250 and fell to ₹135. What fall is that from the peak?
qs.why: From ₹250 to ₹135 is a drop of ₹115, which is 46% of the peak. Falls are measured from the top.
wrong: 13.5% would be a fall to ₹216. The path fell much further than that from its peak of ₹250.
35% would leave the fund near ₹162. The actual low of ₹135 is a deeper fall.
54% is how much of the peak was left, not how much was lost. The loss is the other part.

qs.prompt: Why be careful with a thematic NFO launched after a big run?
options: NFOs are banned after strong markets
Themes often launch near their top, so buyers can pay a high price
The fund house charges no fee on NFOs, so there is little to gain
Thematic funds cannot hold large companies
qs.why: Fund houses launch what is popular, and popularity peaks after a run. New buyers can arrive just before a fall.
wrong: No such ban exists. The caution is about timing and price, not a rule.
Fees are charged on NFOs like any fund. A new fund has no track record to judge.
Thematic funds can hold large companies. The concern is concentration in a single idea.

title: Value, contra and dividend yield: style funds
concept: A value fund buys stocks that look cheap compared with earnings or assets. A contra fund bets against the crowd on out-of-favour stocks.
Each of these must hold at least 65% in equity. A fund can follow value or contra, but not both labels.
Value can lag for years when growth stocks lead, then catch up. Patience is the price of the style.
A dividend yield fund holds high-dividend stocks. The dividend does not make it less risky.
A client who needs steady results every year may be unhappy with a style that goes in and out of favour.

client.quote: "The value fund has trailed the market for three years. Should I sell?"
client.context: Client losing patience with a style.

talk: "Value styles do go through long dry spells, and that is exactly when most people leave. Let's check whether the fund is doing what it promised, not whether it is winning this year."
remember: Dividend yield is not low risk.

qs.prompt: A value fund tends to buy:
options: Stocks that look cheap against fundamentals
qs.why: Value investing targets stocks priced low compared with earnings or assets.
