qs.prompt: A style fund that trails for three years should be judged on:
options: Whether it follows its stated style and process
qs.why: Judge the fund on its approach and long-term record, not one stretch.

qs.prompt: A dividend yield fund is:
options: Still an equity fund with market risk
qs.why: High-dividend stocks can still fall.

qs.prompt: A value fund has trailed the market for three years. Which step is most sensible?
options: Sell now, since three years of lag proves the style is broken
Check if it still does what it promised, not if it is winning
Switch to last year's top fund so that the lag ends right away
Add more money each time the lag grows, with no review at all
qs.why: The test is behaviour against promise: does it still buy cheap stocks and hold them with discipline? Yearly rank is a poor guide.
wrong: Value styles go through long dry spells. Three years of lag alone does not prove that the fund has stopped doing its job.
Last year's top fund is often a growth fund at its peak. Chasing it replaces patience with a timing bet.
Adding without a review treats the lag as a signal to buy. Skipping the check can hide a real problem.

qs.prompt: How many of the labels 'value' and 'contra' can one fund use?
options: Both, since value and contra are really the same style
Only one of the two, and each needs at least 65% in equity
Neither, since SEBI has banned both labels for all funds
As many labels as the fund house likes to put on it
qs.why: A fund can follow value or contra, but not both labels, and each must hold at least 65% in equity.
wrong: They are different styles. Value looks for cheap stocks, contra bets against the crowd on stocks out of favour.
The labels are allowed. SEBI uses them as separate categories with their own rules.
The labels are limited by SEBI's category rules, so a fund house cannot mix and match them.

qs.prompt: A client believes a dividend yield fund must be safer because it pays dividends. What is the honest answer?
options: It is safer, because dividends keep coming in when prices fall
The dividend does not make it less risky, and the NAV can still fall
It is guaranteed to pay a fixed income to investors every year
It is exactly as safe as a bank fixed deposit of the same size
qs.why: The fund holds equity, so the market can hurt the NAV. A payout from stocks is not a shield against that.
wrong: Dividends depend on company profits. In a bad year they can be cut, and prices can drop at the same time.
No guarantee exists for a mutual fund's income. Dividends vary from year to year.
A fixed deposit has a promised rate from a bank. A dividend yield fund has neither a promised rate nor that safety.

qs.prompt: Which client is likely to be unhappy with a value style?
options: One who needs steady results every single year
One with fifteen years to invest and no need for the money
One who can sit through a dry spell of several years
One who looks at the fund only once a year
qs.why: The style goes in and out of favour, so a year-to-year steady result is exactly what it cannot offer.
wrong: Fifteen years is long enough to ride through several dry spells, which suits the style well.
Patience is what the style asks for. A client who can wait is a good match.
Looking once a year fits a style that takes years to pay off, and it limits the urge to react.

title: Choosing an equity fund: a simple, honest method
concept: Start with the goal and horizon, then pick the category. Only then compare funds.
Compare funds in the same category over several rolling periods, not a single calendar year.
Look at consistency, downside in bad years, portfolio concentration, and cost, not just the headline return.
Check the fund's age, the manager's tenure and the fund size. Very large size can hurt mid and small cap funds.
Hold a small number of funds. Many overlapping funds add paperwork, not diversification.

client.quote: "Here are 12 funds my colleague suggested. Can I buy all of them?"
client.context: Client over-diversifying.

talk: "Twelve funds will likely hold many of the same stocks. Let's pick a few that do different jobs, and check overlap before buying."

qs.prompt: What should you decide first when picking an equity fund?
qs.why: Goal and horizon decide the category and the risk.

qs.prompt: Why check overlap between funds?
options: Funds may hold the same stocks, so diversification is less than it looks
qs.why: Overlap shows how much of the portfolio is duplicated.

qs.prompt: A better way to read fund performance than a single year is:
options: Rolling returns across many start dates
qs.why: Rolling returns show how consistent a fund has been through cycles.

qs.prompt: A friend suggests twelve equity funds. What is the best response?
options: Buy all twelve, since more funds always means more spread
Check the overlap, then pick a few that do different jobs
Buy the six with the highest returns of the last year
Buy one fund from each fund house, to keep it fair
qs.why: Overlap shows how many stocks repeat. A few funds with different jobs add real spread and are simple to follow.
wrong: More names rarely mean more spread. If the funds hold the same stocks, a fall hits all of them together.
Last year's winners are often at their peak. A one-year return says little about the next decade.
Fund houses are not a measure of spread. Two funds from different houses can hold the same stocks.

qs.prompt: What is the better way to compare two equity funds in the same category?
options: Their return in the last calendar year, taken by itself
Whichever fund house spends more on its advertising
Whichever one has the more famous fund manager running it
Rolling returns over several periods, plus downside and cost
qs.why: Rolling periods show consistency, the bad-year numbers show risk, and cost shows what is kept. Together they paint a fair picture.
wrong: A single year can be a lucky one. It hides how the fund behaved across good and bad markets.
Advertising spend has no link to how a fund performs. It is paid from fees at some level.
A famous name tells you little. Check the manager's tenure and how the fund held up in bad years.

qs.prompt: In the made-up holdings, twelve funds owned only 78 different stocks. What does this suggest?
options: Same-category funds hold many of the same stocks, so extras add little
Every fund that is added brings an almost entirely new set of stocks
Twelve is the ideal number of funds for an investor of any kind
Overlap of holdings is a problem seen only in debt mutual funds
qs.why: The first few funds add most of the spread. After that, more funds repeat the same companies and cost time.
wrong: The bars show the opposite. The count of new stocks grows slowly because most are already owned.
No ideal number fits everyone. The right number depends on the jobs the funds do, not a count.
Equity funds overlap often, especially in the same category where managers look at the same large companies.

qs.prompt: Why can a very large size hurt a mid or small cap fund?
options: A larger fund must pay a higher rate of tax on the gains it makes
Large funds are not allowed to hold any small company stocks at all
Large positions in thinly traded stocks move the price as they trade
The fund house is forced to close down any scheme once it gets big
qs.why: Mid and small stocks trade in smaller volumes. A big fund buying or selling can push the price, which raises its costs.
wrong: Tax does not rise with fund size. The concern is about trading, not about a larger tax bill.
Large funds are allowed to hold small stocks. The difficulty is in trading them in volume.
A fund is not closed for being large. Some funds limit new money so that the strategy still works.

title: The hybrid family at a glance
concept: Hybrid funds mix equity and debt, and some also hold gold or other assets. The category tells you the rough mix.
Aggressive hybrid: 65% to 80% equity, the rest debt. Conservative hybrid: 10% to 25% equity, the rest mostly debt.
Balanced advantage (dynamic asset allocation) changes its equity share with market valuations. Equity savings holds equity, arbitrage and debt.
Arbitrage funds hold hedged equity and are taxed like equity funds. They behave like low-risk debt funds with stable returns.
Multi asset funds must hold at least three asset classes, with at least 10% in each.

client.quote: "I want something between FD and equity. What are my options?"
client.context: Cautious investor stepping into markets.

talk: "There are a few middle paths. A conservative hybrid has a little equity, a balanced advantage fund moves its equity share with valuations, and an aggressive hybrid is mostly equity. Let's match one to how much fall you can handle."

qs.prompt: An aggressive hybrid fund holds how much in equity?
qs.why: The category range is 65% to 80% equity.

qs.prompt: A balanced advantage fund:
options: Changes equity exposure with market valuations
qs.why: Dynamic asset allocation shifts equity share through cycles.

qs.prompt: A multi asset fund must hold:
options: At least 10% in each of three or more asset classes
qs.why: SEBI requires three asset classes with a minimum of 10% each.

qs.prompt: A factsheet shows a fund with 50% in equity, 30% in debt and 20% in gold. Meena asks which category it is and why it is not an aggressive hybrid. What is the right answer?
options: Balanced advantage, since a fund with equity near half is always called dynamic
Conservative hybrid, since debt and gold together form a large share
Multi asset, since it holds three asset classes with at least 10% in each
Aggressive hybrid, since it holds more than one asset class together
qs.why: Three classes, each at 10% or more, is the multi asset test. Aggressive needs 65% to 80% equity, which this lacks.
wrong: Balanced advantage is defined by a model that moves equity with valuations, not by sitting near half equity.
Conservative hybrid keeps equity at only 10% to 25%. Here equity is 50%, so it falls outside that range.
Holding several classes is not enough. An aggressive hybrid needs 65% to 80% in equity, and this fund has 50%.

qs.prompt: Meena says she will panic if ₹1 lakh ever shows less than ₹90,000. In a bad stretch like the film, only one holding keeps her above that line. Which one?
options: Conservative hybrid, which fell only about 3%, to roughly ₹97,000
Aggressive hybrid, whose debt part protects it against any real fall
Equity fund, since it rebounds fastest once the fall is over
Any hybrid, since every hybrid holds some debt to cushion falls
qs.why: A 15% equity share fell only about 3% in the film. ₹1 lakh would show about ₹97,000, inside her limit.
wrong: With 70% in equity the film's aggressive hybrid fell about 19%. ₹1 lakh would show nearly ₹81,000.
The equity fund fell about 28% and left ₹72,000 on paper. A quick rebound does not stop the panic before it.
Hybrids differ widely. A 70% equity hybrid can fall nearly as far as equity, so having some debt is not enough.

qs.prompt: A client says: "A hybrid gives FD-like safety with equity-like growth, so I will put my emergency money in it." What is the honest reply?
options: Hybrids are safe, as the debt part is guaranteed by the fund house
Only aggressive hybrids fall, so a conservative one is as safe as an FD
Hybrids never fall by more than 10% because of the rules set by SEBI
A hybrid can fall, and how far depends on how much equity it holds
qs.why: It admits a hybrid can fall and ties the size of the fall to the equity share, which is the useful guide.
wrong: No guarantee exists. Debt can fall in value when rates rise and can default, so the debt part carries risk too.
A conservative hybrid falls less, but still holds equity and risky debt. It is not an FD and can show a loss.
No rule caps a fall at 10%. Category rules set the equity range, not the loss a fund may suffer.

qs.prompt: Rohan sees two funds both named "Balanced" and assumes they hold the same mix. Which check tells him what each really holds?
options: The fund house, since one house runs all its funds the same way
The category and the actual equity share on each factsheet
The last one-year return, since it reveals the equity share
The size of each fund, since bigger funds hold more equity
qs.why: The category sets the allowed range and the factsheet shows the live mix. A name alone proves nothing.
wrong: One house runs many funds with different mandates. The house name does not fix a fund's equity share.
A one-year return reflects the market that year. It does not reveal what the fund actually holds.
Fund size says how much money is in the fund, not how it is split between equity and debt.

title: How arbitrage funds work
concept: The fund buys a stock in the cash market and sells the same stock in the futures market at a higher price. The gap between them is locked in as profit.
Because the position is hedged, the fund barely moves with the stock market. Returns track short-term interest rates.
At least 65% is in equity-related instruments, so the fund is taxed as an equity fund. This is the main attraction for investors in high tax slabs.
Returns can dip when the futures premium narrows, such as when markets are weak and there is less demand for leverage.
It is a short-term parking option, not a growth engine.

client.quote: "Can I park ₹20 lakh for a year in something safer than equity but better taxed than an FD?"
client.context: High-bracket client with idle cash.

talk: "An arbitrage fund can fit. It's hedged, so it moves little with markets, and it is taxed as equity. Returns stay near short-term rates, so expect FD-like numbers, not equity growth."

qs.prompt: An arbitrage fund earns by:
options: Capturing the gap between cash and futures prices
qs.why: It buys in cash and sells futures to lock in the spread.

qs.prompt: Arbitrage funds are taxed as:
qs.why: They hold at least 65% in equity-related instruments, so equity tax rules apply.

qs.prompt: What do arbitrage fund returns usually resemble?
qs.why: The hedged spread tends to track short-term rates.

qs.prompt: An arbitrage fund buys a share at ₹1,000 and sells its futures at ₹1,005. By month end the share has fallen to ₹950 and the futures price has merged with it. What does the fund make on this share?
options: ₹50 loss, as the share price fell and the fund owns that share
₹5 gain, as a ₹50 share loss is met by a ₹55 futures gain
₹55 gain, as the futures sale made money while the share fell
Nothing, because a hedged position never earns or loses a rupee
qs.why: The share loses ₹50, the futures sale gains ₹55, and the locked gap of ₹5 remains.
wrong: The hedge matters. The ₹50 fall on the share is offset by a profit on the futures sale it sold.
The ₹55 futures gain is real, but the ₹50 share loss cancels most of it, leaving only ₹5.
The gap between the two prices is the profit, so a hedged position still earns that small sum.

qs.prompt: Rohan is in the 30% slab and will redeem after 12 months. Which reply to his ₹20 lakh question is honest?
options: It will certainly beat an FD, since equity tax is always lower
It is exempt from tax, since equity funds are taxed unlike income
It may leave more after tax than an FD, at similar returns
It will grow like equity over the year, with a hedge as a bonus
qs.why: It claims only what the example shows: a lower tax rate helps, while the return stays near short-term rates.
wrong: If the futures premium narrows, the return can fall below an FD's, so a sure win cannot be promised.
Equity taxation is not zero. Short-term gains at 12 months or less are taxed at 20% plus cess in the example.
A hedged fund does not chase equity growth. Its return follows short-term rates, so this promise is wrong.

qs.prompt: In a weak market, an arbitrage fund's returns slip from about 7% to about 5.5% a year. No stock it holds has crashed. What explains the dip?
options: The hedge has failed, so the fund is now losing on its stocks
The fund has moved most of its money into small caps for returns
Rates always rise when equity falls, which cuts the fund's income
Cash and futures prices drew closer, so less gap is locked in
qs.why: The fund earns the gap between cash and futures prices. In weak markets demand for leverage falls and the gap shrinks.
wrong: A hedge that has failed would cause sharp losses, not a slow slide. This fund just earns a thinner gap.
Arbitrage funds stay hedged and do not shift into small caps. Their earnings come from the price gap.
Rates and equity markets do not move in lockstep. The dip here comes from the shrinking futures premium.

qs.prompt: A client wants to put money in an arbitrage fund for ten years, because it is taxed as equity. What should the adviser say?
options: It is ideal, since equity taxation also brings equity-like returns
It suits parking cash, but a ten-year goal needs a growth fund
It works, as the futures gap grows larger each year it is held
It works only if she invests by SIP and never redeems early
qs.why: Returns track short-term rates, so over ten years it will trail the growth a long-term goal needs.
wrong: Equity tax treatment is about tax rules, not returns. The fund still earns near short-term rates.
The gap between cash and futures is small and does not compound upward the longer the fund is held.
A SIP changes how money goes in, not what the fund earns. The return stays near short-term rates.

title: Balanced advantage funds: how the dial turns
concept: A balanced advantage fund moves its net equity between low and high levels. When markets look expensive it reduces equity, and when they look cheap it increases it.
It uses a model, often based on valuations such as price to earnings or price to book, to set the equity level.
Hedging with futures keeps the tax status equity-like while the net equity level changes.
It can reduce the pain in a fall, but it can also lag in a strong rally because it holds back at high valuations.
Compare funds by their model, how often it changes, and how it behaved in 2020 and other stress periods.

client.quote: "Does this fund protect me when markets fall?"
client.context: Client wants downside protection.

talk: "It tries to reduce risk when valuations are high, so falls are often smaller than in a pure equity fund. It doesn't remove losses, and in strong rallies it can trail."

qs.prompt: A balanced advantage fund lowers equity when:
qs.why: Models reduce equity as markets get pricey.

qs.prompt: A downside of a balanced advantage fund is:
options: It can trail in strong rallies
qs.why: Holding back at high valuations can mean missing part of a rally.

qs.prompt: To compare balanced advantage funds, look at:
options: The model and its behaviour in past falls
qs.why: The allocation model drives outcomes. Check its record in stress periods.

qs.prompt: The market's price to earnings ratio rises from 20 to 28, and a balanced advantage fund's model cuts net equity from 50% to 30%. What is the likely effect on a client over the next two years?
options: Larger falls if prices drop, since cutting equity locks in a return
No change either way, since the tax status keeps its return fixed
Smaller falls if prices drop, but a lag if the rally continues
Higher returns in a rally, since selling equity high adds gains
qs.why: With less equity, a fall hurts less. If prices keep rising, the lower equity share earns less than a full equity fund.
wrong: Cutting equity lowers exposure to a fall. Nothing about the move locks in a fixed return for the fund.
Tax status does not fix returns. The equity share changed, so the fund's ups and downs change with it.
Selling early can miss further gains. In a rally that keeps going, the fund with less equity trails.

qs.prompt: In the made-up decade, the dial fund fell about 8% in year 3 but gained only about 18% in each of the two big rally years, while equity gained 28% and 35%. A client says the fund is the weaker one. What is the best reply?
options: Agree, since lagging in a rally shows the model has totally failed
It lagged only because the fund charges more when markets rise
Ignore the rally years, since only the worst year counts
Its job is a smoother ride, so judge it across the whole cycle
qs.why: Holding back at high prices is the design. The cost shows in the rally and the benefit shows in the fall.
wrong: Lagging in a rally is expected for this type, so one rally year is not proof of a broken model.
A fund's expense ratio is a fixed yearly percentage. It does not rise with the market.
Both the fall and the rally years matter. Choosing only one year would give a false picture.

qs.prompt: Rohan is choosing between two balanced advantage funds. Which comparison is most useful?
options: Each fund's last one-year return, since it shows the better model
Each model, how often it shifts equity, and its 2020 record
The fund house's brand, since big houses build better models
The number of units in each fund, since more units show more skill
qs.why: The model and its record in a hard year show how the fund tries to protect. That is what the category promises.
wrong: A one-year return reflects one market's mood. It says little about whether the model works through a cycle.
A big name does not show how a model reads valuations. Two funds in one house can differ.
The number of units reflects a fund's unit price and size, not the skill of its model.

qs.prompt: A balanced advantage fund cuts its net equity to 30% by selling futures against the shares it holds. A client asks if it will now be taxed like a debt fund. What is correct?
options: Yes, the net equity of 30% is below 35%, so slab-rate tax applies
It depends on the client's slab, which fixes the fund's tax status
Hedging keeps gross equity high, so it stays equity-like for tax
It becomes tax-exempt, since hedged equity does not count as equity
qs.why: Futures hedges cut the net level while shares stay held, so the fund can keep its equity-style tax status.
wrong: The equity share used for tax counts the shares held, not the net level after futures hedges.
A fund's tax category depends on what it holds. The client's slab changes the rate, not the category.
Hedged equity is still equity-related and does not give the fund a tax exemption.

title: Equity savings and conservative hybrids
concept: An equity savings fund holds equity, arbitrage and debt. Net equity is usually in a modest range, and the fund is taxed as an equity fund if 65% is in equity and arbitrage together.
A conservative hybrid holds mostly debt with a small slice of equity. Its gains are generally taxed at slab rate, like a debt fund.
These suit people who want a bit of equity upside with lower swings, such as retirees or first-time investors.
The debt part carries credit and interest rate risk. Check its quality.
Returns will be modest. Expect steady, not spectacular.

client.quote: "My father is 70 and wants better than an FD but cannot take big falls."
client.context: Retiree seeking gentle growth.

talk: "A conservative hybrid or equity savings fund could suit. They hold some equity for growth with a larger debt or arbitrage base. Expect moderate returns and small falls, not zero."

qs.prompt: An equity savings fund holds:
qs.why: It blends the three to dampen swings.

qs.prompt: A conservative hybrid is mainly:
options: Equity with a small debt portion
Debt with a small equity portion
qs.why: The category keeps 10% to 25% in equity.

qs.prompt: Who might suit a conservative hybrid?
options: A retiree wanting modest growth with small falls
qs.why: Lower volatility fits those who dislike big falls.

qs.prompt: Rohan's father says he would be upset if ₹10 lakh ever showed below ₹9 lakh. In the film's bad year, which holding stays above that line?
options: An aggressive hybrid with 70% equity, at about ₹7.9 lakh
A conservative hybrid with 15% equity, at about ₹9.5 lakh
An equity fund with every rupee in shares, at about ₹7 lakh
Every hybrid does, since all hold some debt to cushion falls
qs.why: A 15% equity share loses about 5.4% in that year, so ₹10 lakh falls to about ₹9.5 lakh.
wrong: With 70% in equity, a 30% fall costs about 21%, leaving nearly ₹7.9 lakh, well below the line.
A full equity fund loses 30%, leaving ₹7 lakh. Calm funds exist because this fall is hard for some people.
Hybrids differ in equity share. A 70% equity hybrid still falls hard, so having some debt is not enough.

qs.prompt: An equity savings fund holds 25% in equity, 42% in arbitrage and 33% in debt. The client assumes it is taxed like a debt fund because equity is only 25%. What is right?
options: He is right, since the debt and equity shares fix the tax rate
Tax depends only on unhedged equity, which is 25% here
The investor chooses the tax status when buying the units
Equity plus arbitrage is 67%, so it gets equity-fund taxation
qs.why: The 65% line counts equity and arbitrage together, and 25% plus 42% is 67%, so equity taxation applies.
wrong: It looks right at first, but arbitrage is hedged equity and counts toward the 65% line, so the claim fails.
The test is equity and arbitrage together, not unhedged equity alone, so the 25% figure is the wrong base.
Tax status follows what the fund holds. The investor cannot choose it, whatever the plan or option.

qs.prompt: A conservative hybrid holds only 15% in equity, yet it fell more than expected after a bond in its debt portfolio was marked down. What did the buyer miss?
options: The equity part was too small, so the fund could not recover
Conservative hybrids hold only government bonds, which cannot fall
The debt part has credit and rate risk, so check its quality
Funds with little equity cannot be hurt by anything but equity
qs.why: A debt part can fall on a rate rise or a poor-quality bond. Checking its credit quality is part of choosing.
wrong: A bigger equity share would have added risk. The fall came from the debt portfolio, not from too little equity.
Conservative hybrids may hold corporate bonds, and even government bonds change in price with rates.
The debt part can lose value too. Calling the fund equity-only for risk purposes is a mistake.

qs.prompt: The father's conservative hybrid gained 14% in a strong year. He now expects 14% every year. What should Rohan tell him?
options: That was a strong equity year, so expect steady, modest gains
Expect 14% a year, since most of the fund sits in stable debt
Expect more than 14%, since a good year lifts the next year too
Expect exactly the same as an FD, since the fund is mostly debt
qs.why: The equity kicker helped that year. In a typical year the debt base sets a steadier, more modest return.
wrong: Debt does not guarantee 14%. This year's return came from a strong equity run, which will not repeat on demand.
A good year does not lift the next one. Returns do not carry forward from year to year.
A conservative hybrid still holds some equity and may fall or rise differently from an FD, so it is not the same.

title: Taxing hybrids: the 65% line
concept: A fund with at least 65% in equity-related instruments is taxed as an equity fund. Gains over one year are long-term.
Equity LTCG over the annual exemption is taxed at 12.5%, and short-term gains at 20% (confirm current rates with a tax advisor).

Funds with 35% to 65% in equity sit in between: gains held over 24 months are long-term at 12.5%, otherwise slab rate. Funds with mostly debt (equity below 35%) are generally taxed at slab rate whatever the holding period.
Arbitrage and equity savings funds use the 65% line, which is why they exist in their tax-efficient form.
Always check the fund's tax status, not just its name.

client.quote: "Will I pay tax like an FD on this hybrid fund?"
client.context: Client asking about tax.

talk: "It depends on the equity share. At 65% or more, it's taxed like an equity fund. Below that, the rules differ and many such funds are taxed at your slab rate. Please confirm with your CA for your own situation."
remember: Check the fund, not the name.

qs.prompt: A hybrid fund is taxed as equity when equity-related holdings are at least:
qs.why: The 65% threshold decides equity treatment.

qs.prompt: A hybrid fund with only 20% in equity and the rest in debt is generally taxed:
options: At slab rate on gains, whatever the holding period
qs.why: With mostly debt holdings, gains are generally taxed at the investor's slab rate. Confirm with a tax advisor.

qs.prompt: To know a fund's tax treatment you should check:
options: Its actual asset mix and category
qs.why: Tax follows holdings, not the name.

qs.prompt: Rohan's fund holds 70% in equity and 30% in debt. He sells after 14 months with a gain of ₹2,00,000. He is in the 30% slab. Ignoring the annual exemption and counting 4% cess on the tax, what is the tax?
options: ₹41,600, a short-term equity gain at 20% plus cess
₹26,000, a long-term equity gain at 12.5% plus cess
₹62,400, a gain taxed at his 30% slab rate plus cess
₹13,000, since only half the gain is taxed after a year
qs.why: 70% is above the 65% line and 14 months is over a year, so 12.5% plus cess on ₹2 lakh is ₹26,000.
wrong: The 20% rate applies only up to a year. He held it for 14 months, so the gain is long-term.
Slab rate applies to funds with less than 65% equity. This one is above the line, so it does not apply.
No rule taxes half the gain. The whole gain is taxed, over the exemption, at the long-term rate.

qs.prompt: Meena holds a fund with 50% in equity and sells after 18 months, with a gain of ₹1,00,000 at the 30% slab. What is the useful point for her?
options: It is already long-term, since it was held over 12 months
It is taxed at 20% as a short-term gain, whatever the time
It is exempt from tax, since only funds above 65% equity pay
It is at slab rate now, but turns long-term at 24 months
qs.why: Between 35% and 65% the long-term line is 24 months. Waiting six more months could cut the tax from ₹31,200 to ₹13,000.
wrong: Twelve months applies to funds with 65% or more in equity. This fund is below that line, so 24 months is needed.
The 20% short-term rate belongs to funds at 65% or more. This fund's short-term gain goes at slab rate.
Gains here are taxable. The 65% line decides which rates apply, not whether tax is due.

qs.prompt: A fund called "Balanced Income" holds 20% in equity. A client assumes it gets equity tax treatment after one year. What is the right correction?
options: The name says balanced, so the middle 24-month rule applies
After one year, any hybrid gets equity rates, whatever it holds
Under 35% in equity, slab rate generally applies at any time
It would be taxed as equity once the client's slab is above 20%
qs.why: Below 35% in equity the fund is generally taxed like a debt fund, and a longer hold does not change that.
wrong: A name is no test. The middle rule applies to funds with 35% to 65% in equity, and this one holds only 20%.
The one-year rule needs 65% or more in equity. A hybrid with 20% in equity does not qualify.
Slab does not change the fund's category. The category comes from the fund's holdings.

qs.prompt: A fund holds 64% in equity and 36% in debt. It is one point under the 65% line. Rohan sells after 13 months. How is the gain taxed?
options: At the long-term equity rate, as it is nearly 65% and over a year
At slab rate: it is in the 35% to 65% band, under 24 months
At the short-term rate of 20%, since 13 months is short for equity
Not at all, since funds under 65% equity are exempt from tax
qs.why: The 65% line is a hard cut. At 64% the 24-month rule applies, so at 13 months the gain is at slab rate.
wrong: A fund close to the line gets no equity rate. It must reach 65%, so a one-point gap changes the tax a lot.
The 20% short-term rate also needs 65% or more in equity. A fund at 64% does not qualify.
No exemption exists for a fund's equity share. The share only decides which tax rules apply.

title: Matching a hybrid to the client
concept: Start with the shortfall the client can handle, then pick the hybrid whose worst falls fit it.
For a first-time investor, a balanced advantage or aggressive hybrid can be an easy entry that reduces regret.
For idle cash with a year or less, arbitrage may fit. For more than three years, plain equity or hybrid funds can suit.
Avoid stacking several hybrids that hold the same assets.
Review once a year and rebalance the whole portfolio, not each fund.

client.quote: "I'm nervous about equity. Where do I begin?"
client.context: First-time investor.

talk: "We'll start with a hybrid that holds some equity but cushions the falls, and add a pure equity fund once you are comfortable. We'll review every year."
remember: Fit the fall, not the return.

qs.prompt: For a nervous first-time investor, a sensible start is:
options: A hybrid with a cushioned equity share
qs.why: Hybrid funds ease people into equity.

qs.prompt: Holding many hybrids with similar assets mainly gives:
qs.why: Similar portfolios duplicate the same exposure.

qs.prompt: How often should a portfolio be reviewed at minimum?
qs.why: An annual review is a sensible minimum.

qs.prompt: Meena can bear about ₹60,000 of fall on ₹5 lakh, and wants as much equity growth as that limit allows. The worst falls in the record are about 5% for a conservative hybrid, 11% for a balanced advantage fund, 22% for an aggressive hybrid and 35% for an equity fund. Which fits?
options: A conservative hybrid, with a worst fall of 5%, or ₹25,000
An aggressive hybrid, with a worst fall of 22%, or ₹1.1 lakh
A balanced advantage fund, worst fall 11%, or ₹55,000
An equity fund, since its high growth will make up for the fall
qs.why: It uses most of her limit: ₹55,000 of fall against ₹60,000 she can bear, so it gives the most growth that fits.
wrong: It fits comfortably, but it leaves growth unused. She asked for as much as her limit allows, which is a larger share.
A ₹1.1 lakh fall is nearly twice what she can bear, so she would likely sell at the bottom.
A 35% fall means ₹1.75 lakh on paper. Growth that comes later does not help a person who sold in the dip.

qs.prompt: Rohan has ₹8 lakh he needs in 10 months for a house deposit. He wants it to earn a little more than a savings account. Which fits best?
options: An aggressive hybrid, since it earns the most of any hybrid
A balanced advantage fund, since it cuts equity when risk is high
A multi asset fund, since gold and debt protect equity falls
An arbitrage fund, since the money is needed within a year
qs.why: With a deadline under a year, a hedged fund that barely moves with markets fits better than one that holds real equity.
wrong: In ten months a fall may not recover before the money is due, so a fund with 65% to 80% equity is risky here.
It lowers equity at high prices but can still fall by double digits. Ten months is too short to wait for recovery.
It spreads risk, but equity is still part of it. Falls can still occur and cannot be waited out in ten months.

qs.prompt: A client holds three hybrids: two aggressive hybrids and one balanced advantage fund. All three hold many of the same large company shares. What should the adviser suggest?
options: Keep all three, as each fund house runs its own style of investing
Check the overlap, then keep one or two and drop the duplicates
Add a fourth hybrid so that the overlap is spread more widely
Switch all three into one conservative hybrid, to remove all risk
qs.why: Funds that hold the same assets add cost and tracking effort but little extra spread of risk. Merging them keeps it simple.
wrong: Different houses can still hold the same shares. Three funds with the same holdings are one bet, paid for three times.
A fourth hybrid adds another cost and more overlap. The question is whether each fund does something different.
A conservative hybrid still carries equity and debt risk, so risk is not removed. It also changes the plan's mix.

qs.prompt: At the yearly review, Meena sees her aggressive hybrid's equity share has drifted from 72% to 68% inside the fund. She asks if she should sell units to restore it. What is the sound reply?
options: Yes, rebalance each fund every year or its category changes
Yes, sell units whenever the share moves more than one point
No, never review a hybrid, as the manager does everything
The manager handles it. Check the whole portfolio's mix
qs.why: The fund's mix inside its range is the manager's job. Her review looks at the overall split across all funds.
wrong: A fund stays in its category while its share is within the allowed range, here 65% to 80%, and 68% is within it.
One point of drift is normal. Selling on that basis would cost tax and effort with no gain for the plan.
A yearly check of the whole portfolio is still needed. The manager does not know her goals or other holdings.

title: SIP myths and what rupee-cost averaging really does
concept: An SIP invests a fixed amount at regular dates. When the NAV is low you get more units, when it is high you get fewer, so your average cost per unit sits below the average price.
This lowers the stress of timing. It does not guarantee a profit or protect against a long fall.
SIP returns are measured with XIRR, since each instalment has a different holding period.
An SIP works best over long periods, through at least one full market cycle.
Stopping an SIP in a fall is the most common way to lose the benefit.

client.quote: "Markets are down 15%. Should I pause my SIP?"
client.context: Client scared by a fall.

talk: "A fall is when the same amount buys more units. Pausing means you stop buying at lower prices. If your goal is still far away, staying the course is usually the plan."

qs.prompt: In an SIP, a lower NAV means:
options: You get more units for the same amount
qs.why: Fixed money buys more units when prices are low.

qs.prompt: Which measure fits SIP returns best?
qs.why: XIRR accounts for the different dates of each instalment.

qs.prompt: SIPs cannot:
qs.why: No investment method removes market risk.

qs.prompt: Rohan's six instalments of ₹5,000 were made at NAVs of ₹100, 90, 80, 85, 95 and 105. His average cost came to about ₹91.7, below the ₹92.5 average of those NAVs. Why?
options: The fund house gives a small discount on each instalment that you pay on time
Fixed money buys more units when the NAV is low, fewer when high
Units from an SIP are always allotted at the lowest NAV recorded in the month
The high months and the low months cancel out, leaving a lower overall figure
qs.why: Fixed money divided by a low NAV gives more units, so cheap months carry more weight in the average cost.
wrong: No discount exists. Every instalment is allotted at that day's NAV, so the saving cannot come from a price cut.
Allotment follows the NAV of the day the money is accepted. It is never chosen as the month's lowest price.
Months do not cancel out. If they did, the cost would equal the plain average, which is ₹92.5 here.

qs.prompt: After a 15% fall, Rohan's cousin says: stop the SIP now and restart when the market looks safe. What does stopping really do?
options: It protects the units he already holds from any further fall in the market
It cancels the units he already holds at the next NAV the fund declares
It has no effect, since units from an SIP are bought at average prices anyway
It stops him buying at today's lower prices and leaves a restart date to guess
qs.why: Fewer instalments mean fewer units at low NAVs, and the restart date is a timing guess that SIPs exist to avoid.
wrong: Units he holds still move with the NAV. Stopping the SIP only changes what he buys from now on.
Existing units stay in his folio until he redeems them. Pausing an SIP does not cancel anything.
Each instalment is bought at that day's NAV, not at an average, so skipping one means skipping a cheap buy.

qs.prompt: A client's two-year SIP shows a loss. Markets are 13% lower and most of her instalments were bought at higher prices. Which reply is honest?
options: A SIP cannot show a loss, so the statement she received must be a printing mistake
It will certainly recover within six months, so there is nothing to worry about at all
An SIP is a method, so it follows the fund: a paper loss now, with time on her side
SIPs only work in rising markets, so she should move all of it to a fixed deposit now
qs.why: It names the method, admits the paper loss and points to the holding period, which is the part that is true.
wrong: Any fund can show a loss on paper when the NAV is below the average cost. The statement is likely right.
No one can promise a recovery date. A confident promise that fails costs the client's trust.
SIPs also buy through falls. Moving everything away after a drop turns a paper loss into a real one.

qs.prompt: Rohan's SIP has run for three years. Which figure measures his return fairly?
options: XIRR, because each instalment has been invested for a different time
The simple average of all the NAVs he bought at over the three years
Today's NAV minus the NAV of his first instalment, shown as a percentage
The expense ratio of the fund, since it shows what he earned each year
qs.why: XIRR gives each instalment its own start date, so the return reflects how long every rupee was invested.
wrong: A plain average ignores how many units were bought at each NAV and how long each instalment has been held.
His later instalments started at other prices, so one NAV difference misses most of what he bought.
The expense ratio is a yearly cost taken from the fund. It says nothing about his own return.

title: Step-up SIPs: letting investing grow with income
concept: A step-up SIP raises the instalment by a set amount or percentage each year, such as 10%.
Because income usually rises over time, a step-up lets the investment keep pace without effort.
The final corpus can be far larger than a flat SIP, even with a small yearly step.
Set the step to something the client can sustain. A step that is too high can cause missed instalments.
Reviewing the step each year, along with the goal, keeps the plan honest.

client.quote: "I can only invest ₹10,000 now, but my salary will grow."
client.context: Young earner with a rising income.

talk: "Start at ₹10,000 and raise it 10% each year. You'll hardly feel the change, and the corpus at the end can be much larger than a flat SIP."

qs.prompt: A step-up SIP:
options: Raises the instalment on a schedule
qs.why: The instalment increases by a fixed amount or percentage.

qs.prompt: The main benefit of a step-up is:
options: The investment keeps pace with growing income
qs.why: Raising contributions matches rising income.

qs.prompt: A risk of setting a step-up too high is:
options: Missed instalments when cash flow is tight
qs.why: A step you cannot sustain can lead to a stopped SIP.

qs.prompt: Rohan's 10% step-up SIP ends ten years about ₹10 lakh ahead of his flat SIP. What explains most of that gap?
options: Step-up SIPs earn a higher rate of return than flat SIPs in the same fund
It invests about ₹7 lakh more, and the extra goes in as income rises
Banks pay a loyalty bonus when the instalment rises every single year
The fund house waives its expense ratio on the extra stepped-up amount
qs.why: Total invested is ₹19.1 lakh against ₹12 lakh. More money working for longer is where most of the gap comes from.
wrong: Return depends on the fund, not on how the instalment is set. Both SIPs here earn the same assumed rate.
No such bonus exists. Banks only run the mandate, and the instalment size has no effect on any payout.
Expense ratio is charged on the whole fund value either way. There is no waiver for a stepped-up amount.

qs.prompt: A client earns ₹40,000 a month and expects raises of about 6% a year. He asks for a 25% yearly step-up to build wealth faster. What do you say?
options: Agree to 25%, since a bigger step always builds a bigger corpus for him
Suggest a step near his raises, 5 to 8% a year, and review it yearly
Tell him step-ups are only meant for people who earn above ₹1 lakh a month
Suggest a flat SIP instead, because any step-up adds extra risk to the fund
qs.why: A step near his income growth feels light, so he is likely to keep it. The yearly review lets him adjust.
wrong: A step he cannot keep up leads to missed instalments, and a stopped SIP gives a smaller corpus than a modest step.
Step-ups work at any income. What matters is that the step fits the cash he really has to spare.
A step-up changes how much goes in, not what the fund holds. It adds no risk beyond the fund's own.

qs.prompt: Rohan starts at ₹10,000 a month and steps up by 10% each year. What is his monthly instalment in year 4?
qs.why: Each year multiplies by 1.10: ₹11,000, then ₹12,100, then ₹13,310 in year 4. The steps compound.
wrong: ₹13,000 adds ₹1,000 a year to the first amount. A step-up of 10% grows on the latest instalment each time.
₹14,000 treats the step as 10% a year for four full years on the first amount, which counts one year too many.
₹12,100 is the year 3 figure. Year 1 has no step, so year 4 has taken three steps, not two.

qs.prompt: Which risk comes from setting the yearly step too high?
options: Missed instalments when cash is tight, which can stop the SIP
A lower NAV on the units bought later in the year
The fund house cancelling the mandate for being too large
A higher tax rate on the gains from the larger instalments
qs.why: A bounced or skipped instalment breaks the habit, and repeated misses can cancel the SIP, so the corpus falls short.
wrong: NAV follows the market, not the size of the instalment. A larger step does not change the price you pay.
Fund houses accept any amount above the minimum. They do not cancel a mandate for being too large.
Tax depends on how long you hold and the gain made, not on how big each instalment was.

title: Lump sum, SIP or STP: choosing how to enter
concept: A lump sum puts all the money in at once. It does well if markets rise soon after, and badly if they fall.
An SIP spreads new savings over time. It suits regular income.
An STP (systematic transfer plan) moves a lump sum from a safe fund, often liquid or short duration, to an equity fund in instalments.
No method wins every time. The best one is the one the client can stick with.
STP gives a client with a large lump sum comfort. The money waiting in debt keeps earning something.

client.quote: "I got ₹30 lakh from a property sale. Invest it all today?"
client.context: Client with a large lump sum.

talk: "We can park it in a liquid fund and move it into equity over, say, six to twelve months through an STP. You earn something on the waiting money, and you won't regret a single day's entry."
remember: STP: debt to equity in steps.
Best method is the one they follow.

qs.prompt: An STP moves money:
options: From one scheme to another in instalments
From a bank to a stock
qs.why: STP transfers units from a source fund into a target fund over time.

qs.prompt: Who benefits most from an STP?
options: Someone with a large lump sum
qs.why: STP smooths entry for a lump sum.

qs.prompt: The best way to invest is:
options: The one the client can stay with
qs.why: Behaviour matters more than the exact method.

qs.prompt: Meena has ₹30 lakh and is afraid of a fall just after she invests. Which plan fits her fear best?
options: Put all of it into equity today, so that no single day of gains is missed
Hold it in a liquid fund and move it to equity in monthly steps with an STP
Start an SIP for the full ₹30 lakh from her bank account in the first month
Keep it in a savings account until the market looks cheap enough to enter
qs.why: An STP gives her a fixed entry plan, earns something while the money waits, and cuts the regret of a single bad entry day.
wrong: A lump sum is a fair choice for someone who can sit through a fall. Meena has said she cannot, so it is a poor fit.
An SIP is built from regular income. It cannot be used to invest a sum already in hand, because the mandate is a few thousand rupees.
Waiting for a cheap market is a timing guess. The money earns little, and 'cheap' is clear only afterwards.

qs.prompt: A market rise of 15% arrives in the month after Meena starts her 12-month STP. How does she compare with someone who invested the whole ₹30 lakh that day?
options: She earns more, because the STP buys the units at lower prices than the lump sum did
She earns the same, because both of them put the same money in on the same day
She earns less this time, as most of her money was still in the liquid fund
She loses money, because an STP cannot make a gain when the market is rising
qs.why: A rising market rewards money that was already invested. She trades some of that gain for a smoother entry.
wrong: The STP buys at whatever the price is each month. In a market that only rises it buys at higher prices, not lower.
The two do not put the same money in at the same time. Most of her money was still in the liquid fund as the market rose.
She still gains on the part moved over, plus interest on the rest. The STP does not stop gains, it only delays some.

qs.prompt: What is the usual choice for the 'from' fund in an STP?
options: A sector fund with a high-growth theme
A liquid or short-duration debt fund
A fund with a high exit load
qs.why: These funds hold the money steadily and can be redeemed quickly, which suits money that moves out on a schedule.
wrong: A sector fund moves a lot. The waiting money should be calm, otherwise the parking spot is as risky as the destination.
An exit load would take a cut on each monthly transfer. The parking fund should charge little to leave.
Gold can swing in price and does not give the steady, small return that waiting money should earn.

qs.prompt: Which statement about lump sum, SIP and STP is honest?
options: The STP is the best method in every market
A lump sum always beats an SIP because more money works from day one
The best method is the one the investor can follow without panic
An SIP removes the risk that markets fall
qs.why: A plan the investor sticks with beats a better plan that is dropped halfway. Match the method to the person.
wrong: In rising markets the lump sum can win. No method wins every time, so 'always the best' is a false promise.
Lump sums win when markets rise soon and lose when they fall. 'Always' is wrong in both directions.
An SIP spreads out the price you pay, but it does not stop the market from falling or protect against loss.

title: SWP: turning a corpus into an income
concept: A systematic withdrawal plan (SWP) redeems a fixed amount from a fund every month, quarter or year.
Each withdrawal is part gain and part capital, so only the gain portion is taxed.
The fund keeps growing while you withdraw, so a modest rate can last a long time.
A high withdrawal rate in a falling market eats the corpus fast. This is sequence risk.
Keep one to two years of withdrawals in a lower-risk fund so you are never forced to sell equity in a fall.

client.quote: "Can I take ₹50,000 a month from my ₹1 crore corpus?"
client.context: Retiree planning income.

talk: "That's 6% a year. It may work, but if markets fall early it could run down quickly. A safer plan keeps two years of withdrawals in a steady fund and the rest invested for growth."

qs.prompt: In an SWP, what part of each withdrawal is taxed?
qs.why: Each redemption is part capital and part gain.

qs.prompt: Sequence risk means:
options: Early falls while withdrawing can drain the corpus
qs.why: Poor returns early in withdrawal do lasting damage.

qs.prompt: A sensible protection for an SWP is:
options: Holding one to two years of withdrawals in a steadier fund
qs.why: A buffer avoids selling equity at the bottom.

qs.prompt: Dadi's ₹1 crore falls 25% in her first year, and she keeps withdrawing ₹6 lakh a year. Why does this hurt more than the same fall in year 15?
options: An early fall shrinks the pile that all later withdrawals are paid from
Funds charge a higher expense ratio in the early years of a plan
Withdrawals made in year one are taxed more heavily than later ones
The market always recovers faster in the later years of any plan
qs.why: Withdrawals take money out while prices are low, so fewer units are left to recover when the market turns. This is sequence risk.
wrong: Expense ratio is a yearly percentage of the fund's value. It does not depend on which year the withdrawal falls in.
Tax is on the gain portion of each withdrawal. It does not rise because the market fell in the first year.
No one can say later years recover faster. The point is that a fall hurts more when a withdrawal plan is already running.

qs.prompt: Dadi redeems ₹1,00,000 from an equity fund. The units she sold had cost ₹60,000. How is the withdrawal taxed?
options: Nothing is taxed because it is her own money
Only the ₹40,000 gain portion counts as capital gain
Only the ₹60,000 she originally invested is taxed
qs.why: Each SWP payment is part cost and part gain. Only the gain is taxed, at the capital gains rate that applies to her holding period.
wrong: The part that was her own capital is returned to her. Taxing the whole amount would count that capital as profit.
Her capital comes back untaxed, but the gain on it does count. Tax rules apply to the profit in each withdrawal.
The ₹60,000 is her cost and is not taxed. Taxing it would charge her on money she already paid tax on.

qs.prompt: Dadi asks for ₹50,000 a month from ₹1 crore. What is the sound reply?
options: That is only 6% a year, so the money will certainly last as long as she lives
It is 6% a year and may work, but an early fall could drain it, so hold a buffer
Never withdraw more than ₹10,000 a month from any corpus, whatever its size
An SWP only works with a bank fixed deposit and not with a mutual fund
qs.why: It names the rate, admits the risk of an early fall and gives a plan: a buffer and a yearly review.
wrong: 'As long as she lives' is a promise nobody can keep. If returns come in below withdrawals, the corpus shrinks.
There is no universal limit like this. The safe rate depends on the corpus, the mix of funds and the time she needs it.
An SWP is a feature of mutual funds. A bank fixed deposit has its own way of paying interest each month.

qs.prompt: Why keep one to two years of withdrawals in a lower-risk fund?
options: It raises the return earned by the equity part of the whole corpus
So she never has to sell equity after a fall to pay her monthly needs
It removes the tax that would otherwise apply to each withdrawal
It lets her withdraw more each month than the plan would allow
qs.why: In a falling market, bills are paid from the calm fund while equity has time to recover.
wrong: The buffer earns a low return. It supports the plan in a fall, it does not raise what equity earns.
The tax on gains still applies to each redemption, whichever fund it comes from.
The buffer cannot raise a safe rate. A rate that is too high stays too high.

title: Goals first: from time horizon to asset mix
concept: Write down the goal, the amount needed in future rupees, and the date. Inflation raises the target.
Goals under three years usually belong in low-risk funds. Goals over seven years can hold more equity.
The shorter the horizon, the less you can afford a fall near the end. Shift to safer funds as the date nears.
Keep a separate fund or folio for each goal so progress is easy to see.
Review the goal each year. A change in income or cost should change the plan.

client.quote: "I want ₹50 lakh for my daughter's college in 12 years."
client.context: Parent with a clear goal.

talk: "We should adjust ₹50 lakh for inflation first, then work out the monthly amount. Over 12 years you can hold mostly equity for the first part, then move into safer funds over the last three years."

qs.prompt: For a goal two years away, funds are usually chosen from:
qs.why: Short horizons cannot absorb equity falls.

qs.prompt: Why adjust a goal for inflation?
options: Future costs are higher than today's
qs.why: The money needed will be larger in future rupees.

qs.prompt: What should happen to a goal portfolio as the date nears?
qs.why: Protect what has been gained as the date approaches.

qs.prompt: A college costs ₹50 lakh today. With about 6% yearly inflation, roughly what will it cost in 12 years?
qs.why: Each year multiplies by 1.06, and twelve years gives about double. Inflation compounds, just like returns.
wrong: ₹53 lakh is one year of inflation, not twelve. The price rises every year, and each rise builds on the last.
₹86 lakh adds 6% of ₹50 lakh for twelve years, without letting each year's rise build on the one before.
₹62 lakh is far below even the simple sum. Twelve years of rising prices cannot add only a quarter.

qs.prompt: A family needs a car down payment of ₹4 lakh in 18 months. Where does the money belong?
options: Mostly in equity, to chase the highest return available
In a low-risk fund such as a liquid or short-duration fund
In a sector fund, since a short goal needs a quick gain
In gold, since gold keeps rising whenever shares fall
qs.why: A short goal needs the money to be steady and easy to get. Low-risk funds fit that need.
wrong: With 18 months to go, a 20% fall leaves no time to recover, and the car cannot wait for the market.
Sector funds swing a lot and can stay down for years. That is the opposite of what a short goal needs.
Gold can fall too. No asset only rises, so none is safe to bet a short goal on.

qs.prompt: Why does the plan move money from equity to safer funds in the last three years before the goal?
options: Equity stops earning anything in the last three years before a goal
A late fall leaves no time to recover, so what is saved needs protecting
SEBI requires goal-based investments to turn safer as the date nears
Safer funds always earn more than equity near the end of a goal
qs.why: The closer the date, the less time to recover. Moving to safer funds locks in much of what has been built.
wrong: Equity does not stop. The reason is the risk of a fall at the wrong time, not the end of returns.
SEBI has no such rule for an ordinary investor's goal. This is a planning habit, not a regulation.
Safer funds usually earn less. The trade is a lower return for a lower risk of loss when it matters.

qs.prompt: Why keep a separate fund or folio for each goal?
options: Funds held in separate folios earn higher returns than a single folio
Progress on each goal is easy to see, and no goal is raided for another
It lowers the expense ratio that is charged on each separate folio
It lets the investor skip the yearly review of each goal's plan
qs.why: With one pot, it is hard to tell which goal is on track and easy to borrow from the wrong one.
wrong: A folio is only a record. The return depends on the fund, not on how many folios hold it.
Expense ratios are set by the fund and do not change with the number of folios.
Goals change, so each folio still needs a yearly look at income, cost and date.

title: SIP discipline: pauses, bounces and restarts
concept: An SIP is paid through a bank mandate. If the account lacks money on the date, the instalment bounces and the bank may charge a fee.
Three missed instalments in a row can cancel the SIP in many schemes, depending on the rules.
A pause or skip option exists in some schemes. Use it for genuine cash needs, not for market fear.
Pick an SIP date a few days after salary arrives.
Keep an emergency fund so you never have to stop an SIP or redeem equity in a hurry.

client.quote: "My SIP failed twice. Is it cancelled?"
client.context: Client with missed instalments.

talk: "One more failure and many schemes cancel it. Let's move the date to just after your salary and make sure the account has a buffer. We'll restart it today."

qs.prompt: A good SIP date is:
options: The last day of the quarter
A few days after salary arrives
qs.why: Matching cash inflow avoids bounces.

qs.prompt: A bounced SIP instalment means:
options: The bank account lacked funds on the date
qs.why: Insufficient balance causes the mandate to fail.

qs.prompt: An emergency fund helps SIPs by:
qs.why: Cash reserves keep long-term investing intact.

qs.prompt: Rohan's salary credits on the 7th and his SIP debits on the 5th. What is the best fix?
options: Move the SIP date to a few days after salary arrives
Change to a different fund house
Keep the date and top up the account on the 4th each month
Stop the SIP and invest a lump sum each year
qs.why: A debit date shortly after payday matches money to the mandate, and it is a one-time change.
wrong: The fund house is not the problem. The date falls before the money arrives, whichever house it is.
Topping up on the 4th works only if he remembers every month. One slip and it bounces again.
A yearly lump sum gives up the habit and the averaging that made the SIP worth doing.

qs.prompt: Rohan's SIP has bounced twice. He is told 'a third miss in a row may cancel it'. What should he do?
options: Wait to see whether a third instalment also fails before doing anything
Change the date, keep a buffer, and check the mandate is still active
Cancel the SIP himself so that the record on his folio stays clean
Start a second SIP in another fund to make up for the missed ones
qs.why: Moving the date and keeping a cushion fix the cause, and checking the mandate shows nothing has already lapsed.
wrong: Waiting risks the third miss and the loss of the SIP. The fix is available now.
Cancelling ends the habit he wants to keep. Bounces are about timing, not about the SIP being a bad idea.
A second SIP adds a second mandate to bounce, and fixes nothing about the date.

qs.prompt: When is a 'pause' or 'skip' option on an SIP a fair use?
options: When the market falls sharply and he feels nervous about his units
For a genuine cash need, such as a medical bill, with a plan to restart
Whenever he sees an advertisement for a better fund than his own
Whenever the NAV has gone up compared with the month before
qs.why: A real cash need is what the option is for, and a restart date keeps the habit.
wrong: A fall is when the same instalment buys more units. Pausing out of nerves means skipping the cheap months.
Chasing a new fund each month adds cost and timing guesses, and the SIP loses its steady habit.
A higher NAV means fewer units this month, not a reason to stop. Over time, high and low months even out.

qs.prompt: Why does an emergency fund protect an SIP?
options: It pays the fund's own expense ratio each year on his behalf
So a sudden bill does not force him to stop or sell equity in a hurry
It raises the return the SIP earns on every instalment he makes
It cancels the mandate automatically whenever a crisis arrives
qs.why: With six months of cash set aside, a bill never touches the SIP or forces a sale at a bad price.
wrong: The expense ratio is deducted from the fund itself, so an emergency fund has no role in paying it at all.
An emergency fund earns a small return of its own. It does not change what the SIP earns.
A mandate stays active until he cancels it, or repeated misses end it. A cash buffer helps avoid those misses.

title: What passive investing really is
concept: A passive fund copies an index instead of trying to beat it. If the index holds 50 stocks in certain weights, the fund holds the same.
Costs are lower because there is no research team picking stocks.
The fund's return will be close to the index return, minus costs and tracking error.
Passive does not mean safe. An index fund falls when its index falls.
Over long periods, many active funds in efficient segments, such as large caps, have struggled to beat their index after costs.

client.quote: "If index funds are so cheap, why do you sell active funds?"
client.context: Sceptical client.

talk: "Index funds are a great core, especially in large caps. In other areas a good active manager has more room to add value. We can hold both and keep the costs sensible."

qs.prompt: A passive fund aims to:
options: Beat the index by a wide margin
qs.why: Index funds mirror their benchmark.

qs.prompt: Why are index funds cheap?
qs.why: Lower management effort means a lower expense ratio.

qs.prompt: An index fund in a falling market will:
qs.why: Passive funds carry the same market risk as their index.

qs.prompt: Two funds each earn 12% a year before costs. One charges 0.2% and the other 1.5%. Rohan invests ₹10 lakh in each for 20 years. About how much more does the cheaper fund leave?
options: About ₹2.6 lakh, which is 1.3% of ₹10 lakh for 20 years
About ₹19 lakh, since the drag compounds each year
About ₹13,000, which is one year of the cost gap
Almost nothing, as both funds earned 12% before costs
qs.why: At 11.8% the index fund grows to about ₹93 lakh, and at 10.5% the active fund reaches about ₹74 lakh. Gap about ₹19 lakh.
wrong: That adds up simple costs and misses compounding. A lower yearly return also shrinks every later year's base.
The yearly gap is 1.3% of ₹10 lakh, which is ₹13,000 in year one. It keeps growing as the pile grows.
Costs come out of the return. Equal returns before costs do not mean equal returns after them.

qs.prompt: An index returned 14.0% in a year. Meena's index fund on that index returned 13.8%. Where did the 0.2% go?
options: The manager's poor stock picks, which pulled the fund down
The fund holds different shares from the index in a different mix
A fee charged by the stock exchange on each unit she holds
Mostly the fund's expense ratio, plus small tracking effects
qs.why: An index fund's return is the index return minus its costs and a little tracking error.
wrong: An index fund has no stock picking to get wrong. Its shares come from the index list.
If it held different shares it would not be an index fund. It copies the index in the same weights.
The fund's costs are in the expense ratio. Nothing like a per-unit exchange fee is charged to her.

qs.prompt: Rohan says: "If index funds are cheap and active funds lag, why hold any active fund?" Which reply is sound?
options: Index for the core, active where managers have more room
Hold only active funds, as managers add value in every segment
Hold only index funds, since they never fall as active funds do
Index funds suit only beginners; active funds suit experts
qs.why: Passive suits efficient areas like large caps, while active has more room in less crowded segments such as small caps.
wrong: In efficient areas such as large caps many active funds have struggled to beat their index after costs.
An index fund falls whenever its index falls. Cost is lower, but the risk of the market remains.
Skill level does not decide this. The choice is about which segment and what it costs.

qs.prompt: Meena has ₹10 lakh in a Nifty index fund and the Nifty falls 30%. Which sentence fits best?
options: Her fund will fall less, since an index fund holds only top shares
Her fund will stay near ₹10 lakh, since its costs are so low
Her fund will show about ₹7 lakh, since it falls with the index
Her fund will show a loss only if the fund manager makes errors
qs.why: An index fund tracks the index, so about 30% less, minus tiny costs. Passive does not mean safe.
wrong: Holding top shares does not protect a fund. If the index drops 30%, those shares drop with it.
Low cost helps over many years, but it does not shield a fund from a falling market.
There is no manager error to blame. The fund is built to follow the index down as well as up.

title: Index fund or ETF: same idea, different wrapper
concept: An index fund is bought and sold with the AMC at the day's NAV, like any other fund. SIPs work easily.
An ETF trades on the stock exchange all day and needs a demat account. You pay the market price, which can differ slightly from NAV.
ETFs have a small bid-ask spread when you trade, and low liquidity can make it wider.
Index funds suit SIP investors. ETFs suit people who trade with a demat and want intraday prices.
Both can have the same tracking quality. The expense ratio and tracking difference matter more than the wrapper.

client.quote: "Should I buy the Nifty ETF or the Nifty index fund?"
client.context: Client with a demat account.

talk: "For a monthly SIP, the index fund is simpler. If you invest in lump sums through your demat, the ETF can be a bit cheaper, but watch the spread and trade in liquid hours."

qs.prompt: An ETF is bought:
options: Only from the AMC at NAV
On the stock exchange through a demat account
qs.why: ETFs trade on exchanges.

qs.prompt: A cost of trading an ETF is:
qs.why: The gap between buying and selling prices.

qs.prompt: For a small monthly SIP, the easier choice is:
qs.why: Index funds allow auto-debit SIPs.

qs.prompt: Rohan wants a ₹5,000 SIP in a Nifty fund, running for ten years with no monthly effort. He has a demat account. Which is the simpler route?
options: The ETF, since a demat account sets up the monthly buy itself
The index fund, since its SIP debits and buys on its own
The ETF, since it is always cheaper than an index fund
Either one, since both need a manual order each month
qs.why: The fund house runs the SIP and buys units at NAV, so he does nothing after the mandate is set.
wrong: An ETF is bought on the exchange, so he has to place an order each month unless his broker offers a plan.
An ETF may have a lower expense ratio, but the spread and effort can cancel that. It is not always cheaper.
Only the ETF needs a manual order. The index fund is built for a standing monthly instruction.

qs.prompt: Meena buys ₹5,00,000 of an ETF at its ask of ₹250 a unit. The NAV at that moment is ₹249. About how much more did she pay than the NAV value of what she bought?
options: About ₹500, as the gap is about 0.1% of the buy
About ₹5,000, as an ETF buy always costs 1% extra
About ₹2,000: ₹1 more on each of 2,000 units
Nothing extra, since an ETF trades at NAV by rule
qs.why: ₹5,00,000 buys 2,000 units at ₹250. A ₹1 gap above NAV on each unit is ₹2,000, about 0.4%.
wrong: The gap is about 0.4%, not 0.1%. ₹1 on a ₹249 unit is 0.4%, and 0.4% of ₹5 lakh is ₹2,000.
No fixed 1% charge exists. The extra paid is whatever gap there is between price and NAV.
An ETF can trade a little above or below NAV. Here it traded above, and she paid for the gap.

qs.prompt: Rohan will invest a ₹10 lakh lump sum for ten years. The ETF's expense ratio is 0.05% and its spread about 0.05% each time he trades. The index fund's expense ratio is 0.20% with no spread. Ignoring brokerage, which statement is right?
options: The index fund costs less, since it has no spread to pay
They cost the same, since both follow the very same index
The ETF always costs more, since it trades on an exchange
The ETF likely costs less in total, if it stays liquid
qs.why: Over ten years the ETF costs about 0.6% (expenses plus spreads) against 2% for the fund, by simple sums.
wrong: No spread saves only about 0.1%, while the ETF's lower yearly cost saves about 1.5% over ten years.
Same index does not mean same cost. Expense ratio and spread differ, and they add up over years.
Trading adds a spread, but on a liquid ETF it is tiny. The lower yearly cost outweighs it.

qs.prompt: An ETF on the Nifty trades at ₹249.90 while its NAV is ₹250.00 near the close. A client asks if the ETF is broken. What is the sound reply?
options: A small gap is normal in a busy ETF, if it stays small
Yes, since an ETF must trade at exactly its NAV all day
Yes, since the fund house is hiding losses until day end
No, since any gap, even one of 5%, would be normal
qs.why: A gap of about 0.04% is within a normal spread. Thin ETFs can show wider gaps, so size and volume are worth a check.
wrong: No rule forces trading at NAV. Buyers and sellers set the price, and arbitrage keeps it close to the NAV.
NAV is computed from the value of the holdings, so the fund house cannot hide losses in this way.
A 5% gap would be a warning sign for liquidity. A gap of a few paise is the normal kind.

title: Tracking error and tracking difference
concept: Tracking difference is the gap between the fund's return and the index return over a period. It is mostly the expense ratio plus small frictions.
Tracking error is how much that gap wiggles from day to day. A low number means the fund follows its index closely.
A fund with a low expense ratio can still have poor tracking if it is badly managed.
Compare funds on the same index using tracking difference over one to three years.
Cash drag, delays in rebalancing and dividends can add to the gap.

client.quote: "Both funds track the Nifty 50. Why do their returns differ?"
client.context: Client puzzled by two index funds.

talk: "The difference is mostly cost and small tracking effects. Over time, the cheaper and tighter one will usually end up a little ahead."
remember: Error = how jumpy the gap is.

qs.prompt: Tracking difference is:
options: The gap between fund and index return
qs.why: It measures how far the fund's return lags or leads the index.

qs.prompt: A low tracking error means:
options: The fund follows its index closely
qs.why: Small, steady deviations mean close tracking.

qs.prompt: Which usually explains most of a passive fund's tracking difference?
qs.why: The fee is the main drag on tracking the index.

qs.prompt: Over three years the Nifty 50 index gave 40.0%. Meena's two index funds gave 39.4% and 38.1%. Which statement is correct?
options: The second fund has the lower tracking error, as it earned less
Both lag by the same amount, since the index is the same
The first fund lags by about 0.6 points, the second 1.9
The first fund beat the index, since 39.4% is close to 40%
qs.why: Tracking difference is the gap to the index: 40.0 minus 39.4 is 0.6, and 40.0 minus 38.1 is 1.9.
wrong: A lower return does not mean a lower tracking error. Tracking error is about how jumpy the daily gap is.
Their returns differ, so their gaps differ. The same index does not mean the same tracking difference.
Neither fund beat the index. Both gave less than 40%, and an index fund is expected to lag a little.

qs.prompt: Fund X has the lowest expense ratio of all Nifty 50 funds. Yet its daily returns often differ from the index by a visible margin. What does this show?
options: Low cost does not ensure tight tracking, so check error too
A cheap fund must have a low tracking error by definition
The index must be wrong, since the fund is cheap and follows it
Tracking error matters only for ETFs, not for index funds
qs.why: A fund can charge little and still run loosely, with cash drag or late rebalancing. Both numbers are worth a look.
wrong: Cost and tracking are separate. A cheap fund managed carelessly can still show a jumpy gap to its index.
The index is a fixed list with fixed weights. The gap comes from how the fund copies it, not from the index.
Tracking error applies to every fund that copies an index, whether sold as an index fund or an ETF.

qs.prompt: Meena's index fund charges 0.20% a year but trailed its index by 0.45% last year. Where might the other 0.25% come from?
options: A hidden charge the fund house adds on top of the expense ratio
Cash drag, rebalancing delays and the timing of dividends
The manager's wrong calls about which shares to hold in it
SEBI deducts the difference from every index fund each year
qs.why: Small frictions add to the gap: cash waiting to be invested, delays after index changes, and dividend timing.
wrong: The expense ratio is disclosed and capped by rules. The extra gap comes from how the fund copies the index.
An index fund does not choose shares, so no calls were made. It follows the index list.
No regulator deducts from index funds. Normal frictions in copying explain the gap.

qs.prompt: Two funds follow the same index. Fund P has expense 0.30% and tracking difference 0.35%. Fund Q has expense 0.15% and tracking difference 0.40%. Which would an informed adviser prefer?
options: Fund Q, since its expense ratio is lower and that is what counts
Either, since 0.05% a year is too small to bother with
Neither, since an index fund always lags by its expense ratio
Fund P, whose tracking difference is lower, so it leaves more
qs.why: The investor earns index minus tracking difference. P trails by 0.35% and Q by 0.40%, so P leaves more.
wrong: Expense ratio is one part of the gap. Q's actual gap is larger, so its lower fee was not enough.
0.05% a year compounds over decades. It is small each year and still real, so it is a fair tiebreaker.
The gap is mostly the expense ratio, plus friction. Funds differ, so comparing them is useful.

title: Smart beta and factor funds
concept: Smart beta funds follow an index built on a rule, such as low volatility, quality, momentum or value, rather than just market size.
They are passive in how they are run, but active in what rule they chose.
Each factor goes through long cycles. Momentum can lead for years and then fall sharply.
Costs are usually higher than a plain index fund, and many are new with short records.
Use them as small satellite holdings and understand the rule before you buy.

client.quote: "This momentum index fund gave 40% last year. Should I switch?"
client.context: Client chasing a factor.

talk: "Factors go through strong and weak years. Momentum can reverse fast. We can add a small slice if you understand the rule and accept it may lag for years."

qs.prompt: A smart beta fund follows:
options: An index built on a rule like value or momentum
qs.why: Factors define the index rules.

qs.prompt: A risk of factor funds is:
options: A factor can lag for years
qs.why: Factor performance runs in cycles.

qs.prompt: Smart beta funds are usually best as:
qs.why: They should complement a core holding.

qs.prompt: After a 40% year, Rohan puts ₹5 lakh into a momentum index fund. In the next two made-up years it falls 32% and then 12%. About what is his money worth?
options: About ₹2.8 lakh, as 32% plus 12% is a 44% fall
About ₹3.4 lakh, as only the 32% fall really counts
About ₹3.0 lakh, as each fall hits the reduced sum
About ₹4.4 lakh, as the fund still shows a 3-year gain
qs.why: ₹5 lakh times 0.68 times 0.88 is about ₹2.99 lakh. The second fall applies to the smaller sum.
wrong: Adding the falls gives 44%, which would leave ₹2.8 lakh. A second fall acts on the reduced amount, so this is too low.
₹3.4 lakh is where the money stands after the 32% fall alone. The next 12% fall takes it lower.
The 40% gain came before he invested. Only the two falls count for his ₹5 lakh, so ₹4.4 lakh is far too high.

qs.prompt: Meena asks what makes a momentum index fund "smart beta". Which description is accurate?
options: An active fund where a manager picks shares with good news
A plain index fund under a new name, with the same holdings
A fund that guarantees to beat the market using past winners
Passive in how it runs, active in which rule it follows
qs.why: The fund mechanically copies a rule-based index, but someone chose the rule, so an active decision sits behind it.
