title: Interest rate types

story.headline: Her EMI never changed. Her loan quietly grew four years longer.
paras: Shalini took a 20-year home loan of ₹30 lakh at a floating rate of 8.5%. Her EMI was ₹26,035, and for two years it never changed. She assumed all was well.

Then she looked at her annual statement. Her rate was now 9.5%, and the months remaining were 264, not the 216 she expected. The bank had kept her EMI the same and stretched the loan by 48 months instead.
Nobody had cheated her. This is how a floating-rate loan works when rates rise and the borrower does nothing. But it meant four more years of payments. She had not known she had a choice.

concept: The interest rate on a loan is either fixed or floating. A fixed rate stays the same for the agreed period, so your EMI is certain. It is usually set a little higher, because the lender carries the risk of rates rising. A floating rate moves up and down over the life of the loan.

Floating rates on most new retail loans from banks are linked to an outside benchmark, most often the Reserve Bank's repo rate. Your rate is the benchmark plus a spread. When the Reserve Bank raises or cuts the repo rate, your rate follows at the next reset, typically within three months.

When your rate rises, something has to give. Either the EMI goes up, or the tenure gets longer, or a bit of both. Lenders often extend the tenure by default because the borrower does not feel it. As Shalini found, an unchanged EMI can hide years of extra payments.

You have a say. Lenders are required to tell you about the effect of a rate change and to offer you the choice of a higher EMI, a longer tenure or a mix, as well as the option to prepay in part. If you can afford it, raising the EMI is nearly always cheaper than extending the loan.

Which should you choose? Floating suits long loans, where rates will rise and fall many times and you benefit when they fall. Fixed suits short loans, or anyone whose budget cannot absorb a higher EMI. Whichever you hold, read your loan statement once a year: check the rate, the EMI and, above all, the months remaining.

client.quote: “My rate went up and so did my loan tenure. Why?”
client.context: A client whose floating-rate loan reset.

talk: “Your rate is tied to the repo rate, so it rose when the repo rate rose. The lender kept your EMI steady by adding months. You can ask to raise the EMI instead and keep your original end date. If you can afford it, that costs far less overall.”
remember: Fixed: certain EMI, usually a higher rate. Floating: moves with the benchmark.
Rate up means higher EMI or longer tenure. You can choose.
A steady EMI can hide a growing loan.
Raising the EMI is usually cheaper than extending the tenure.
Check rate, EMI and months remaining once a year.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Fixed rate”?
options: Credit utilisation is the share of your credit limit that you are using. Keeping it low, often below 30%, helps your score.
A fixed rate stays the same for an agreed period, so your EMI is predictable even if market rates move.
A processing fee is a one-time charge by the lender when sanctioning a loan, usually a percentage of the loan amount.
The interest rate is the cost of borrowing, shown as a yearly percentage of the outstanding loan.
qs.why: Fixed rate: A fixed rate stays the same for an agreed period, so your EMI is predictable even if market rates move.

qs.prompt: A borrower’s loan rate falls after the central bank cuts its policy rate. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is Floating rate. A floating rate changes with an external benchmark, so your EMI or tenure can go up or down when market rates change.

qs.prompt: Which statement about “Repo-linked rate” is correct?
options: A repo-linked lending rate is a floating rate tied to the RBI’s repo rate, so changes in the repo rate pass through to borrowers.
A repo-linked rate is set by the borrower’s employer.
Credit utilisation is how often you apply for loans.
The principal is the interest you pay on the loan.
qs.why: Correct: A repo-linked lending rate is a floating rate tied to the RBI’s repo rate, so changes in the repo rate pass through to borrowers. The other statements are common misunderstandings.

qs.prompt: The repo rate rises by 0.5%. Prakash has a repo-linked floating-rate home loan. What should he expect?
options: Nothing changes until the loan is renewed
His rate rises at the next reset, lifting his EMI or his tenure
His EMI falls because banks pass on the benefit
His loan automatically converts to a fixed rate until the repo rate falls
qs.why: A repo-linked rate is the repo rate plus a spread, so it moves when the repo rate moves. The lender then raises the EMI, extends the tenure, or both.
wrong: Floating rates reset during the loan, typically within three months of a change.
A rise in the benchmark raises the borrower's cost. EMIs fall only when rates are cut.
Conversion happens only if the borrower asks for it, and may carry a fee.

qs.prompt: After a rate rise, Rekha's lender says: “Your EMI stays the same.” What should she check next?
options: Whether her credit score has improved
Whether the processing fee has been refunded
How many months are now left on the loan
Whether the property value has gone up
qs.why: If the rate is higher and the EMI is unchanged, the tenure must have been extended. The number of months remaining shows the real cost of doing nothing.
wrong: Her score is unrelated to how the lender absorbed this rate change.
Processing fees are a one-time charge and are not refunded when rates move.
The property's value does not change what she owes or for how long.

qs.prompt: Who is a fixed-rate loan most suitable for?
options: Someone with a tight budget taking a three-year car loan
Someone taking a 25-year loan who expects rates to fall
Someone who plans to prepay the whole loan within months
Someone who wants the lowest possible starting rate
qs.why: A fixed rate gives certainty. On a short loan with no spare room in the budget, knowing the exact EMI matters more than the chance of a slightly lower rate.
wrong: Over a long loan, and with rates expected to fall, floating lets the borrower benefit.
Fixed-rate loans can carry prepayment charges, so they suit this borrower least.
Fixed rates usually start a little higher than floating rates.

qs.prompt: Mohan's floating rate has risen. He can afford ₹2,000 more a month. Which choice costs him the least in total?
options: Keep the EMI and let the tenure extend
Stop paying until rates fall again
Take a personal loan to cover the difference
Raise the EMI and keep the original end date
qs.why: A higher EMI repays principal faster, so less interest builds up. Extending the tenure means paying interest for many additional months.
wrong: This feels painless but adds years of instalments.
Missing EMIs brings penalties and damages his credit score.
A personal loan costs more than the home loan it would be supporting.

qs.prompt: The repo rate rises and Meena's floating-rate loan resets. What can happen?
options: Her rate stays the same until the loan ends
Her loan is cancelled and the bank refunds her
Her rate rises, so the EMI or the tenure goes up
Her principal is cut by the same amount
qs.why: The rate follows the benchmark, so either the EMI or the tenure has to give.
wrong: A floating rate does not stay still, since it follows the benchmark at resets.
A rate change does not cancel a loan or bring any refund to the borrower.
The principal is what she borrowed, and a rate change does not reduce it.

qs.prompt: Rohan's EMI stayed the same after a rate rise. What is the likely reason?
options: The tenure was lengthened without much notice
The rate did not change at all during those years
The bank paid the extra interest from its own funds
His principal was cleared by the bank after the reset
qs.why: A longer tenure absorbs the higher interest, so the EMI can stay unchanged.
wrong: The rate rose, so something else had to take the higher cost.
Banks do not pay a borrower's extra interest from their own pocket.
The principal is not cleared by a rate change, so this does not fit.

qs.prompt: Meena can afford a higher EMI after a rate rise. What is usually the cheaper choice?
options: Let the tenure grow and keep the EMI
Stop paying until the rate falls again
Take a fresh loan to pay the old one
Raise the EMI, keep the tenure
qs.why: A higher EMI keeps the years short, so less interest builds up in the end.
wrong: A longer tenure feels painless but adds interest in every extra year.
Stopping payment brings penalties and harms her credit record.
A fresh loan adds new costs and fees, and does not fix the rate issue.

qs.prompt: Which borrower is better placed to choose a fixed rate?
options: Someone who hopes to guess where rates are going
Someone whose budget cannot take a higher EMI
Someone who never reads the loan statement
Someone who wants the longest possible tenure
qs.why: A fixed rate gives a steady EMI, which suits a tight budget.
wrong: Guessing future rates is not a plan, and nobody can do it well.
Reading the statement matters under both types of rate.
Tenure is a separate choice and does not decide fixed or floating.

example.title: Shalini's loan when the rate rose from 8.5% to 9.5%
example.intro: ₹30 lakh, 20 years, two years already paid. Balance: ₹28.75 lakh.
head: Her choice
Result
rows: Keep the end date: raise the EMI
Extra instalments she avoids by raising it

title: Reducing the cost of a loan

story.headline: A ₹3 lakh bonus, used once, ended his home loan three and a half years early.
paras: Three years into his 20-year, ₹30 lakh home loan at 9%, Rahul received a bonus of ₹3 lakh. He was tempted by a new car's down payment. A colleague suggested he look at his loan statement first.
He still owed ₹28.15 lakh. After 36 EMIs totalling ₹9.7 lakh, the loan had fallen by less than ₹2 lakh. The rest had gone as interest.

He put the ₹3 lakh into the loan and kept his EMI the same. The bank's new schedule showed the loan ending 43 months earlier, with ₹8.7 lakh less interest. One payment of ₹3 lakh had saved nearly three times its own size.

concept: The cost of a loan is not fixed on the day you sign. There are three ways to bring it down afterwards, and most borrowers never use them.

Prepayment means paying extra towards the principal, beyond your EMIs. Every rupee prepaid stops earning interest for the lender for the rest of the loan. That is why it works best early, when the balance is high and many years remain. Even small regular prepayments, such as one extra EMI a year, shorten a long loan by years.

When you prepay, choose to keep the EMI and shorten the tenure, unless your budget is under strain. This gives the largest saving. On floating-rate loans taken by individuals, lenders are not allowed to charge a prepayment penalty. Fixed-rate loans may carry one, so read the terms.

A balance transfer moves your loan to another lender offering a lower rate. It is worth doing when the rate gap is meaningful and many years remain. Count every cost first: processing fee, legal and valuation charges. Before you move, ask your own lender to match the rate. Often they will, for a small fee.

Judge every loan by its total cost of borrowing: interest plus processing fees, insurance sold with the loan, and any other charges. Lenders must give you a Key Facts Statement showing the annual percentage rate, which includes these. A loan with a lower headline rate and heavy fees can cost more than one with a higher rate and none. Before prepaying, though, keep your emergency fund intact. Money put into a loan cannot be taken out again.

title: Credit scores

story.headline: He earned ₹1.8 lakh a month. The bank still said no.
paras: Aditya, a software lead in Hyderabad, applied for a home loan and was confident. He earned well and had never defaulted on anything. The bank declined.

He downloaded his credit report and found the reasons. His score was 668. He had paid his credit card bill late three times in two years, “only by a few days”, when travelling. His two cards were regularly used up to 80% of their limits. And in the past month he had applied to five lenders to compare offers.

None of this felt serious at the time. Together it told lenders that he was stretched and hunting for credit. A year of on-time payments and lower card use later, his score was 771, and the same bank offered him a better rate than he had first asked for.

concept: A credit score is a three-digit number, from 300 to 900, that sums up how you have handled borrowed money. Lenders check it before approving any loan or card, and it affects not just whether you get the loan but the rate you are offered. Around 750 and above is generally treated as good.

The score is built from your credit report, a record kept by credit bureaus of every loan and card in your name and every payment you made or missed. Income is not part of it. A high earner who pays late scores lower than a modest earner who never does.

Four habits drive most of the score. First, pay on time, every time: payment history carries the most weight, and even a few days late is recorded. Second, use only a small part of your card limit. This is credit utilisation, and staying under about 30% is a good guide. Third, do not apply to many lenders in a short time. Each application creates a hard enquiry, and several together look like distress. Fourth, keep old accounts: a long, clean history helps.

Checking your own report does not lower your score. You are entitled to one free full report a year from each credit bureau. Read it for errors: a loan you never took, a payment wrongly marked late, a closed account shown as open. Raise a dispute with the bureau; wrong entries can be corrected.

A score is rebuilt the same way it is damaged: slowly, through behaviour. There are no shortcuts, and anyone offering to “fix your score fast” for a fee is selling nothing. Set every card and EMI to auto-pay, bring card use down, and time does the rest.

title: Cards and borrowing smart

story.headline: “Minimum amount due: ₹2,500.” She paid it for a year and owed more than when she started.
paras: Zoya's card bill after her sister's wedding was ₹50,000. The statement said in bold: minimum amount due ₹2,500. That seemed kind. She paid it, and kept putting about ₹1,700 of fuel on the card each month as usual.
A year later she had paid ₹30,000 to the card company. Her balance was close to ₹60,000.

The card charged 3% a month on whatever she had not paid. In the first month that was ₹1,500 of interest. Of her ₹2,500, only ₹1,000 reduced the debt. And because she was carrying a balance, her new purchases started attracting interest too, with no interest-free days. The minimum due had kept her account in good standing and her debt alive.

concept: Not all borrowing is equal. Knowing the kind of debt you are taking tells you most of what you need to know about its cost.

A secured loan is backed by something the lender can take if you do not pay: a home, a car, gold, a fixed deposit. Because the lender's risk is lower, the rate is lower. An unsecured loan has nothing behind it but your promise. Personal loans, credit cards and most pay-later schemes are unsecured, and so they cost much more.

A credit card is revolving credit: you can borrow, repay and borrow again up to a limit. Used well, it is free. Pay the full statement amount by the due date and you pay no interest at all, while building a strong credit history. Used badly, it is the costliest common debt there is, often 3% or more a month.

The minimum amount due is the trap. It is a small slice of the bill, set so that the account is not marked overdue. Interest runs on everything left unpaid. Once you carry a balance, the interest-free period usually stops for new purchases as well. If you cannot pay in full, pay as much as you possibly can and stop using the card until it is cleared. Converting a large balance into a fixed EMI plan or a lower-rate personal loan can cut the cost sharply.

Before any new loan, lenders work out how much of your income already goes to repayments. A common ceiling is 40% to 50%. Use a stricter test for yourself. Borrow for things that last or grow: a home, education, a business tool. Avoid borrowing for things that are gone before the loan is: holidays, phones, celebrations. Save for those instead.

title: Who counts as an NRI
concept: Status is decided separately for foreign exchange law and for tax.

NRI. A non-resident Indian is an Indian citizen who lives outside India for work, business or other reasons that suggest a long stay abroad. For example: an engineer leaves India for a multi-year posting in Singapore.

FEMA. The Foreign Exchange Management Act governs foreign exchange transactions in India, including the accounts and investments NRIs may hold. For example: a rule on how an NRI may bring money into India comes from the foreign exchange law.

Residential status for tax. Tax residential status depends on days spent in India in a year and earlier years, and decides whether global income is taxed in India. For example: a person’s Indian tax treatment changes after she spends fewer days in India.

OCI. An Overseas Citizen of India is a person of Indian origin holding a foreign passport and a lifelong visa-like card. For most investment rules, OCIs are treated like NRIs. For example: a US citizen of Indian origin holds a card allowing lifelong travel to India.

title: NRE, NRO and FCNR accounts
concept: Choose the account by where the money comes from and where you want it to go.

NRE account. An NRE account is a rupee account for money earned abroad. Balances and interest are freely repatriable, and the interest is generally tax-free in India. For example: an NRI deposits her foreign salary in a rupee account that she can send back abroad easily.

NRO account. An NRO account is a rupee account for income earned in India, such as rent or dividends. Interest is taxable and repatriation is limited to set annual amounts. For example: an NRI’s rental income from a flat in India is credited to a rupee account with limits on sending it abroad.

FCNR(B) deposit. An FCNR(B) deposit is a fixed deposit in a foreign currency, so the investor is protected from exchange-rate changes against rupee. For example: an NRI places a deposit in US dollars with an Indian bank and avoids rupee risk.

Repatriation. Repatriation means sending money from India back to your country of residence. Rules differ by account and source of funds. For example: an NRI moves savings from an NRE account to her overseas bank.

NRI mutual fund investing. NRIs can invest in Indian mutual funds, but some fund houses do not accept investors from certain countries, such as the US and Canada, because of local regulations. For example: a fund house declines an application from a person living in the United States.

title: Tax for NRIs
concept: Indian income is taxed in India; the tax at home may depend on a treaty.

DTAA. A double taxation avoidance agreement is a treaty between two countries that prevents the same income from being fully taxed in both. For example: an NRI claims credit in her country of residence for tax already paid in India.

TDS on NRIs. Tax deducted at source on NRI income, such as capital gains, is usually at higher rates than for residents, and the NRI can claim a refund if too much was deducted. For example: a buyer deducts tax at a high rate when paying an NRI for a property.

Tax residency certificate. A tax residency certificate is issued by your country of residence to prove you are a tax resident there, often needed to claim treaty benefits. For example: an NRI shows the paper from her country’s tax office to claim a lower rate under the treaty.

Indian-source income. Indian-source income is income earned or arising in India, such as rent from property or interest on an NRO account, and is taxable in India. For example: an NRI’s rent from a flat in Pune is taxable in India.

NRI KYC. NRI KYC is the identity and address verification, including passport, visa and overseas address, needed to open accounts and invest. For example: an NRI submits passport and overseas address proof to a fund house.

Power of attorney. A power of attorney lets a trusted person in India act on your behalf for specified tasks. It should be limited and carefully drafted. For example: an NRI authorises a relative in India to handle a bank formality for her.

Repatriation limit. Funds in an NRO account can be repatriated abroad up to a yearly limit, currently one million US dollars per financial year, subject to conditions and documents. For example: an NRI sells inherited property in India and sends the proceeds abroad within the annual limit.

title: Who is an NRI
concept: Two laws use the word NRI differently: FEMA for money rules and the Income Tax Act for tax.

NRI under FEMA. NRI under FEMA is a person of Indian origin or citizenship who lives outside India for work, business, study or another purpose of uncertain duration. For example: a software engineer from Pune who has moved to Dubai on a work visa for several years is treated as an NRI for banking and investing rules.

Residential status for tax. Residential status for tax is decided each year by counting days spent in India, and it decides whether global income is taxed in India. For example: a person who spends fewer days in India than the test requires is treated as a non-resident for that year.

OCI cardholder. An OCI cardholder is a foreign citizen of Indian origin who holds a lifelong Overseas Citizen of India card, and is treated like an NRI for many banking and investment rules. For example: a Canadian citizen born in India uses an OCI card to open an NRO account.

RNOR. RNOR, or resident but not ordinarily resident, is a tax status where mainly income from India, plus some foreign income linked to India, is taxed. For example: a person who returns to India after many years abroad may fall in this status for a few years.

India-sourced income. India-sourced income is income earned or received in India, such as rent, capital gains on Indian assets and NRO interest, and it is taxable for non-residents. For example: an NRI who sells Indian shares pays Indian tax on the gain.

title: Treaties and double tax
concept: Income can be taxed in two countries. Treaties and credits reduce the double bite.

DTAA. DTAA is a double taxation avoidance agreement between two countries that decides who may tax which income and at what rate. For example: an NRI in a treaty country claims a lower tax rate on Indian interest.

Tax residency certificate. A tax residency certificate is a document from the tax authority of your country of residence proving you live there for tax, often needed to claim treaty benefits. For example: an NRI shares this certificate with an Indian bank to get treaty rates applied.

Foreign tax credit. Foreign tax credit lets you reduce tax in one country by the tax already paid on the same income in another. For example: an NRI pays tax in India on rent and claims credit for it when filing in the country of residence.

Tie-breaker rule. A tie-breaker rule is a treaty test, such as permanent home or centre of vital interests, that decides which country treats you as resident when both claim you. For example: a person with homes in two countries uses this test to settle where they are resident.

Return filing. Return filing is submitting your income tax return, which an NRI needs to do when Indian income crosses the exemption limit or when a refund is due. For example: an NRI files a return to claim back excess tax deducted on a sale.

title: The remittance rules
concept: Sending money abroad to invest is allowed within rules set by RBI.

Authorised dealer bank. An authorised dealer bank is a bank permitted by RBI to handle foreign exchange transactions. For example: a resident sends funds through such a bank to an overseas broker.

title: Global risks
concept: Foreign markets bring their own risks on top of normal market risk.
Currency risk. Currency risk is the chance that rupee and foreign currency moves change your return when converted back. For example: a foreign fund gains in dollars but the rupee value rises less.
Concentration risk. Concentration risk is the danger of having too much money in one country, sector or theme. For example: a portfolio holds mostly a few global technology companies.
Tracking error. Tracking error is the gap between what an index fund returns and what the index returns. For example: a fund returns slightly less than its index due to costs.
Subscription limit. A subscription limit is a cap on new money a fund investing overseas can accept, which may pause fresh investments. For example: a fund stops accepting lump sums for a period.

Withholding on dividends. Withholding on dividends is tax deducted by the foreign country before a dividend reaches you. For example: a foreign dividend arrives after tax has been cut.
Foreign tax credit. Foreign tax credit lets you offset tax paid abroad against Indian tax on the same income, as the rules allow. For example: a resident claims credit for tax withheld on a dividend.

title: Staying safe
concept: Global investing attracts scams. A few habits protect you.

Regulated channel. A regulated channel is a broker, bank or fund house authorised by the proper regulator to handle your money. For example: an investor uses an authorised bank and a registered fund house.

Diversification. Diversification is spreading money across assets, countries and sectors so one problem does not sink the portfolio. For example: an investor keeps global funds as one part of a larger plan.

Unregistered app. An unregistered app is a platform with no regulatory approval that promises easy global trading, and it is a common route for fraud. For example: a social media ad promotes a trading app that asks for deposits to a personal account.
Time horizon. Time horizon is how long you can leave money invested, which should match the risk of the investment. For example: a person who needs money in a year avoids volatile global equity.

title: Capital gains basics
concept: A capital gain is the profit on selling an asset. Timing and type decide the tax.
Capital gain. A capital gain is the profit made when you sell an asset for more than its cost. For example: an investor sells shares for more than she paid.

Holding period. Holding period is the time between buying and selling an asset, which decides whether the gain is short term or long term. For example: units sold after a longer holding are treated differently from units sold quickly.

Cost of acquisition. Cost of acquisition is the price you paid for the asset, plus certain costs, used to work out the gain. For example: the purchase price of a fund unit is subtracted from the sale value.
Realised gain. A realised gain is a profit locked in by selling, and only such profits are taxed. For example: a rise in portfolio value is not taxed until units are sold.

Debt fund taxation. Debt fund taxation is the treatment of gains from funds investing mostly in debt, which for many such funds is taxed at the investor’s slab rate. For example: an investor in a debt fund adds the gain to her income.
Dividend taxation. Dividend taxation means dividends are added to your income and taxed at your slab rate. For example: a fund dividend raises the investor’s taxable income.
STT. STT, or securities transaction tax, is a tax charged on buying or selling listed shares and units of equity funds. For example: a small tax is added to every trade on the exchange.

title: Losses and advance tax
concept: Losses can reduce tax if you use them properly.
Set-off. Set-off is adjusting a loss against a gain of the same or allowed type in the same year. For example: a loss on one share reduces the gain on another.

Carry forward. Carry forward is moving an unused loss to later years to offset future gains, usually only if the return was filed on time. For example: a loss this year is used against next year’s gain.

Tax-loss harvesting. Tax-loss harvesting is selling an investment at a loss to offset gains, done carefully and without losing sight of the investing plan. For example: an investor books a loss on a fund to reduce tax on a profit.
Advance tax. Advance tax is tax paid in instalments during the year when the liability is above a threshold. For example: a person with large capital gains pays tax before year end.

qs.prompt: A loss this year is used against next year’s gain. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is Carry forward. Carry forward is moving an unused loss to later years to offset future gains, usually only if the return was filed on time.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Tax-loss harvesting”?
options: This is moving an unused loss to later years to offset future gains, usually only if the return was filed on time.
This is tax paid in instalments during the year when the liability is above a threshold.
This is adjusting a loss against a gain of the same or allowed type in the same year.
This is selling an investment at a loss to offset gains, done carefully and without losing sight of the investing plan.
qs.why: Tax-loss harvesting: Tax-loss harvesting is selling an investment at a loss to offset gains, done carefully and without losing sight of the investing plan.

qs.prompt: Rohan has a ₹40,000 gain on one fund and a ₹10,000 loss on another, same type, same year. What is taxed?
qs.why: The loss is set off against the gain, leaving ₹30,000 to tax.

qs.prompt: Meena has a loss she cannot use this year. What must she do to carry it forward?

qs.prompt: Rohan sells a fund at a loss only to cut tax, and then wants to invest again for the same goal. What should he keep in mind?

That he must never hold the fund again
That tax rules do not apply to him
Costs and his plan, not just the tax
qs.why: Selling has costs and may break his plan.
wrong: A loss is not good in itself. It only offsets a gain.
No rule forbids holding it again, but the plan should lead.
Tax rules apply to every taxpayer, whatever the case.

qs.prompt: Dadi expects large capital gains this year. What does advance tax ask of her?

Pay tax in instalments during the year
Pay only when the tax office sends a letter

title: Regimes and filing
concept: Choosing a regime and filing on time keeps you clear with the tax office.

Old and new regime. The old and new regimes are two ways of computing tax, where the old allows more deductions and the new offers different slab rates. For example: a taxpayer compares both to see which gives a lower bill.
Deduction. A deduction is an amount the law allows you to subtract from income to reduce tax. For example: a qualifying investment reduces taxable income under the old regime.
ELSS lock-in. ELSS lock-in is the three-year period during which units of an ELSS tax-saving fund cannot be redeemed. For example: an investor buys an ELSS fund and cannot sell for three years.

Filing deadline. A filing deadline is the last date to submit a return without penalty, and missing it can cost you loss carry-forward. For example: a taxpayer files before the due date to carry forward a loss.

client.quote: “Which regime should I choose?”
client.context: A salaried client at filing time.

talk: “Compare both with your real numbers. If you use many deductions the old one may win. If not, the new one can be simpler.”
remember: ELSS locks money for three years.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Old and new regime”?
options: This is the three-year period during which units of an ELSS tax-saving fund cannot be redeemed.
This is the last date to submit a return without penalty, and missing it can cost you loss carry-forward.
This is an amount the law allows you to subtract from income to reduce tax.
This are two ways of computing tax, where the old allows more deductions and the new offers different slab rates.
qs.why: Old and new regime: The old and new regimes are two ways of computing tax, where the old allows more deductions and the new offers different slab rates.

qs.prompt: A qualifying investment reduces taxable income under the old regime. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is Deduction. A deduction is an amount the law allows you to subtract from income to reduce tax.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “ELSS lock-in”?
options: This is the three-year period during which units of an ELSS tax-saving fund cannot be redeemed.
This is the last date to submit a return without penalty, and missing it can cost you loss carry-forward.
This are two ways of computing tax, where the old allows more deductions and the new offers different slab rates.
This is an amount the law allows you to subtract from income to reduce tax.
qs.why: ELSS lock-in: ELSS lock-in is the three-year period during which units of an ELSS tax-saving fund cannot be redeemed.

Pick the old regime, since it is older

The lock-in ends after three years, not at retirement.

qs.prompt: Meena is in the new regime. Does an ELSS investment cut her tax under the old-regime deduction?
options: No, only the old regime allows it
Yes, in every regime without exception
Yes, but only after five years
Only if she tells her bank first
qs.why: That deduction applies only if she chooses the old regime.
wrong: Deductions differ between regimes, so not every regime allows it.
The time period is not what decides this. The regime is.
Her bank does not decide which deduction she gets.

qs.prompt: Rohan has a loss to carry forward but files his return after the due date. What may happen?
options: Nothing, since the due date is only a suggestion
The loss is paid back to him in cash
He may lose the right to carry the loss forward
The loss turns into a gain

title: The retirement goal
concept: A good plan starts with a number and a reason.

Retirement corpus. A retirement corpus is the total savings you need at retirement to support your expenses for the rest of your life. For example: a couple estimates the amount they need to fund monthly costs after work.
Inflation. Inflation is the rise in prices over time, which reduces what each rupee can buy. For example: a monthly expense of today is much higher after many years.
Longevity risk. Longevity risk is the chance of outliving your savings. For example: a retiree lives longer than the plan expected.

Withdrawal rate. A withdrawal rate is the percentage of your savings you draw each year, a rule of thumb and not a guarantee. For example: a retiree draws a modest share of the corpus each year to make it last.

client.quote: “How much do I need to retire?”
client.context: A client in their thirties.

talk: “Start with today’s monthly spending, adjust for inflation and the years you will need it. That gives a target we can plan towards.”

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Retirement corpus”?
options: This is the percentage of your savings you draw each year, a rule of thumb and not a guarantee.
This is the rise in prices over time, which reduces what each rupee can buy.
This is the chance of outliving your savings.
This is the total savings you need at retirement to support your expenses for the rest of your life.
qs.why: Retirement corpus: A retirement corpus is the total savings you need at retirement to support your expenses for the rest of your life.

qs.prompt: A monthly expense of today is much higher after many years. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is Inflation. Inflation is the rise in prices over time, which reduces what each rupee can buy.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Longevity risk”?
options: This is the total savings you need at retirement to support your expenses for the rest of your life.
This is the rise in prices over time, which reduces what each rupee can buy.
This is the chance of outliving your savings.
This is the percentage of your savings you draw each year, a rule of thumb and not a guarantee.
qs.why: Longevity risk: Longevity risk is the chance of outliving your savings.

qs.prompt: Rohan spends ₹40,000 a month and will retire in 20 years. What is wrong with planning for ₹40,000 then?
options: Retirees never spend anything on food or travel

Prices will rise, so the same life costs more
qs.why: Inflation lifts prices every year, so the same life needs a bigger monthly sum.
wrong: Retirees still spend on food, health and daily needs, so costs do not vanish.

A bank does not pay a retiree's bills, so the plan must cover them.

qs.prompt: What does longevity risk mean?
options: The chance that markets rise for many years
The chance of outliving your savings

The risk of a loan growing in size
qs.why: Living longer than planned means savings must last for more years.
wrong: Rising markets are good news and not a risk to your savings.

A loan growing is a different risk and not about the length of life.

qs.prompt: A retiree withdraws far more than the plan allows in the first years. What is likely?
options: The corpus grows faster, since money is moving
Inflation stops for the whole period
The corpus may run out before life ends
The withdrawal rate has no effect on the pot
qs.why: Heavy early draws shrink the pot, leaving less to earn and to last.
wrong: Money withdrawn no longer earns, so the pot grows slower and not faster.
Inflation goes on whatever the retiree does with the withdrawals.
The rate of withdrawal matters a lot to how long the pot lasts.

qs.prompt: Meena's yearly spend at retirement is ₹10 lakh. Using the 25-times rule, what pot does it point to?
qs.why: Ten lakh times twenty-five is ₹2.5 crore, matching a draw of about 4%.
wrong: ₹25 lakh is only two and a half years of her spending.
₹10 crore is forty times her yearly spend, far above the rule.
₹1 crore would last about ten years at her spending.

title: EPF and PPF
concept: Two long-term savings routes backed by rules and the government.

EPF. EPF is the employees’ provident fund, where employee and employer contribute a share of salary towards retirement. For example: a salaried person sees a monthly contribution to the provident fund in the payslip.

VPF. VPF is voluntary provident fund, where an employee adds extra contribution to the provident fund beyond the required share. For example: an employee chooses to put more of the salary into the fund.

PPF. PPF is the public provident fund, a government-backed long-term savings account with a rate set periodically. For example: a self-employed person opens a government-backed 15-year savings account for steady savings.
PPF maturity. PPF maturity is the 15-year term after which the account matures, with options to extend. For example: an investor’s PPF account matures after fifteen years.

client.quote: “Is PPF enough for retirement?”
client.context: A client who relies only on PPF.

talk: “PPF is a stable base, but its contribution limit and rate may not beat inflation on their own. Most people blend it with other investments.”
remember: Rates are reset by the government.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “EPF”?
options: This is the public provident fund, a government-backed long-term savings account with a rate set periodically.
This is the employees’ provident fund, where employee and employer contribute a share of salary towards retirement.
This is voluntary provident fund, where an employee adds extra contribution to the provident fund beyond the required share.
This is the 15-year term after which the account matures, with options to extend.
qs.why: EPF: EPF is the employees’ provident fund, where employee and employer contribute a share of salary towards retirement.

qs.prompt: An employee chooses to put more of the salary into the fund. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is VPF. VPF is voluntary provident fund, where an employee adds extra contribution to the provident fund beyond the required share.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “PPF”?
options: This is the public provident fund, a government-backed long-term savings account with a rate set periodically.
This is voluntary provident fund, where an employee adds extra contribution to the provident fund beyond the required share.
This is the employees’ provident fund, where employee and employer contribute a share of salary towards retirement.
This is the 15-year term after which the account matures, with options to extend.
qs.why: PPF: PPF is the public provident fund, a government-backed long-term savings account with a rate set periodically.

qs.why: PPF is open to individuals, whether or not they have a job with an employer.

Extend it in blocks of five years, or withdraw it
Only withdraw it, since extension is not allowed
Move it into a credit card account

The rate is set by her bank's branch manager
The rate rises whenever she pays more
The rate can change over the years
qs.why: The government reviews and sets the rate, so it may move in future.
wrong: A rate reviewed from time to time is not locked for the whole term.
A branch manager does not set the PPF rate. The government does.
The rate does not depend on how much she pays in.

title: NPS
concept: NPS is a pension scheme that you build until retirement and convert partly into a pension.
NPS. NPS is the National Pension System, a voluntary pension scheme regulated by PFRDA. For example: a professional opens a voluntary pension account regulated by PFRDA to build a retirement fund.
Tier I and Tier II. Tier I is the main retirement account with withdrawal rules, and Tier II is a flexible account without the same restrictions. For example: a saver keeps long-term money in Tier I.

Asset choice. Asset choice in NPS is the option to decide how much goes to equity, corporate bonds and government securities, within limits, or to use an automatic life-stage option. For example: a young saver picks a higher share for equity.

Annuity. An annuity is a product that pays a regular pension in return for a lump sum, and NPS rules require part of the corpus to be used this way at exit. For example: a retiree uses part of the corpus to buy a pension.

client.quote: “Can I take all the money out of NPS at retirement?”
client.context: A client who wants a lump sum.

talk: “The rules require part of the corpus to buy an annuity. The rest can be taken as a lump sum within the current rules. Let us check what applies to you.”

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “NPS”?
options: This is the National Pension System, a voluntary pension scheme regulated by PFRDA.
This is a product that pays a regular pension in return for a lump sum, and NPS rules require part of the corpus to be used this way at exit.
Tier I is the main retirement account with withdrawal rules, and Tier II is a flexible account without the same restrictions.
This in NPS is the option to decide how much goes to equity, corporate bonds and government securities, within limits, or to use an automatic life-stage option.
qs.why: NPS: NPS is the National Pension System, a voluntary pension scheme regulated by PFRDA.

qs.prompt: A saver keeps long-term money in Tier I. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is Tier I and Tier II. Tier I is the main retirement account with withdrawal rules, and Tier II is a flexible account without the same restrictions.

options: Tier I is the main retirement account with withdrawal rules, and Tier II is a flexible account without the same restrictions.
This is a product that pays a regular pension in return for a lump sum, and NPS rules require part of the corpus to be used this way at exit.
This in NPS is the option to decide how much goes to equity, corporate bonds and government securities, within limits, or to use an automatic life-stage option.
This is the National Pension System, a voluntary pension scheme regulated by PFRDA.
qs.why: Asset choice: Asset choice in NPS is the option to decide how much goes to equity, corporate bonds and government securities, within limits, or to use an automatic life-stage option.

options: A fixed choice of all equity for good
Using Tier II as the main pot
qs.why: An automatic option shifts the mix with age, so he does not need to.

qs.prompt: Meena reaches NPS exit age. What must she do with part of the pot?
options: Use a set share to buy an annuity
Hand it all over to the government
Reinvest all of it in shares
Leave it idle for another ten years
qs.why: The rules require part of the pot to buy an annuity, a regular pension.
wrong: The pot belongs to her, and it is not handed over in full to anyone.
No rule demands reinvesting it all in shares.
Idle money does not meet the rule, which asks for an annuity.

qs.prompt: A friend says NPS Tier I and Tier II are the same. What is the difference?
options: Tier I is for the old, and Tier II for the young
Tier II must be kept for sixty years
There is no difference between them
Tier I has withdrawal rules, and Tier II is flexible

Tier II has no such lock, so it is the flexible one.

qs.why: PFRDA is the pension regulator that oversees NPS in India.
wrong: SEBI regulates securities markets and not the pension system.

title: Other pension tools
concept: Several smaller tools can support income after work.
SCSS. SCSS is the senior citizens savings scheme, a government-backed savings scheme for older people with regular interest. For example: a retiree places a lump sum in it for quarterly interest.

Atal Pension Yojana. Atal Pension Yojana is a government pension scheme that pays a fixed monthly pension after 60 for contributions made earlier. For example: a worker in the unorganised sector joins it for a basic pension.
Gratuity. Gratuity is a lump sum paid by an employer to an employee after long service, under the rules. For example: an employee receives it when leaving a company after many years.
SWP. SWP is a systematic withdrawal plan that pays a fixed amount from a mutual fund at regular intervals. For example: a retiree sets a monthly withdrawal from a fund.

client.quote: “What gives me monthly income after retirement?”
client.context: A client close to retirement.

talk: “Typically a mix: interest from safe schemes, an annuity or pension, and a withdrawal plan from funds. We design the mix around your expenses.”
remember: Use a mix of income sources.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “SCSS”?
options: This is a government pension scheme that pays a fixed monthly pension after 60 for contributions made earlier.
This is a lump sum paid by an employer to an employee after long service, under the rules.
This is the senior citizens savings scheme, a government-backed savings scheme for older people with regular interest.
This is a systematic withdrawal plan that pays a fixed amount from a mutual fund at regular intervals.

A gratuity from her former employer

An SCSS account from the company
A home loan on easy terms

wrong: A tax refund is a separate matter between him and the tax office.
An employer does not open an SCSS account for a leaving employee.
A leaving employee is not owed a home loan by his old employer.

qs.prompt: A retiree sets an SWP of ₹30,000 a month from a fund. What should she watch?
options: Whether the fund can keep paying for many years
That the fund never changes in value at all
That the money is paid as a gift

wrong: Fund values do change, so expecting no change is a mistake.
An SWP is her own money coming back, not a gift.

qs.prompt: A domestic worker with no employer pension wants a fixed pension after 60. Which scheme is made for her?
qs.why: Atal Pension Yojana is a government scheme for workers outside formal pension cover.
wrong: SCSS is for people who are already sixty or older, and not for saving earlier.

title: Building the plan
concept: Habits beat timing. A few steps make a plan work.

Start early. Starting early means more years of compounding, so smaller savings can grow to more. For example: someone who begins in the twenties needs a lower monthly amount than someone who begins in the forties.
Step-up SIP. A step-up SIP is a SIP whose amount rises by a set percentage each year. For example: an investor raises the SIP every time income grows.
Age-based allocation. Age-based allocation is shifting from growth assets towards safer assets as retirement nears. For example: a saver reduces equity share in the last years.
Annual review. An annual review is a yearly check of savings, returns and goals so the plan can be adjusted. For example: a couple reviews the plan every birthday.

client.quote: “I am forty and have saved nothing. Is it too late?”
client.context: A client who feels behind.

talk: “It is better to start now than not at all. Higher savings, a step-up each year and a sensible asset mix can still make a real difference.”

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Start early”?
options: This is shifting from growth assets towards safer assets as retirement nears.
This is a yearly check of savings, returns and goals so the plan can be adjusted.
This is a SIP whose amount rises by a set percentage each year.
Starting early means more years of compounding, so smaller savings can grow to more.
qs.why: Start early: Starting early means more years of compounding, so smaller savings can grow to more.

qs.prompt: An investor raises the SIP every time income grows. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is Step-up SIP. A step-up SIP is a SIP whose amount rises by a set percentage each year.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Age-based allocation”?
options: Starting early means more years of compounding, so smaller savings can grow to more.
This is shifting from growth assets towards safer assets as retirement nears.
This is a SIP whose amount rises by a set percentage each year.
This is a yearly check of savings, returns and goals so the plan can be adjusted.
qs.why: Age-based allocation: Age-based allocation is shifting from growth assets towards safer assets as retirement nears.

qs.prompt: Rohan is 30 and Meena is 40. Both want ₹2 crore at 60. Who needs the bigger monthly saving?

Rohan, since young people save more per month

qs.why: Fewer years of compounding means more must be put in each month.
wrong: Starting earlier lowers the monthly need, so Rohan needs less.

qs.prompt: Meena's salary rises 10% each year, but her SIP stays at ₹10,000. What can she do?
options: Stop her SIP until the pay doubles
Use a step-up SIP that rises each year
Move all her money to a savings account
Wait for a year without saving
qs.why: A step-up SIP lifts the amount as income grows, adding to the pot over time.
wrong: Stopping loses years of compounding, which are hard to make up later.
A savings account usually grows slower than a long-term plan.

qs.prompt: Rohan is 55 and retires at 60. Why might he lower his share of equity now?
options: Equity can never rise again after 55
Banks demand it after the age of 55 by rule
Safer assets always beat equity every year

Safer assets are steadier, but they do not always earn more.

qs.prompt: Which habit keeps a retirement plan on track?
options: Looking at the plan only on retirement day
Changing the plan after every news headline
A yearly review of savings, returns and goals
Asking friends what their own plans are
qs.why: A yearly check lets her fix gaps early and adjust to changes in life.
wrong: A single look on the last day leaves no time for any changes.
Reacting to headlines leads to hasty changes and costs.
A friend's plan suits a friend's life, not necessarily hers.

title: Insurance words
concept: A few words appear on every policy.
Premium. A premium is the amount you pay to keep an insurance policy in force. For example: a car owner pays a yearly amount to keep the policy in force.
Sum insured. Sum insured is the maximum amount the insurer will pay under the policy. For example: a health or home policy states the maximum amount it will pay on the first page.
Deductible. A deductible is the part of a loss you pay yourself before the insurer pays. For example: a driver pays the first part of a repair bill.
Renewal. Renewal is continuing the policy for another term by paying the premium before it lapses. For example: a person renews the car policy before the expiry date.

client.quote: “Why is the premium different on two similar policies?”
client.context: A client comparing quotes.

talk: “Premium depends on cover, deductible, add-ons and the insurer’s pricing. Compare what is covered, not only the price.”

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Premium”?
options: This is the maximum amount the insurer will pay under the policy.
This is continuing the policy for another term by paying the premium before it lapses.
This is the part of a loss you pay yourself before the insurer pays.
This is the amount you pay to keep an insurance policy in force.
qs.why: Premium: A premium is the amount you pay to keep an insurance policy in force.

qs.prompt: A health or home policy states the maximum amount it will pay on the first page. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is Sum insured. Sum insured is the maximum amount the insurer will pay under the policy.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Deductible”?
options: This is the amount you pay to keep an insurance policy in force.
This is continuing the policy for another term by paying the premium before it lapses.
This is the part of a loss you pay yourself before the insurer pays.
This is the maximum amount the insurer will pay under the policy.
qs.why: Deductible: A deductible is the part of a loss you pay yourself before the insurer pays.

qs.prompt: Meena's repair bill is ₹40,000 and her deductible is ₹10,000. What does the insurer pay?
qs.why: The insurer pays the bill less her deductible: ₹40,000 less ₹10,000.
wrong: ₹40,000 would ignore the deductible she has agreed to carry.
₹10,000 is her own share, and not what the insurer pays.
₹50,000 adds the deductible to the bill, which is wrong.

qs.prompt: What is the sum insured?
options: The premium that Rohan pays every year
The amount of tax saved on the premium paid
The commission earned by the agent who sold it
qs.why: It is the upper limit of what the insurer will pay for a claim.
wrong: The premium is what Rohan pays. The sum insured is what he can claim.
Tax savings, if any, are a separate matter from the sum insured.
An agent's commission is not related to what the policy pays.

qs.prompt: Meena forgets to renew her policy and the date passes. What may happen?
options: It continues for another term at no cost
The policy may lapse, and cover can stop
The insurer pays double at the next claim
The sum insured grows to make up for it
qs.why: Renewal needs the premium before it lapses, or cover stops.
wrong: A term continues only if the premium is paid on time.
No insurer pays double for a missed renewal.
A sum insured does not grow on its own, whatever happens.

qs.prompt: Rohan picks a higher deductible to cut his premium. What is the trade-off?
options: A higher premium and a much bigger payout
No change in what he pays or in what he gets
The insurer pays his deductible for him each time
A lower premium, with more paid by him
qs.why: A larger deductible lowers the premium, but he bears more of every loss.
wrong: A higher deductible does not raise the premium or the payout.
It changes both what he pays each year and what he pays at a claim.
The point of a deductible is that he pays it himself.

title: Motor insurance
concept: Motor insurance has a compulsory part and an optional part.
Third-party cover. Third-party cover is the compulsory motor cover that pays for injury or damage you cause to others. For example: a driver who damages another person’s car is covered for that loss.
Own damage cover. Own damage cover pays for damage to your own vehicle, such as from an accident, fire or theft, as the policy states. For example: a policy pays repair costs after a collision.

IDV. IDV, or insured declared value, is the vehicle’s agreed value, which is the maximum payout if it is stolen or declared a total loss. For example: an older car is agreed at a lower value than a new one for the maximum payout on theft.
No-claim bonus. A no-claim bonus is a discount on premium for each claim-free year. For example: a driver with no claims gets a lower premium at renewal.

client.quote: “Is third-party cover enough?”
client.context: A client who wants to save money.

talk: “It meets the legal requirement, but it does not pay for your own vehicle. Own damage cover protects your car as well.”

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Third-party cover”?
options: This is the vehicle’s agreed value, which is the maximum payout if it is stolen or declared a total loss.
This is a discount on premium for each claim-free year.
This pays for damage to your own vehicle, such as from an accident, fire or theft, as the policy states.
This is the compulsory motor cover that pays for injury or damage you cause to others.
qs.why: Third-party cover: Third-party cover is the compulsory motor cover that pays for injury or damage you cause to others.

qs.prompt: A policy pays repair costs after a collision. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is Own damage cover. Own damage cover pays for damage to your own vehicle, such as from an accident, fire or theft, as the policy states.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “IDV”?
options: This pays for damage to your own vehicle, such as from an accident, fire or theft, as the policy states.
This is a discount on premium for each claim-free year.
This is the compulsory motor cover that pays for injury or damage you cause to others.
This is the vehicle’s agreed value, which is the maximum payout if it is stolen or declared a total loss.
qs.why: IDV: IDV, or insured declared value, is the vehicle’s agreed value, which is the maximum payout if it is stolen or declared a total loss.

qs.prompt: Rohan's car damages another person's car in an accident that was his fault. Which cover pays for the other car?
qs.why: Third-party cover pays for harm caused to others by his vehicle.
wrong: Own damage cover is for his own vehicle and not for others.
A no-claim bonus is a discount on the premium and is not a payout.
IDV is the agreed value of his own car, used for theft and total loss.

qs.prompt: Meena's car is stolen. What decides the most she can get back?
options: The price of fuel in that month
The number of seats in the car itself
The colour that she chose for it
qs.why: The IDV is the agreed value, and it is the most paid for theft or total loss.
wrong: Fuel prices have no link to the amount paid for a stolen car.
Seats do not decide the payout. The agreed value does.
Colour does not decide what the policy pays for a stolen car.

qs.prompt: Rohan has not made any claim for two years. What does he usually gain at renewal?
options: A higher deductible without any choice
A bigger bill for the same cover
qs.why: A no-claim bonus lowers the premium after a year with no claim.
wrong: A bonus does not push the deductible up unless he chooses.
A record with no claims does not make the bill any bigger.
Having no claims does not end a policy in any way.

qs.prompt: Meena sets her car's IDV much lower to save on the premium. What is the risk?
options: The cover becomes compulsory by law
The third-party cover stops at once
Her no-claim bonus is cancelled too
qs.why: A lower IDV cuts the premium, but it also lowers the most she can receive.
wrong: Cover does not become compulsory by the IDV she sets.
Third-party cover is a legal requirement and is not changed by IDV.
An IDV choice does not cancel a no-claim bonus.

title: Home and property
concept: A home is often the biggest asset. Cover should match its real value.

Fire and allied perils. Fire and allied perils cover is protection against fire and related risks such as lightning, floods and similar listed events. For example: a policy pays for damage after a fire in the house.
Home contents. Home contents cover protects furniture, appliances and belongings inside the house. For example: a policy pays when a theft takes the television.

Reinstatement value. Reinstatement value is the cost to rebuild or replace an asset as new, while market value is what it would sell for. For example: a policy pays to rebuild a damaged wall at current cost.

Underinsurance. Underinsurance is when the sum insured is lower than the true value, which can reduce the claim payout in proportion. For example: a house is insured for half its value and a claim is paid at a reduced share.

client.quote: “I insured the house for less to save premium.”
client.context: A client who chose a low cover.

talk: “A lower sum insured can cut the claim in proportion. It is safer to insure for the real value.”

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Fire and allied perils”?
options: This is when the sum insured is lower than the true value, which can reduce the claim payout in proportion.
This is the cost to rebuild or replace an asset as new, while market value is what it would sell for.
This cover is protection against fire and related risks such as lightning, floods and similar listed events.
This cover protects furniture, appliances and belongings inside the house.
qs.why: Fire and allied perils: Fire and allied perils cover is protection against fire and related risks such as lightning, floods and similar listed events.

qs.prompt: A policy pays when a theft takes the television. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is Home contents. Home contents cover protects furniture, appliances and belongings inside the house.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Reinstatement value”?
options: This cover protects furniture, appliances and belongings inside the house.
This is when the sum insured is lower than the true value, which can reduce the claim payout in proportion.
This cover is protection against fire and related risks such as lightning, floods and similar listed events.
This is the cost to rebuild or replace an asset as new, while market value is what it would sell for.
qs.why: Reinstatement value: Reinstatement value is the cost to rebuild or replace an asset as new, while market value is what it would sell for.

qs.prompt: Meena's flat is insured for ₹30 lakh, but it would cost ₹60 lakh to rebuild. A ₹10 lakh loss occurs. What is likely?
options: A full payment of ₹10 lakh in all
qs.why: With half the cover needed, the claim may be paid in the same proportion.
wrong: A full payment ignores the underinsurance clause that many policies carry.
A policy still pays something, so no payment is not the likely result.
The sum insured is a ceiling, and it is not paid when the loss is lower.

qs.prompt: What does reinstatement value mean?
options: What the property would sell for today
The price that was paid long ago
The value that the tax office sets
The cost to rebuild or replace as new
qs.why: It is the cost of rebuilding or replacing, as new, at current prices.
wrong: That is market value, which can be very different from the rebuilding cost.
The old purchase price may be far below today's rebuilding cost.
A tax office value is a separate matter and may differ from rebuilding cost.

qs.prompt: Rohan's television is stolen from his flat. Which cover is meant for this?
qs.why: Contents cover protects belongings inside the home, including against theft.
wrong: A fire policy pays for fire and allied perils, not for a theft.
Motor third-party cover is about vehicles, not belongings in a flat.
A term plan pays on death, and it does not cover belongings.

qs.prompt: Dadi buys a home policy. Which sum insured is a better guide?
options: The cost to rebuild the building
The price a buyer might pay today
The lowest figure that saves premium
A round figure that sounds good
qs.why: Rebuilding cost is what is needed to restore the house after a loss.
wrong: Market price includes land and location, which are not rebuilt.
The lowest figure invites underinsurance and a cut in the claim.
A round figure may not match the real cost of rebuilding.

title: Travel and accident cover
concept: Short-term risks have their own products.
Travel insurance. Travel insurance covers medical costs, trip delays, lost baggage and similar problems during a trip. For example: a traveller abroad gets treated for illness and claims the cost.
Personal accident cover. Personal accident cover pays a sum if an accident causes death or disability. For example: a policy pays a sum after a serious injury.
Cashless claim. A cashless claim is one where the insurer pays the provider directly, so you avoid paying upfront. For example: a hospital bills the insurer for approved treatment.
Reimbursement claim. A reimbursement claim is one where you pay first and send bills to the insurer for repayment. For example: a traveller pays a clinic and later files the bills.

client.quote: “Do I need travel insurance for a short trip?”
client.context: A client planning a holiday.

talk: “Medical costs abroad can be high. A small premium protects against large bills and trip problems.”

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Travel insurance”?
options: This is one where you pay first and send bills to the insurer for repayment.
This is one where the insurer pays the provider directly, so you avoid paying upfront.
This pays a sum if an accident causes death or disability.
This covers medical costs, trip delays, lost baggage and similar problems during a trip.
qs.why: Travel insurance: Travel insurance covers medical costs, trip delays, lost baggage and similar problems during a trip.

qs.prompt: A policy pays a sum after a serious injury. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is Personal accident cover. Personal accident cover pays a sum if an accident causes death or disability.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Cashless claim”?
options: This is one where the insurer pays the provider directly, so you avoid paying upfront.
This is one where you pay first and send bills to the insurer for repayment.
This covers medical costs, trip delays, lost baggage and similar problems during a trip.
This pays a sum if an accident causes death or disability.
qs.why: Cashless claim: A cashless claim is one where the insurer pays the provider directly, so you avoid paying upfront.

qs.prompt: Meena gets treated at a network hospital and the insurer pays the hospital directly. What is this?
qs.why: The insurer pays the provider directly, so she avoids paying upfront.
wrong: In reimbursement she pays first and is repaid later, which did not happen here.
A deductible is the part of a loss that she pays herself.
A renewal is continuing a policy for another term.

qs.prompt: Rohan pays a clinic abroad from his own pocket. What should he do to claim?
options: Tell the clinic to bill the insurer next year
Wait to see if the insurer calls him up
Keep the bills, and file a reimbursement claim
Throw away the bills to save some space
qs.why: He paid first, so he files a reimbursement claim with the bills.
wrong: A clinic abroad will not usually wait for an insurer a year later.
The insurer cannot pay until a claim with proof is filed.
Without bills, a reimbursement claim cannot be supported.

qs.prompt: Which cover pays a sum if an accident causes a serious disability?
qs.why: Personal accident cover pays on death or disability caused by an accident.
wrong: Home contents cover protects belongings and not a person's health.
Third-party motor cover pays for harm caused to others.
Fire cover protects property against fire and similar events.

qs.prompt: Meena's bag is lost on a trip. Which cover may help?
qs.why: Travel insurance can include lost baggage and delays, as the policy says.
wrong: Accident cover pays on death or disability, and not for lost bags.
A term plan pays only on death, so it does not help here.
Fire cover is for the home, so it does not apply to a lost bag.

title: Making a claim
concept: A claim goes smoothly when you act quickly and keep records.
Claim intimation. Claim intimation is informing the insurer about a loss promptly, within the time the policy allows. For example: a driver calls the insurer soon after an accident.
Surveyor. A surveyor is a licensed person appointed by the insurer to assess the loss. For example: a licensed person appointed by the insurer inspects the damaged vehicle.
Exclusion. An exclusion is a situation the policy does not cover. For example: a policy does not pay for damage from a listed excluded cause.

Free-look period. A free-look period is a short time after buying a policy in which you can review it and return it for a refund, subject to terms. For example: a buyer reads the policy documents and cancels within the period.

client.quote: “My claim was rejected for an exclusion.”
client.context: A client who did not read the policy.

talk: “Always read the exclusions before buying. If you think the rejection is wrong, we can raise it with the insurer and, if needed, the insurance ombudsman.”

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Claim intimation”?
options: This is a licensed person appointed by the insurer to assess the loss.
This is a situation the policy does not cover.
This is informing the insurer about a loss promptly, within the time the policy allows.
This is a short time after buying a policy in which you can review it and return it for a refund, subject to terms.
qs.why: Claim intimation: Claim intimation is informing the insurer about a loss promptly, within the time the policy allows.

qs.prompt: A licensed person appointed by the insurer inspects the damaged vehicle. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is Surveyor. A surveyor is a licensed person appointed by the insurer to assess the loss.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Exclusion”?
options: This is a short time after buying a policy in which you can review it and return it for a refund, subject to terms.
This is a situation the policy does not cover.
This is a licensed person appointed by the insurer to assess the loss.
This is informing the insurer about a loss promptly, within the time the policy allows.
qs.why: Exclusion: An exclusion is a situation the policy does not cover.

qs.prompt: Meena's vehicle is damaged in an accident. What should she do first?
options: Repair it first and tell them later
Wait for the insurer to call her
Sell the vehicle as it is
qs.why: Claim intimation within the allowed time keeps her claim valid.
wrong: Repairing first stops the insurer from assessing the damage.

qs.prompt: Who is the surveyor in a claim?
options: A licensed person the insurer appoints
A person selected by the repair shop
qs.why: A surveyor is licensed and is appointed by the insurer.
wrong: A friend has no licence or role in assessing a loss.
A repair shop's person would not be an independent assessor.
A newspaper person has no role in a claim at all.

qs.prompt: Rohan's claim is for a cause that the policy lists as an exclusion. What is likely?
options: The insurer pays double the amount
The sum insured is raised at once
The insurer may not pay for that cause
qs.why: An exclusion is a situation the policy does not cover.
wrong: Insurers do not pay extra for an excluded cause.
A claim does not raise the sum insured on any basis.
Exclusions stay in force, and are not cancelled by a claim.

qs.prompt: Meena buys a new policy and finds that the terms differ from what she was told. What can she do?
options: Do nothing, since the money is paid
Use the review window to return it
Wait until a claim and then complain
Tear up the papers and forget them
qs.why: A short review window lets her return it for a refund, under terms.
wrong: Paying does not take away her right to review it.
Waiting until a claim is too late, as the window is short.
Tearing up the papers loses the proof she needs.

title: Red flags
concept: Most scams share the same warning signs.
Guaranteed returns. Guaranteed returns is a promise of fixed high profit with no risk, which no genuine market investment can make. For example: a group promises double money in a month.
Urgency pressure. Urgency pressure is rushing you to decide now so you do not have time to check. For example: a caller says the offer ends in one hour.
Unregistered adviser. An unregistered adviser is someone giving investment advice without the registration the law requires. For example: a stranger on social media sells paid stock tips.
Too good to be true. Too good to be true describes an offer whose reward is far above what is normal for the risk. For example: a scheme promises returns far above any bank or fund.

client.quote: “A friend says this scheme pays 10 percent a month.”
client.context: A client excited by a high return.

talk: “Returns that high with no risk are a warning, not an opportunity. Let us check who is behind it before you put in any money.”

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Guaranteed returns”?
options: This is rushing you to decide now so you do not have time to check.
This is someone giving investment advice without the registration the law requires.
This is a promise of fixed high profit with no risk, which no genuine market investment can make.
This describes an offer whose reward is far above what is normal for the risk.
qs.why: Guaranteed returns: Guaranteed returns is a promise of fixed high profit with no risk, which no genuine market investment can make.

qs.prompt: A caller says the offer ends in one hour. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is Urgency pressure. Urgency pressure is rushing you to decide now so you do not have time to check.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Unregistered adviser”?
options: This is rushing you to decide now so you do not have time to check.
This is a promise of fixed high profit with no risk, which no genuine market investment can make.
This is someone giving investment advice without the registration the law requires.
This describes an offer whose reward is far above what is normal for the risk.
qs.why: Unregistered adviser: An unregistered adviser is someone giving investment advice without the registration the law requires.

qs.prompt: A caller says Meena's money will double in a month, with no risk. What does this most likely show?
options: A warning sign of a scam
A special offer for smart investors
A deal that banks cannot match yet
A government scheme with rare access
qs.why: No genuine investment can promise high profit with no risk, so this is a red flag.
wrong: Real investors check claims. A promise this large is not a mark of smartness.

qs.prompt: A message says: 'Join in the next hour or lose your place.' What should Rohan do?
options: Pay quickly to secure the place
Send the link on to his friends
Slow down, since rushing is a trick
Share his bank details to hold it
qs.why: Urgency is used so that he cannot check, so a pause is the safest step.

Forwarding spreads the risk to his friends and does nothing to verify it.

qs.prompt: A social media page sells paid stock tips. Which question matters most before paying?
options: How many followers does the page have today?
How bright and neat are the page photos?
Did a friend of a friend pay for it?
Is he registered, and can I verify it?
qs.why: Paid advice needs a registration that can be checked on the regulator's list.
wrong: Followers can be bought, so the number says little about honesty.
Photos are made to attract and say nothing about the adviser's standing.
A friend's payment is not a check, since friends can be fooled too.

qs.prompt: Meena sees screenshots of big profits in a group. What is the right view?
options: They can be faked, proving nothing
They prove that the group is registered
They show that the profit is guaranteed
qs.why: Screenshots are easy to fake, so they are no evidence at all.
wrong: A picture of a profit does not show that the scheme is real or sound.
Registration is shown on the regulator's list and not in a chat group.
No screenshot can show a guarantee, since no guarantee can be real.

title: Digital fraud
concept: Many frauds happen through your phone.
Phishing. Phishing is a fake message or link that tricks you into sharing passwords, card or bank details. For example: a text claims your account is blocked and asks you to click a link.

UPI collect fraud. UPI collect fraud is a fake request to pay that is shown as money coming to you, which you must never approve with your PIN. For example: a buyer asks you to approve a request to receive payment.
OTP sharing. OTP sharing is giving the one-time password to someone else, which lets them complete a transaction in your name. For example: a caller pretending to be a bank officer asks for the code.

Remote access app. A remote access app is a screen-sharing tool a fraudster asks you to install so they can see and control your phone. For example: a fake support agent asks you to install a tool to fix a problem.

client.quote: “A person from my bank asked for my OTP.”
client.context: A client who got a call.

talk: “No bank will ask for your OTP or PIN. Hang up and call the number on your card or the official website.”
remember: You never need a PIN to receive money.
Do not install tools on request.

options: This is a fake message or link that tricks you into sharing passwords, card or bank details.
This is a fake request to pay that is shown as money coming to you, which you must never approve with your PIN.
This is a screen-sharing tool a fraudster asks you to install so they can see and control your phone.
This is giving the one-time password to someone else, which lets them complete a transaction in your name.
qs.why: Phishing: Phishing is a fake message or link that tricks you into sharing passwords, card or bank details.

qs.prompt: A buyer asks you to approve a request to receive payment. Which idea does this show?
qs.why: This is UPI collect fraud. UPI collect fraud is a fake request to pay that is shown as money coming to you, which you must never approve with your PIN.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “OTP sharing”?
options: This is a fake message or link that tricks you into sharing passwords, card or bank details.
This is a screen-sharing tool a fraudster asks you to install so they can see and control your phone.
This is a fake request to pay that is shown as money coming to you, which you must never approve with your PIN.
This is giving the one-time password to someone else, which lets them complete a transaction in your name.

A refund from the marketplace seller
A collect fraud, where approving pays out

qs.prompt: A caller says he is from Rohan's bank and needs the OTP to stop a fraud. What should Rohan do?

Hang up, and call the bank on its printed number

Ask the caller to send the same message again
qs.why: A real bank never asks for an OTP, so hanging up and calling the printed number is safe.
wrong: The OTP lets the caller complete a payment in his name, so it must stay private.
