Repeating the message adds nothing, since the request itself is the fraud.

qs.prompt: A text says Meena's account is blocked and shows a link to 'update KYC'. What is the safest step?
options: Ignore it, and open the bank's app herself
Click the link, since it came by text message
Reply with her card number to prove who she is
Forward the text to her contacts to warn them
qs.why: A link in a text may lead to a fake page, so she should use the official app or site.
wrong: The text itself is the trick, so the link should not be opened at all.
Sharing her card number gives the fraudster what he came for.
Forwarding can spread the link and does not check whether it is real.

qs.prompt: A 'support agent' asks Rohan to install a screen-sharing app to fix a payment problem. What is the risk?
options: The app will speed up all of his payments
The bank will refund him much sooner
The agent can control his phone
The app will remove his old messages
qs.why: Such tools give a stranger full view and control, including over banking apps.
wrong: A screen-sharing tool does nothing to speed up payments.

title: Investment scams
concept: Some scams look like opportunities.
Ponzi scheme. A Ponzi scheme pays earlier investors using money from new investors, and collapses when new money stops. For example: a scheme pays high returns to early members using fresh deposits.
Pump and dump. A pump and dump is when a group hypes a stock to raise its price and then sells to those who follow. For example: a group urges members to buy a thinly traded stock before selling.
Fake trading app. A fake trading app shows made-up profits to persuade you to deposit more, but you cannot withdraw. For example: an app displays growing profit, then blocks the withdrawal.

Impersonation call. An impersonation call is a call from someone pretending to be an official who threatens you and demands money. For example: a caller claims to be an officer and demands payment to avoid arrest.

client.quote: “An officer says I must pay a fine on a video call or be arrested.”
client.context: A client who got a threatening call.

talk: “Real agencies do not demand money on a video call. Cut the call and tell us or the cyber helpline.”
remember: Officials never demand money on calls.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Ponzi scheme”?
options: This pays earlier investors using money from new investors, and collapses when new money stops.
This is a call from someone pretending to be an official who threatens you and demands money.
This shows made-up profits to persuade you to deposit more, but you cannot withdraw.
This is when a group hypes a stock to raise its price and then sells to those who follow.
qs.why: Ponzi scheme: A Ponzi scheme pays earlier investors using money from new investors, and collapses when new money stops.

qs.prompt: A group urges members to buy a thinly traded stock before selling. Which idea does this show?

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Fake trading app”?
options: This shows made-up profits to persuade you to deposit more, but you cannot withdraw.
This is a call from someone pretending to be an official who threatens you and demands money.
This is when a group hypes a stock to raise its price and then sells to those who follow.
This pays earlier investors using money from new investors, and collapses when new money stops.
qs.why: Fake trading app: A fake trading app shows made-up profits to persuade you to deposit more, but you cannot withdraw.

qs.prompt: A scheme pays old members with money from new members. What is it called?
qs.why: Paying old members from new members' money is the mark of a Ponzi scheme.
wrong: A mutual fund invests in a portfolio of securities, under strict regulation.
A fixed deposit earns interest from the bank's lending business.
A bond is a loan that the issuer repays from its own business.

qs.prompt: A group urges members to buy a little-known stock today, before 'the big jump'. What may be going on?
options: A safe tip from some honest experts
A government plan to lift the stock price
A rule that the stock must rise
A pump and dump, to sell to followers
qs.why: A group can hype a stock, push the price up and then sell to those who follow.

qs.prompt: Rohan's trading app shows growing profit, but blocks his withdrawal and asks for more money first. What is likely?
options: A way to cut his tax
qs.why: Made-up profits and blocked withdrawals are the mark of a fake app.
wrong: Real platforms process withdrawals without asking for more deposits.

A genuine bonus does not come with a demand for more money.

qs.prompt: A caller says he is an officer and demands money to avoid arrest. What should Meena do?
options: Pay quickly to avoid any trouble
Stay on the video call as he asks her
Hang up and report it as a fraud
Share her bank details to prove who she is
qs.why: No genuine officer demands payment over the phone, so she should report it.
wrong: Paying only feeds the fraud, and the demands will grow.
Staying on the line gives the fraudster more time to pressure her.
Her bank details would help the fraudster take money from her.

title: Verify before you trust
concept: A quick check beats a long regret.

Registration check. A registration check is searching the regulator’s official list to confirm that an adviser, broker or fund is registered. For example: a person looks up an adviser on the SEBI website before paying.

Call-back verification. Call-back verification is hanging up and calling the official number yourself to confirm a request. For example: a person calls the bank’s printed number after a suspicious call.

title: If it happens
concept: Speed matters. Quick action can stop money from leaving.

Cyber helpline 1930. The cyber helpline 1930 is the national number for reporting financial cyber fraud quickly, with a matching online portal for complaints. For example: a victim calls it right after a fraudulent transfer.
Block and freeze. Block and freeze means calling your bank at once to stop cards, UPI or accounts being misused. For example: a person blocks a card after sharing details.

title: Why plan
concept: Without a plan, the law decides who gets what and how fast.

Estate. An estate is everything a person owns at death, such as property, savings, investments and belongings. For example: a person’s house, accounts and shares together make up everything they leave behind.

Intestate succession. Intestate succession is how assets pass under personal law when a person dies without a valid will. For example: a man dies without a will and his heirs inherit by the rules that apply to his religion.
Legal heir. A legal heir is a person entitled by law or a will to inherit from the deceased. For example: a spouse and children are among those entitled by law to inherit.

Succession certificate. A succession certificate is a court document that confirms who can claim certain assets such as bank balances and securities of the deceased. For example: a family obtains it to claim an account when there is no will.

title: Wills
concept: A will is the main tool to state who receives what.
Will. A will is a legal declaration of how a person wants their assets to pass after death. For example: a woman writes a legal declaration naming who gets her flat and savings.
Executor. An executor is the person named in a will to carry out its instructions. For example: a trusted friend is named to manage the distribution.

Witnesses. Witnesses are people who watch the maker sign a will and sign it themselves, and the law requires at least two. For example: two adults watch the maker sign and then sign the document themselves.
Codicil. A codicil is a document that changes or adds to an existing will. For example: a person adds a new bank account to the existing document through a short supplement.

title: Nomination and joint holding
concept: Nominations help move assets, but they do not always decide ownership.

Nominee. A nominee is a person named to receive an asset on the holder’s death, but the nominee is not always its final owner, as the will or law can decide. For example: a bank pays a deposit to the person named on the account, who then holds it for the heirs as the law requires.
Joint holder. A joint holder is a person who shares an account or asset with another, and in some modes the survivor continues to hold it. For example: a couple holds a demat account jointly.
Transmission. Transmission is the process of moving assets to heirs or nominees after the holder’s death. For example: a fund house transfers units to the legal heir after documents are submitted.
Mode of holding. Mode of holding is how joint accounts are operated, such as either or survivor or anyone or survivor. For example: a couple chooses either or survivor for convenience.

title: Family structures
concept: Some families use structures to organise and pass wealth.

HUF. An HUF is a Hindu undivided family, a separate entity for tax that applies to Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh families. For example: a family earns some income through a separate tax entity with its own PAN.

Family trust. A family trust is an arrangement in which trustees hold assets for the benefit of named beneficiaries as set out in the deed. For example: parents place assets in a trust for their children.
Gift deed. A gift deed is a document that transfers an asset to another person without payment. For example: a parent gifts a flat to a child by a registered deed.

Family settlement. A family settlement is an agreement among family members that settles how property is shared and avoids disputes. For example: siblings sign an agreement on the division of an ancestral house.

title: Bond basics
concept: A bond is a loan you give to a borrower in return for interest.

Bond. A bond is a loan an investor gives to a government or company, which promises interest and the return of the principal. For example: an investor lends money to a company and receives interest and the principal back later.
Coupon. A coupon is the regular interest a bond pays, usually stated as a percentage of face value. For example: a security pays a fixed interest percentage every year.
Face value. Face value is the amount printed on a bond that is repaid at maturity. For example: a security printed at one lakh repays that amount at the end.
Maturity. Maturity is the date on which the bond’s principal is repaid. For example: a bond matures after ten years and returns the principal.

title: Yield, price and rates
concept: Bond prices move in the opposite direction to interest rates.

Yield to maturity. Yield to maturity is the annual return you earn if you buy a bond at its current price and hold it to maturity. For example: a bond bought below face value has a higher yield than its coupon.
Interest rate risk. Interest rate risk is the chance that rising rates push bond prices down. For example: prices of existing bonds fall when new bonds pay more interest.

Duration. Duration measures how sensitive a bond’s price is to changes in interest rates, where a higher figure means more sensitivity. For example: a long-term bond falls more than a short-term bond when rates rise.
Reinvestment risk. Reinvestment risk is the chance that interest received must be reinvested at lower rates. For example: a coupon is reinvested at a lower rate than before.

title: Government securities
concept: Government borrowing is a core part of the bond market.
G-Sec. A G-Sec is a government security, a bond issued by the central government with very low credit risk. For example: an investor buys a ten-year government bond.
Treasury bill. A treasury bill is a short-term government security sold at a discount and repaid at face value. For example: a buyer pays less than face value and receives the full value at the end.
State development loan. A state development loan is a bond issued by a state government to raise money. For example: a state borrows by issuing bonds through an auction.
RBI Retail Direct. RBI Retail Direct is a platform where individuals can buy government securities directly. For example: a retail investor opens an account to buy a bond.

title: Corporate bonds and credit
concept: Companies pay more than governments because they carry more risk.
Credit rating. A credit rating is an agency’s opinion of how likely a borrower is to repay on time. For example: a bond with a high rating is seen as safer than one with a low rating.
Default risk. Default risk is the chance that a borrower fails to pay interest or principal. For example: a company misses an interest payment.
Corporate bond. A corporate bond is a bond issued by a company, which usually pays more than a government bond because of added risk. For example: a firm raises money by selling bonds to investors.
Liquidity risk. Liquidity risk is the difficulty of selling an investment quickly at a fair price. For example: an investor cannot find a buyer for a little-traded bond.

title: Deposits, debentures and ladders
concept: Several fixed income choices sit next to bonds.

Fixed deposit. A fixed deposit is a bank deposit that pays fixed interest for a set period, and deposits are insured up to a limit per depositor per bank. For example: a saver places money in a one-year bank deposit.
NCD. An NCD is a non-convertible debenture, a company bond that cannot be converted into shares. For example: a finance company raises funds by selling debt that cannot be turned into shares.
Floating rate bond. A floating rate bond is a bond whose interest resets with a benchmark rate. For example: a bond’s coupon rises when the benchmark rate rises.
Bond laddering. Bond laddering is buying bonds with different maturities so that money comes back at regular intervals. For example: an investor holds bonds maturing in one, three and five years.

title: IPO basics
concept: An IPO is the first time a company sells shares to the public.

IPO. An IPO, or initial public offering, is when a company sells its shares to the public for the first time and gets listed on an exchange. For example: a growing company raises money and lists on the stock exchange.
Primary market. The primary market is where new shares are issued and sold by the company, as in an IPO. For example: an investor buys shares directly from the issuer during the offer.

Secondary market. The secondary market is the exchange where existing shares are bought and sold among investors after listing. For example: an investor sells her shares on the exchange to another investor.
Offer document. An offer document is the prospectus that describes the company, its business, risks and use of funds. For example: an investor reads the risk section before applying.

title: Price and application
concept: The price comes from a band and bids, and the application uses your bank account.
Price band. A price band is the range in which investors can bid for shares in the IPO. For example: the issue states a lower and an upper price for bids.
Book building. Book building is the process of collecting bids within the price band to discover the final issue price. For example: demand from bidders helps set the final price.

Cut-off price. Cut-off price is an option where a retail investor agrees to buy at whatever final price is set within the band. For example: an investor chooses cut-off so the bid is valid at the final price.
ASBA with UPI. ASBA with UPI is a way to apply where the amount is blocked in your bank account and debited only if shares are allotted. For example: an applicant approves a mandate in a UPI app.

Oversubscription. Oversubscription is when investors bid for more shares than are on offer. For example: an issue is subscribed many times its size.
Allotment. Allotment is the process of giving shares to applicants, which can be by lottery for retail investors when the issue is oversubscribed. For example: only some applicants receive shares.
Listing gain. A listing gain is the difference between the listing price and the issue price, which can also be a loss. For example: shares list above the issue price on the first day.

Investor categories. Investor categories are the groups in an IPO, such as retail, non-institutional and qualified institutional buyers, each with a share of the issue. For example: retail applicants bid within the retail limit.

title: Judging an IPO
concept: A few checks beat the headlines.
Fresh issue. A fresh issue is when the company issues new shares and the money goes to the company. For example: a company sells new shares to fund expansion.
Offer for sale. An offer for sale is when existing shareholders sell their shares and the money goes to them, not the company. For example: an early investor sells part of the holding in the IPO.
Use of proceeds. Use of proceeds is the stated plan for how the company will spend the money it raises. For example: the offer document says funds will repay debt and build a plant.
Valuation. Valuation is the price of the company compared with its earnings, assets or similar companies. For example: an investor compares the price with listed peers before applying.

title: The balance sheet
concept: It is a photograph of what a company owns and owes on one day.

Assets. Assets are the things a company owns or is owed that have value, such as cash, stock, plants and customer dues. For example: a retailer's shops, inventory and bank balance sit on one side of its balance sheet.
Liabilities. Liabilities are the amounts a company owes to others, such as loans, supplier bills and taxes due. For example: a firm has a bank loan and unpaid bills to its suppliers.

title: Value versus price
concept: Price is what the market asks today. Value is what the business may be worth.

Intrinsic value. Intrinsic value is the estimated worth of a business based on the cash it can generate in future. For example: an analyst estimates a company is worth ₹800 a share even though it trades at ₹650.
Market price. Market price is the price at which a share trades on the exchange right now. For example: a share changes hands at ₹650 this morning.

Time value of money. Time value of money is the idea that a rupee today is worth more than a rupee received later. For example: receiving ₹100 now is preferred to receiving ₹100 after five years.

title: Discounted cash flow

Discount rate. Discount rate is the yearly return used to convert future cash into today's value, reflecting risk. For example: a riskier business is valued using 13% a year instead of 10%.

concept: Multiples compare a price with earnings, sales or assets.
Price to earnings. Price to earnings is the share price divided by earnings per share. For example: a share priced at ₹300 earns ₹15 a year, so buyers pay 20 times its yearly profit.

title: What a mutual fund is
concept: A mutual fund collects money from many people and invests it together, so each person owns a small share of a larger, spread-out portfolio.

Mutual fund. A mutual fund is a pool of money collected from many investors and invested by a professional in shares, bonds or other assets. For example: five hundred colleagues each put in ₹5,000, and one manager invests the combined ₹25 lakh on their behalf.

Unit. A unit is your share of the fund. You buy it with your money, and how many you own shows how much of the pool is yours. For example: putting in ₹10,000 when one share of the pool costs ₹20 gives you 500 slices of the pool.

NAV. NAV is the price of one unit. It is the fund's total value, after costs, divided by the number of units, and it is worked out every business day. For example: a pool worth ₹200 crore with 10 crore units is priced at ₹20 per unit at the end of the day.

Fund house. A fund house, or AMC, is the company that runs the fund, employs the manager and handles the paperwork, under rules set by SEBI. For example: a company with licensed managers and analysts runs dozens of funds and reports to the market regulator.

SEBI. SEBI is the market regulator. It sets rules on how funds invest, what they disclose and how they treat investors, and the fund's assets are kept separate from the fund house's own money. For example: if the company that runs a fund ran into trouble, the money in the pool would still belong to the unit holders.

talk: “No. Your money buys units of a pool, and the pool's assets are kept separate and overseen by a trustee under SEBI rules. The fund house manages the pool but does not own it.”

title: The kinds of funds
concept: Funds differ by what they hold. That decides how much they can grow and how much they can fall.

Equity fund. An equity fund invests mainly in company shares. It has the highest growth potential and the biggest ups and downs, so it suits goals at least five years away. For example: a fund holding shares of many large companies can rise sharply in a good year and fall in a bad one.

Debt fund. A debt fund lends money by buying bonds and similar instruments. It is usually steadier than an equity fund but is not free of risk. For example: a fund that mostly holds government and company bonds earns interest and moves less than a shares fund.

Hybrid fund. A hybrid fund mixes shares and bonds in one fund, so the manager balances growth and stability for you. For example: a fund keeping about two thirds in shares and the rest in bonds falls less in a bad year than an all-shares fund.

Index fund. An index fund simply copies a market index such as the Nifty 50, holding the same companies in the same proportion. It has no manager picking stocks and usually charges less. For example: a fund that holds the fifty biggest companies in fixed weights moves almost exactly like that list of companies.

ELSS. An ELSS is an equity fund with a three-year lock-in, and under the old tax regime up to ₹1.5 lakh a year invested qualifies for a deduction. For example: a salaried person puts money in a share-based fund that cannot be withdrawn for three years and claims a tax deduction.

title: Risk, return and time
concept: Higher possible growth always comes with a bigger chance of loss. Time and spreading money around are how investors manage that.

Risk. Risk is the chance that your investment ends up worth less than you hoped, or less than you put in, at the time you need it. For example: a person needing money in one year finds the fund down 10% just when the bills arrive.

Riskometer. The riskometer is the label every fund must show, from Low to Very High, telling you how risky the fund's holdings are. For example: a fund holding mostly small company shares carries the top label, while one holding short bonds carries a low one.

Time horizon. Time horizon is how long you can leave the money invested before you need it. The longer it is, the more time prices have to recover from falls. For example: money for a house in two years and money for retirement in twenty years should not sit in the same kind of fund.

Diversification. Diversification means spreading money across many holdings so that one bad company or sector cannot hurt you badly. For example: owning slices of hundreds of businesses means one company's failure barely moves your total.

Volatility. Volatility is how much a price swings up and down. It is the bumpy ride, and it is normal for equity funds even when they do well over the long run. For example: a fund that gains 30% one year and loses 12% the next is bumpy, even if the ten-year result is good.

title: What a fund costs you
concept: Every fund charges a small yearly fee. The amount looks tiny, but over twenty years it can change your final sum by lakhs.

Expense ratio. The expense ratio is the yearly fee, shown as a percentage of your money, that pays for running the fund. It is taken from the fund's value, so you never see a bill. For example: a fund that charges 1.5% a year keeps ₹1,500 from every ₹1 lakh each year before you see any return.

Direct plan. A Direct plan is bought straight from the fund house, with no distributor in between, so it has a lower expense ratio than the Regular plan of the same fund. For example: buying through the fund house's own website gives the same portfolio at a smaller yearly charge.

Regular plan. A Regular plan is bought through a distributor or adviser, whose service is paid out of a higher expense ratio. For example: buying through an agent who helps you choose and review costs a bit more each year inside the fund.

Exit load. An exit load is a fee charged if you sell units within a set period, often a year, to discourage quick selling. For example: selling after eight months attracts a 1% charge, while selling after thirteen months does not.

Growth option. In a Growth option, profits stay in the fund and increase the unit price, instead of being paid out, so they keep compounding. For example: choosing this means no payouts arrive and the unit price simply rises over time as gains build.

title: How to start safely
concept: Starting takes a few steps: a one-time KYC, a choice of fund, a way to pay, and a habit you can keep.

KYC. KYC is a one-time identity check with your PAN and address proof that you must complete before investing in any fund. For example: a new investor completes an online identity check using a PAN and Aadhaar-linked verification before buying her first fund.

Folio. A folio is your account number with a fund house. It records every unit you hold and every purchase and sale. For example: all of one investor's units with a fund house are tracked under a single number.

SIP. An SIP, or systematic investment plan, moves a fixed amount from your bank into a fund on a set date every month, which makes investing a habit. For example: ₹5,000 leaves the account on the 5th of every month and buys units automatically.
Lump sum. A lump sum is putting in a larger amount all at once, instead of in monthly instalments. For example: a bonus of ₹2 lakh is invested in one go on a single day.

Nominee. A nominee is the person you name to receive your units if you die, which saves your family time and paperwork. For example: a father names his daughter, so she can claim his investments without a long legal process.

talk: “Use a monthly SIP for your salary so it becomes a habit. For the bonus, decide the goal first, then invest it in a fund that suits that goal's time frame. Always add a nominee.”

The SIP is certain to make a profit because it collects extra units
qs.why: A fixed amount means lower prices buy more units and higher prices buy fewer.
wrong: The extra units are bought with the same money at a lower price, not given by anyone.

qs.prompt: A father wants his daughter to be able to claim his investments quickly if something happens to him. What should he have done?

Invest only in her name, whatever his own goals may be

Nothing, because units are always claimed by the fund house

wrong: A note with passwords is risky and does not give a legal route to claim the units.

title: Lending your money
concept: A bond is a loan you give to a government or a company. In return, you are promised regular interest and your money back on a set date.
Principal. Principal is the original amount you lend, which you get back when the loan ends. For example: you lend ₹1 lakh and, on the final day, the borrower returns that ₹1 lakh.

Interest. Interest is the payment the borrower makes for using your money, usually stated as a percentage of the principal each year. For example: lending ₹1 lakh at 7% a year earns you ₹7,000 for every year the loan runs.

Bond. A bond is a tradable loan certificate issued by a government or company, which promises interest and repayment on fixed dates. For example: a company raises ₹500 crore by issuing certificates to many lenders, each promising yearly payments and a final return of money.
Coupon. The coupon is the fixed interest rate a bond pays, set when the bond is issued. For example: a bond printed with 8% pays ₹8 each year for every ₹100 of its face value.
Maturity. Maturity is the date on which the bond ends and the borrower returns the principal. For example: a bond issued in 2026 with a ten-year life repays the principal in 2036.

client.quote: “Is a bond the same as a fixed deposit?”
client.context: A saver comparing the two.

talk: “They are close cousins. Both are loans, with interest and a return of money at the end. A bond can be sold to someone else before it ends, and the borrower can be a company or a government, not only a bank.”
remember: A bond is a loan you give.
The borrower pays interest and returns the principal at maturity.
The coupon is the fixed interest rate.

options: This is the fixed interest rate a bond pays, set when the bond is issued.
This is a tradable loan certificate issued by a government or company, which promises interest and repayment on fixed dates.

A rate that changes every year to follow the bank's savings rate
The total return across the whole life of the bond to maturity

wrong: The coupon is set on the face value, not on the price a later buyer pays in the market.

wrong: A bond is a loan, not ownership. Lenders get interest, not a share of profits.

qs.prompt: On the maturity date of a 10-year bond, what should the borrower do?
options: Start paying double interest to reward holders who waited for ten years
Offer new units at a lower price to the people who lent earlier
Return the principal, along with the final interest payment that is due
Cancel the bond and keep the principal as a fee for the loan

Keeping the principal would be a default. A borrower must repay it on the maturity date.

title: Who borrows, and how safe
concept: The safety of a bond depends on who is borrowing and how likely they are to pay you back on time.

Government security. A government security, or G-Sec, is a bond issued by the Government of India. It carries the lowest default risk among rupee bonds because the government can raise money and pay. For example: lending to the central government is treated as the safest rupee loan available.

Corporate bond. A corporate bond is issued by a company. It usually pays a higher interest rate than a government bond because the company is more likely to fail to pay. For example: a company offers 9% while the government offers 7%, and the extra 2% is the reward for taking more risk.

Credit rating. A credit rating is a grade given by a rating agency that shows how likely a borrower is to repay. Higher grades mean safer borrowers. For example: a borrower graded at the top of the scale is considered very likely to repay, while a low grade signals real doubt.
Default. A default happens when a borrower fails to pay interest or return the principal on time. For example: a company misses a scheduled payment and its lenders have to wait or accept a loss.

Credit risk. Credit risk is the chance that the borrower will not pay you back in full and on time. For example: lending to a weak company at a very high rate means a bigger chance of not being repaid.

client.quote: “This company bond pays 11%. Why would I take 7% from the government?”
client.context: A saver tempted by a high rate.

talk: “A high rate is often the price of a higher chance of not getting paid. Look at the credit rating and ask what could go wrong before you chase the rate.”
remember: Government bonds carry the lowest default risk.
A higher rate usually means higher credit risk.
Credit ratings help but are not guarantees.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Government security”?
options: This is a grade given by a rating agency that shows how likely a borrower is to repay. Higher grades mean safer borrowers.
This happens when a borrower fails to pay interest or return the principal on time.

This is a bond issued by the Government of India. It carries the lowest default risk among rupee bonds because the government can raise money and pay.
qs.why: Government security: A government security, or G-Sec, is a bond issued by the Government of India. It carries the lowest default risk among rupee bonds because the government can raise money and pay.

qs.prompt: Which statement best describes “Credit rating”?
options: This happens when a borrower fails to pay interest or return the principal on time.
This is a grade given by a rating agency that shows how likely a borrower is to repay. Higher grades mean safer borrowers.
This is a bond issued by the Government of India. It carries the lowest default risk among rupee bonds because the government can raise money and pay.
This is issued by a company. It usually pays a higher interest rate than a government bond because the company is more likely to fail to pay.
qs.why: Credit rating: A credit rating is a grade given by a rating agency that shows how likely a borrower is to repay. Higher grades mean safer borrowers.

qs.prompt: A company bond pays 11% while a government bond pays 7%. What does the extra 4% most likely signal?

Government rates are low because default risk is low, not because of any hidden losses.
Rates are not random. They reflect the borrower's risk, the term and market conditions.

options: The agency sees low default risk, but it is an opinion, not a guarantee

wrong: Deposit insurance applies to bank deposits. It does not cover bonds, whatever their rating.

qs.prompt: A company misses its scheduled interest payment on a bond. What has happened, and what does it mean for lenders?

A maturity, so lenders receive their principal back early

A default, so lenders may have to wait longer or accept a loss
qs.why: Missing a due payment is a default, and lenders may be paid late, partly, or not at all.
wrong: A missed payment is not routine. Bond terms set fixed dates, and missing one is a serious event.

qs.prompt: For the same time period, which borrower's bond would normally pay the lowest interest rate?
options: A new company with no track record, because it is easiest to start
The Government of India, since it carries the lowest default risk
A mid-sized company with a good rating, since it is well known
A bank's subsidiary that has just been formed this year
qs.why: Lending to the government is treated as the safest rupee loan, so it pays the least extra.
wrong: A new company is riskier, so it must pay more to attract lenders, not less.
A good rating still carries more risk than the government, so the rate would be higher.
A newly formed firm has no history to judge, so lenders would expect a higher rate.

title: Why bond prices move
concept: A bond can be sold before it matures, and its price changes when market interest rates change. That is the main risk in bond funds.

Yield. Yield is the return you actually earn on a bond, given the price you paid and the interest it pays, shown as a yearly percentage. For example: buying a bond below its face value makes the yearly earning on your money higher than its printed interest rate.

Interest rate risk. Interest rate risk is the chance that a bond's price falls because market interest rates have gone up. For example: when new bonds start paying more, an older bond paying less becomes less attractive and sells for a lower price.

Duration. Duration shows how sensitive a bond or bond fund is to a change in interest rates. A longer duration means bigger price swings. For example: a fund holding bonds that end in twenty years moves much more than one holding bonds that end in one year.
Inflation. Inflation is the yearly rise in prices, which reduces what each rupee can buy. For example: if prices rise 6% a year, ₹100 buys what only ₹94 bought a year ago.

Real return. Real return is what your interest earns after taking away inflation, so it shows the growth in what you can actually buy. For example: earning 7% when prices rise 5% leaves you only about 2% better off in buying power.

client.quote: “My bond fund fell even though nothing defaulted. How?”
client.context: An investor puzzled by a fall.

talk: “When market interest rates rise, existing bonds lose value because new bonds pay more. The fall is on paper and fades as the bonds move closer to their end dates, but longer-duration funds feel it more.”
remember: Bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions.
Look at the return after inflation.

options: This is the chance that a bond's price falls because market interest rates have gone up.
This shows how sensitive a bond or bond fund is to a change in interest rates. A longer this means bigger price swings.
This is the yearly rise in prices, which reduces what each rupee can buy.
This is the return you actually earn on a bond, given the price you paid and the interest it pays, shown as a yearly percentage.
qs.why: Yield: Yield is the return you actually earn on a bond, given the price you paid and the interest it pays, shown as a yearly percentage.

qs.why: This is Interest rate risk. Interest rate risk is the chance that a bond's price falls because market interest rates have gone up.

options: This is the yearly rise in prices, which reduces what each rupee can buy.
This shows how sensitive a bond or bond fund is to a change in interest rates. A longer this means bigger price swings.
This is the return you actually earn on a bond, given the price you paid and the interest it pays, shown as a yearly percentage.
This is the chance that a bond's price falls because market interest rates have gone up.
qs.why: Duration: Duration shows how sensitive a bond or bond fund is to a change in interest rates. A longer duration means bigger price swings.

qs.prompt: Market interest rates rise. What usually happens to the price of a bond you already hold?

It stays the same, since a bond's price is fixed once it is issued
It doubles, since the coupon is automatically raised to match the rise
It falls, because new bonds pay more and yours becomes less attractive
qs.why: New bonds pay higher rates, so buyers pay less for your lower-rate bond, and its price falls.
wrong: Rising rates do the opposite. Older, lower-rate bonds are worth less when new ones pay more.

A coupon never changes once set. Nothing about a rate rise adjusts it upward.

qs.prompt: Rates rise by 1%. Fund A holds bonds ending in one year, and Fund B holds bonds ending in twenty years. What is likely?
options: Both fall by the same amount, since the rate rise is the same for each
Fund B falls more, since longer duration means bigger price swings
Fund A falls more, because short bonds are the most exposed to rates
Neither falls, since bond funds are protected from rate changes
qs.why: Longer-dated bonds are more sensitive, so Fund B swings by more than Fund A.
wrong: The same rate change hits bonds differently depending on how long they run.
Short bonds are the least sensitive, since they end soon and can be reinvested at new rates.
Bond funds are not protected. Rising rates can lower their value, as in this example.

qs.prompt: A deposit pays 7% a year while prices rise 6% a year. What is the real return, roughly?
options: About 13%, since interest and inflation are added together
About 7%, because inflation affects only the cost of goods
About 1%, so buying power grows only slightly
About 6%, because inflation is the main part of the earnings
qs.why: Seven percent minus six percent leaves about one percent of real growth in buying power.
wrong: Inflation reduces what money buys. It is taken away from the return, not added to it.
Inflation does reduce what your interest can buy, so the real gain is lower than 7%.
Inflation is not part of the earnings. It is the loss in buying power that you must subtract.

qs.prompt: A ₹100 bond with an 8% coupon is bought for ₹95. How does the yield compare with 8%?
options: Higher, since ₹8 a year and a ₹100 repayment on ₹95 earns more
Lower, because paying less than face value reduces the earnings
Exactly 8%, since the coupon always equals the yield
Zero, since a bond bought below face value pays no interest
qs.why: You pay ₹95 and receive ₹8 a year plus ₹100 at the end, so you earn more than 8% on your money.
wrong: Paying less than face value for the same payments raises the return, not lowers it.
Yield equals the coupon only when the price equals the face value. Here it does not.
A bond pays its coupon whatever price the buyer paid. The interest does not disappear.

title: Deposit, bond or debt fund
concept: There are several ways to lend money. Each trades safety, flexibility and tax in a different way.

Fixed deposit. A fixed deposit is money lent to a bank for a fixed time at a fixed rate. Deposits in a bank are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank. For example: a saver locks ₹3 lakh for two years at a set rate and knows exactly what she will get on the last day.

Debt mutual fund. A debt mutual fund pools many people's money to buy a mix of bonds. Its value moves daily, so it has no fixed return and no deposit insurance. For example: an investor holds units of a fund that owns dozens of bonds, and the unit price drifts up and down.

Liquidity. Liquidity is how quickly you can turn an investment into cash without losing value. For example: money in a savings account can be withdrawn today, while money in a long deposit may cost you a penalty to take out early.

Taxable interest. Interest from a deposit or bond is added to your income and taxed at your slab rate each year. For example: someone in the 30% slab keeps about 70% of every rupee of interest after tax.

Emergency money. Emergency money is a cushion for sudden needs, which should sit in safe, easy-to-reach places, not in long or risky investments. For example: six months of expenses are kept in a savings account or a very short-term fund, not in a long-term bond.

client.quote: “Should I put my emergency money in a debt fund for the better return?”
client.context: A saver stretching for yield.

talk: “Emergency money needs to be there at full value the moment you need it. Keep it in a savings account or a very short-term option, and use debt funds for money you will not need for a few years.”
remember: Deposits have a fixed rate and bank insurance up to a limit.
Debt funds can fall in value and carry no insurance.
Keep emergency money simple and easy to reach.

options: This is money lent to a bank for a fixed time at a fixed rate. Deposits in a bank are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.
This is how quickly you can turn an investment into cash without losing value.
Interest from a deposit or bond is added to your income and taxed at your slab rate each year.
This pools many people's money to buy a mix of bonds. Its value moves daily, so it has no fixed return and no deposit insurance.

This is how quickly you can turn an investment into cash without losing value.
This is money lent to a bank for a fixed time at a fixed rate. Deposits in a bank are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.
Interest from a deposit or bond is added to your income and taxed at your slab rate each year.
qs.why: Liquidity: Liquidity is how quickly you can turn an investment into cash without losing value.

qs.prompt: Meena keeps ₹8 lakh in a single bank, in one deposit. The bank fails. How much is covered by deposit insurance?
options: The full ₹8 lakh, since all deposits are covered without any limit
Up to ₹5 lakh, so spreading deposits across banks can protect more
Nothing, since deposit insurance covers savings accounts only
Up to ₹10 lakh, since the limit applies to each separate deposit
qs.why: The limit is ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, so spreading across banks raises the covered total.
wrong: The cover has a limit. It does not protect the full amount if a depositor holds more.
The cover applies to deposits of all kinds, including fixed deposits, up to the limit.
The limit is per depositor per bank, not per deposit, so extra deposits in the same bank do not add cover.

qs.prompt: Rohan holds a debt fund and sees its value dip 2% in a month. What is the right reading?
options: A mistake by the bank, which must refund the loss to every investor
A sign that deposit insurance has been withdrawn from the fund
Proof that the fund has defaulted, so he must sell at once
Normal for a debt fund, since its value moves with the bonds it holds
qs.why: Fund values move daily with bond prices, so a small dip is part of how it works.
wrong: A debt fund is not a bank deposit, and no one refunds ordinary price moves.
Debt funds never had deposit insurance, so nothing was withdrawn.
A small dip is usually a price move, not a default. A default would be a separate event.

qs.prompt: Meena earns ₹10,000 interest on a deposit and is in the 30% tax slab. What is the effect?
options: She keeps about ₹7,000, since interest is added to income and taxed
She keeps the full ₹10,000, since deposit interest is outside tax
She keeps ₹3,000, since the tax is charged on her principal instead
She keeps ₹10,000 this year and pays the tax in the next
qs.why: Interest is added to income and taxed at the slab, so 30% tax leaves about ₹7,000.
wrong: Interest is taxable income, so it does not go untaxed, whatever the slab.
Tax applies to the interest earned, not to the principal she deposited.
Interest is taxed in the year it is earned, so waiting a year does not change the position.

qs.prompt: Rohan wants his emergency money to earn a little more. Which choice is the best?
options: Put it in a long-term bond fund, since it pays more than a deposit
Lock it in a five-year deposit, for the highest rate available
Keep it in a savings account or very short-term option, easy to reach
Invest it in a company bond with the top interest rate in the market
qs.why: Emergency money must be there at full value on short notice, so simple and quick wins.
wrong: A long-term fund can fall just when he needs the money, which defeats the purpose.
A long lock-in makes the money hard to reach, and exit usually brings a penalty.
A top rate usually means higher risk, which is wrong for money that must be there for sure.

title: Choosing with a goal
concept: Match the tool to the goal. How soon you need the money, and how much worry you can handle, point to the right choice.

Goal matching. Goal matching means choosing an investment based on when you need the money and how much fall you can accept, not on the highest advertised rate. For example: money for a wedding in two years goes into something steady, while money for retirement in twenty can take more risk.

Laddering. Laddering means splitting money across deposits or bonds that end at different dates, so some money becomes free every year. For example: four equal deposits ending in one, two, three and four years give you cash each year and let you renew at current rates.

Issuer spread. Issuer spread means not putting all your lending with one borrower, so one default cannot hurt you badly. For example: lending across several banks and companies means one failure costs you a small part, not everything.

Quality check. A quality check means reading the credit rating and what a bond fund actually holds before you invest. For example: before buying a fund, an investor reads the list of its holdings and sees mostly top-rated borrowers.

Short-term fund. A short-term fund holds bonds that end soon, so it reacts less to interest rate changes and is steadier than a long-term bond fund. For example: a fund holding bonds that end within a year or two swings far less than one holding twenty-year bonds.

client.quote: “I have ₹10 lakh to keep safely for five years. What should I do?”
client.context: A cautious saver with a medium time frame.

talk: “Split it across a few places, such as deposits at different banks, a ladder of end dates, and a high-quality debt fund, and check what each holds. That spreads both bank risk and interest rate risk.”
remember: Match the tool to the goal and the time you have.
Read the rating and the holdings first.

This means choosing an investment based on when you need the money and how much fall you can accept, not on the highest advertised rate.
This means splitting money across deposits or bonds that end at different dates, so some money becomes free every year.

Choose a very long bond fund, since it pays the most each year

qs.prompt: Dadi puts ₹10 lakh into four deposits ending in 1, 2, 3 and 4 years. What is the main benefit of this ladder?
options: Some money comes due every year, giving cash access and a chance to renew
It raises the interest rate on every deposit above the going rate
It removes any chance of losing money at the bank, even above the limit
It makes all the interest on these deposits tax-exempt in each year
qs.why: Each year a part ends, so cash is near, and it can be renewed at the then-current rate.
wrong: A ladder does not raise the rate. Each deposit earns the rate that applied when it was made.
A ladder spreads end dates. It does not remove bank risk, so the insurance limit still matters.
Interest remains taxable whatever the ladder, so no tax saving comes from the structure.

qs.prompt: Meena lends ₹6 lakh, all of it to one company through a single bond. What is the main weakness?
options: The interest will be lower, since big loans always pay less
The bond cannot be repaid, since it is larger than the usual size
There is no weakness, because a single rated bond is as safe as any
One failure could cost her much of the money, so spreading is wiser
qs.why: With everything lent to one borrower, a default hits the whole sum, and spreading limits the damage.
wrong: Loan size does not set the rate. The borrower's risk and the term mostly do.
Bonds of this size are routinely repaid. The size is not the weakness here.
A rating lowers risk but cannot remove it, so concentration is still a weakness.

qs.prompt: Before buying a debt fund, Rohan reads its list of holdings. What is he checking?
options: Whether the fund's name is easy to remember when he talks about it later
Which borrowers it lends to, and whether the credit quality is high
How many people work at the fund house, since more staff means less risk
